An unimaginable idea: When does God ignore idolatry by Jews?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
22:35:47 UTC
07:35:47 KST

It is on very rare occasions that I encounter an idea that absolutely startles me.
This week, while studying the Ohr HaChaim by Rabbi Hayyim ben Moshe ibn Attar (1696-1743) on Parashat Ha’azinu with a hevruta, I encountered such an idea.
In the verse “The Lord alone did guide him, no alien god at His side” (Deuteronomy 32:12; JPS translation), R. Hayyim introduces a midrash (Bereshit Rabbah 38:6):
“Rebbi says: Peace is great, as even if Israel engages in idol worship but there is peace among them, the Omnipresent says, ‘it is, as it were, that I have no power over them since there is peace among them,’ as it is stated: ‘Ephraim is attached to idols, leave him’ (Hosea 4:17).
'Their heart has separated, now they will be punished'
“But once there was divisiveness between them, what does it say? ‘Their heart has separated, now they will be punished’ (Hosea 10:2). You thus learn: Peace is great, and dispute is despised.”
Rabbi Hayyim incorporates this idea in the verse of Ha’azinu, offering a novel translation: “When the nation is unified, God will grant it (the nation) remission; (when the nation is unified) then God does not focus even on idolatry in their midst.”
Is this not extraordinary? All the prophets – from Moses through Malachi – rail against the sin of idolatry. It is one of the three cardinal sins for which the halacha calls upon a person to surrender his life rather than submit to idolatrous practice.
God will even overlook its idolatrous conduct if the Jews are united
And yet, this midrash says that if the Jewish nation is united, God will even overlook its idolatrous conduct!
The Jewish people give serious thought to a host of issues – all of which are important: Judicial reform vs non-Judicial reform; two-state solution vs only one; settlement of Judea and Samaria vs no settlement; sovereignty over the greater Israel or not; exemptions from the draft for Torah study or no exemption; updating the doctrine of purity of arms or not.
These are all issues over which very rational people can feel passionately and argue persuasively.
Yet Rabbi Hayyim urges us to remain a unified nation; a people that does not block highways or burn tires, engage in vandalism against those with whom we may differ, or delegitimize other Jews with whom we differ.
Our challenge is to follow in God’s path – just as He is one, so must we, the Jewish people, remain one. In an ideal world, the Jewish people would be unified in embracing the covenant between God and Israel.
But now we may have to aspire to unity for the sake of our survival in a very hostile world.■
The writer is founding principal (retired) of The Frisch School in Paramus, New Jersey.

Music icon John Farnham to miss tribute concert in his honour due to poor health
In short:
John Farnham will miss a tribute concert dedicated to his career due to poor health, the singer's family has confirmed.
The Australian music icon has been in poor health for several years and his family confirmed he required 24-hour medical care at home.
Some of the biggest names in Australian music, including Jimmy Barnes, Tina Arena, Human Nature, Jessica Mauboy, Kate Ceberano and Ross Wilson, are performing at the charity concert.
Australian music legend John Farnham will miss a tribute concert dedicated to his career due to poor health, the singer's family has confirmed ahead of the Melbourne event.
The concert, dubbed The Songs of John Farnham: A Living Legend, will be held at Rod Laver Arena this evening, with funds raised on the night going towards the cancer service that supported Farnham during his cancer battle.
In a statement posted on social media, Farnham's wife, Jill, and sons, Robert and James, wrote that the singer was "deeply moved" by the musical tribute but would be too unwell to attend the arena spectacular.
His family confirmed the 77-year-old You're the Voice singer required continuous oxygen support and was receiving 24-hour nursing care.
"Many people have been asking whether John will be involved in the concert or attending tomorrow night to watch it all happen," the Farnham family statement said.
"Unfortunately, he will not be able to attend and, as a family, we feel it is important to provide an update on John's health to help explain why.
"John's health has deteriorated in recent months. He now requires continuous oxygen support and uses a wheelchair for mobility.
"It has also become necessary for John to receive 24-hour nursing care at home, ensuring trained support is always available when he needs it."
Some of the biggest names in Australian entertainment are scheduled to take centre stage at the Farnham tribute tonight, including Jimmy Barnes, Tina Arena, Human Nature, Jessica Mauboy, Kate Ceberano and Ross Wilson.
International stars, including Canadian singer Celine Dion and American crooner Richard Marx, are also taking part in the event, which will raise funds for Head and Neck Cancer Australia.
"We have kept these matters private while our family has adjusted to John's changing needs. However, we now feel it is important that John's fans and supporters understand his circumstances and why he cannot be there this weekend," the Farnham family said.
"If things were different, John would have loved nothing more than to attend the concert. He would undoubtedly have been a little overwhelmed by all the fuss, but he would also have wanted to thank everyone involved in person.
"As a family, we have decided that it is best for John to remain at home, where he can be safe and comfortable."
Australian pop band Human Nature, who featured in John Farnham's song Every Time You Cry, said they "can't wait" to celebrate the 77-year-old's career at tonight's concert.
"This weekend, we celebrate the extraordinary music and legacy of the one and only John Farnham — a true living legend and a hero to us all," the band said in a social media post.
"It's impossible not to feel emotional, and incredibly humbled, to have played even a small part in John's remarkable career.
"John, we love you. Thank you for welcoming us into your world."
The original yellow Wiggle, Greg Page, said in a social media post: "All our love and understanding is being sent to John and his family".
Farnham is one of Australia's most successful performers, with his 1986 album, Whispering Jack, selling more than 1.6 million copies.
The British-born singer was named 1987 Australian of the Year by then-prime minister Bob Hawke, and has won more than 20 ARIA awards.
In 2024 Farnham released an autobiography, The Voice Inside, which details the monumental triumphs of his career as well as the immense struggles he has faced.

In particular, deceased civilians are declared to have been "Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel" or to have "died of illnesses." The report's authors also cynically claim that Ukrainian soldiers deliberately killed elderly people in the Kyiv region in order to later blame russia for it
They emphasize that the occupiers are disguising the fake report as a "legal document" containing "irrefutable evidence" in order to give it weight in the information space. At the same time, russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson maria zakharova has already stated that they intend to use this pseudo-investigation at the UN General Assembly as an official position.
"Such measures are part of the Kremlin's systematic strategy. In an attempt to blur the evidentially confirmed mass killings of civilians, russia is creating a parallel information reality to justify its own war crimes before a foreign audience," the CCD concludes.

An American perspective: Why Yom Kippur still brings Jews together, even without belief - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
22:17:06 UTC
07:17:06 KST

In rabbinic usage, Yom Kippur is sometimes simply called Hayom – the Day. It’s a way of setting it apart from every other day – even Shabbat, which is itself set apart from every day except Yom Kippur.
But what is the purpose of ranking time this way? Isn’t all time, in fact, the same, and isn’t it only we humans, with our imagination, who invent these distinctions?
And yet, we make these distinctions all the time. And we make them because they are important. We believe in the distinctions. We know, for example, that time spent with our children and grandchildren has a higher value than time scrolling through social media with our minds seized by, say, images of famous people, expensive cars, or arguments that grow violent.
We know that some times are categorically superior to others: a brit milah, a baby naming, a loved one’s wedding, a birth, or the ceremony at the conclusion of life.
It’s in these instances that we see how time can contain life in its fullness, or conversely, in its shallowness. We are made viscerally aware of the value of time, of a moment, of a day. And so it is with Yom Kippur, the Day.
The power of Yom Kippur to create belonging
When I grew up in Minnesota in the 60s and 70s, many and perhaps most Jews I knew went to synagogue just two days a year, on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur.
Some saw this as troubling. You might have heard that “Ed Shapiro, that nebuch, only goes to shul twice a year!” The thing about this imagined Shapiro wasn’t that he only went to synagogue twice a year; it was that he went at all.
Think about that with an open mind.
After some 3,300 years, almost 2,000 of them in exile, Shapiro, a Jew, a regular person, not a rabbinical scholar or a saint, living an otherwise completely secular life, feels compelled to leave the comfort of his armchair, the luxury of his big-screen TV with its televised golf game, to go to a place where they chanted in an ancient language, one that he did not understand.
It’s there he will go to pray to a God Shapiro doesn’t believe in. And yet there’s Ed, sitting when it’s time to sit, standing when it’s time to stand. Sweating and yawning.
Schuckling and looking at his watch.
This, all this, is the essence of The Day. A purely trans-intellectual takeover of the body and mind by an alien – and yet, somehow, totally familiar – feeling that he, our fictional Ed Shapiro, is a Jew and that Jews not only go to shul on Yom Kippur, but they also fast.
Ridiculous as it sounds to the outsider, Ed, a man of hearty appetite, will go without food or water for 25 hours. The truly fascinating thing, and I think the word “miraculous” is not out of place here, is that he does this based on a command from an unseen and un-believed-in Deity. That he doesn’t know why doesn’t make it any less impressive. In a very real sense, it makes it all the more impressive. After all, who really understands any of this?
In fact, if someone prevented Shapiro from attending shul – let’s say there was a gathering of people, perhaps not especially difficult to imagine these days, who stood in front of the prayer house and used their bodies to barricade the entrance – Shapiro, not what you’d call a heroic type, would very likely risk his physical well-being to force his way in.
A lesson in belonging, not belief
WHEN I WAS about 12 and didn’t want to go to synagogue on Yom Kippur, or really, at any time, my dad once told me a similar thing. “Pete, imagine they wouldn’t let you go inside.”
I have to admit, it was a hugely compelling thing to hear, especially given the regularity of swastikas, carved or drawn with permanent marker, found at my school. It wasn’t a lesson in belief. It was a lesson in belonging, and it worked on me exactly the way it must have worked on Shapiro, whoever he was.
This unknowable, unbelieved-in God has somehow made His presence and His will known and largely obeyed, after millennia of exilic existence, to Jews.
And they, sometimes without a deep knowledge of their traditions, continue to insist on being part of the Jewish people and that their children take part in the tradition. I am one of those Jews too, though my own road there has taken me to a different place than Shapiro’s.
No longer a teenager by any stretch of the imagination, I observe Shabbat, kashrut, and the Jews holidays. I put on tefillin every weekday morning. And I agree, hour to hour, to wrestle with the idea of God, with trying to “know” God.
In fact, even when I was young, I wrestled and wrestled hard – once going to a seafood restaurant with my cousin on the Day for all-you-can-eat fried shrimp. Why? Looking back, I rebelled because I cared. I wasn’t “parve” about any of it.
Just as no one can fully understand God, no one can fully explain Ed Shapiro, and millions liked him. Like me. Like us.
This is only one of the beauties, the honor of being part of our glorious, resilient, courageous, brilliant, and faithful peoplehood, a peoplehood some today insist doesn’t exist.
We hear from those who seem not to wish us well that we are only “a religion,” that Judaism (how I dislike the false “ism” inherent in that term) is not a nation, not a peoplehood. “I have no qualms with Jews, only Israel,” they say.
Ed Shapiro knows different. Ed feels the difference. And it’s in part that difference that makes Yom Kippur, Hayom, the Day.
It is the Day when God calls us together, calls His Am Segulah, His treasured nation, together to start another year afresh, to be sealed and inscribed for a good year.
To a year of health, joy, children, rejoicing, and true peace. To true shalem, when it will be effortless to see and to feel the wholeness of the world and our place within it.
May we be so inscribed.
The writer is a Grammy- and Emmy-nominated rock & roll performer, songwriter, film composer, visual artist, and award-winning author. He has been profiled in Time Magazine, Rolling Stone, The Wall Street Journal, Tablet, and NPR. His newest book is Suspended by No String: A Songwriter’s Reflections on Faith, Aliveness, and Wonder (Regalo Press/Simon and Schuster). Follow him at peterhimmelman.substack.com

The Ebenezer Scrooge model: Can Yom Kippur really bring repentance and change?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
22:17:00 UTC
07:17:00 KST

After nearly 25 hours without food or drink, in the culmination of prayers that emphasize the fragility of life, the supremacy of God, and the risk of divine punishment, synagogue-goers on Yom Kippur are exhausted, humble, and perhaps filled with remorse and trepidation. The shofar blasts hundreds of sounds and leaves a deep, echoing resonance in the soul.
But a week later, have those worshipers changed their behavior for the better? Do people really transform themselves? Repentance isn’t simply regret; it is regret that produces transformation.
Ironically, a fictional story written by 19th-century English writer and journalist Charles Dickens, one of the leading novelists of the Victorian era, did an outstanding job illustrating consequential moral change.
His 1843 novella A Christmas Carol can provide a vivid, instantly recognizable human story about Ebenezer (which means “stone of help” in Hebrew) Scrooge, whose surname is regarded as a catchword for avarice and bitterness toward society and who constantly shouted “Bah! Humbug!” to express his disgust with many traditions.
Wealthy from running a warehouse, he pays his clerk, Bob Cratchit, a paltry wage while living cheaply in the quarters of his dead business partner, Jacob Marley. When two men ask him for charity on Christmas Eve, he gives them the cold shoulder.
But at night, Marley’s ghost visits Scrooge and warns him that three spirits will appear before him and demand that he change his character. If not, Scrooge will be bound in heavy chains.
After being shown scenes of his loveless childhood, the ruthless way he treats others in the present, his future lonely death, and his neglected gravestone, Scrooge repents and performs good deeds as a way of life.
Yom Kippur has no ghosts, of course, but it does something rather similar. It asks us to confront who we were, who we have become, and who we might yet become.
His transformation isn’t merely feeling sorry. He undergoes something: a psychological process of recognition, confrontation with himself, an emotional awakening, a decision to change, and then changed behavior.
What does it really take to change?
Prof. Mario Mikulincer, a well-known Hebrew University of Jerusalem (HUJI) psychologist and researcher who serves as the academic director of the university’s Israel Center for Addiction and Mental Health, described this same process.
The Argentina-born psychologist explained that there is a natural human inclination not to feel sorry about misdeeds or admit mistakes. The brain’s executive function is to admit mistakes and improve.
Stress, fatigue, and routine wear down the prefrontal cortex that controls executive function, allowing the basal ganglia that control body movements and process emotions to take over.
“Habits,” he said, “operate automatically. When intention conflicts with habit under stress, habit almost always wins. People who succeed don’t have superior willpower; they build superior environments and friction-free routines.”
Having no food or drink on Yom Kippur provides the time to think about oneself and the future.
“Hunger reduces the amount of glucose in the body, so it reduces executive function. This can make people more impulsive,” he noted. “But it also gives you time to have thoughts that overcome the physical, to think of life and death, one’s existence, and anxiety.
“It can also help you to identify with the poor, who are often hungry. The religiously observant believe that God is surveying what we do and can help lead us to better behavior. That can lead to the expression of remorse and determination to be a better person.”
Mikulincer added that it was “a brilliant move” that Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, was accompanied by a long fast, as it promotes introspection. “When stress, exhaustion, or emotional triggers hit, executive function undergoes depletion, allowing habitual patterns to hijack behavior.”
Repentance is more than feeling sorry
RABBI MOSHE BEN MAIMON (Maimonides, or the Rambam) wrote in his book Hilchot Teshuvah (The Laws of Repentance) about the yetzer hara (the primal drive). He stated that genuine repentance is not just feeling remorse; with the same capability one has to sin, one must actively choose differently. The psychologist noted that “this is part of executive function.”
Psychologists also refer to the “False Hope Syndrome” in which people set unrealistically high expectations for self-transformation because deciding to change provides an immediate, cheap surge of dopamine and moral relief.
When the initial euphoria fades, the reality of effort sets in, leading to relapse, said Mikulincer. “A person can overcome physical temptations. I think everybody can change, but it’s hard to move immediately from black to white and meet all your goals. If the goals aren’t realistic, they’re better off working step by step.”
Guilt makes people think, “I did something bad,” and this motivates self-improvement. But shame makes them think, “I am bad,” which triggers defensiveness and behavioral paralysis.
“People should feel guilt so they can repair,” he commented. “Repentance is a powerful Jewish theme. A good measure of it improves behavior, but a pathological amount is harmful. If a person feels shame, he hides and has to lie, and then it’s very hard to improve. Self-loathing actually stops people from changing, and shame triggers denial, addiction, and anger.”
The repetitive, collective nature of the Yom Kippur confessional (viddui) uses plural language (“We have trespassed, we have betrayed, we have stolen, we have spoken slander ... We have turned away from Your commandments and from Your good laws, and it has yielded us no benefit,” recited aloud many times during the Yom Kippur service).
Psychologically, listing misdeeds out loud forces a person to bridge the gap between internal denial and objective reality – a necessary first step in any therapeutic recovery program.
“It’s brilliant, because it is said in the plural,” the psychologist continued. “One is part of a community, of something bigger, so you can shoulder the burden.”
Another well-known prayer is Unetanneh Tokef, which balances the terrifying fragility of human life with an impressive openness to change. It emphasizes that human nature is inherently flawed, but the door to transformation never closes.
Deeply ingrained behaviors are automated pathways in the brain. Asking someone to “just stop” a bad habit without replacing the underlying trigger and reward is neurobiologically unrealistic.
“The brain is plastic and can grow,” said Mikulincer. “With practice, prayer, medication, or deep breathing, you can produce brain change, but one must stick to it and have self-discipline.”
The final prayer, Ne’ilah (closing), said as the sun sets, gives those present in the synagogue the feeling that time is running out and directly confronts human self-deception and helplessness, causing worshippers to ask for divine assistance when willpower alone fails.
Some people emerge stronger after hardship while others don’t.
Mikulincer suggested that “suffering can destroy people, but if they overcome it, they can become stronger. Personality traits can really change; kindness and even optimism can be learned – at any age. Decades ago, it was thought that the brain is set like plaster by age 30. The brain has been proven to have neuroplasticity, the ability to change and create new synapses.”
Mikulincer spends all his professional time doing research, not treating patients. In 2021, he researched the phenomenon of people who abandoned a religious way of life and, this year, those who have become observant due to exposure to war and terror.
Asked if he has studied prisoners and whether they can be helped to change their behavior significantly, he said he hasn’t, “but maybe will do it. It’s an interesting subject to explore.”
Asked what would be the single most effective first step to take if one wants to become a better person in the new year, he concluded: “Forgive yourself more, be less critical, feel healthy guilt, admit mistakes, and give a chance for something to happen.”
Can a crisis really change us?
LIKE MIKULINCER (who is not religiously observant), Dr. Aaron Cherniak is also a licensed psychologist at the Israel Center for Addiction and Mental Health. He is the director of research at the Shaare Nefesh Resilience Center (affiliated with the Shaare Zedek Medical Center) and a modern Orthodox rabbi ordained at New York’s Yeshiva University.
He asserted that personality can change after adulthood, but it’s more gradual than dramatic. Traits like conscientiousness and emotional stability do shift over the lifespan, especially around major life transitions. But lasting change tends to come from sustained new behavior, not a single moment of insight.”
Making promises on Yom Kippur “gives us the instant gratification of feeling like ‘better’ people instantaneously, even though nothing about us has changed. The habits we have formed and our pattern of seeking immediate gratification do not change just because we have made a sincere commitment.
“Real growth happens with consistent choices to maintain that commitment over time, notwithstanding the challenge of doing so. None of this is to diminish the power of profound moments of insight that remind us that we desire change and can change.”
“Crises,” Cherniak continued, “are one of the more reliable catalysts for real personality and behavioral change, precisely because they disrupt routine and force a kind of reckoning that everyday life rarely demands.
“But permanence isn’t guaranteed by the crisis itself; it depends on whether the person has the support, meaning-making, and follow-through to consolidate that shift into something lasting, rather than reverting once the acute period passes.”
Prolonged stress keeps the nervous system oriented toward threat and survival, which narrows attention and depletes the cognitive resources – planning, impulse control, flexible thinking – that deliberate change relies on.
It also drains the kind of bandwidth needed to build new habits, since chronic stress tends to push people back toward familiar, well-worn coping behaviors rather than newer, less automatic ones, simply because the familiar option requires less effort under strain.
Timing matters. Attempting significant change during a period of acute, ongoing stress is much harder than during a period of relative stability, and it’s often more realistic to focus on stabilizing first before expecting deep behavioral change to take hold.”
Change doesn’t require motivation to come first; behavior, he said. “What we call motivation is driven largely by a sense of progress, not just by wanting something in the abstract – taking a step, even a small one, generates momentum that fuels the next step, so motivation is as much a byproduct of action as a precondition for it.”
Asked why intelligent people repeatedly make the same mistakes, Cherniak suggested that “intelligence and self-control run on different systems. Knowing better doesn’t mean acting better. Under stress or temptation, fast emotional and reward circuits tend to override slow, deliberate reasoning, no matter how sharp that reasoning is.”
He disagrees with the claim that some people cannot change for the better. “There are real obstacles to change – environmental instability, or a total lack of support and stability – not some fixed incapacity in the person. And often underneath those, the deeper barrier is a person’s own belief that they can’t change.
“There’s a teaching from Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik on this: he wrote that when Elisha ben Abuyah – the sage who became known as the ‘Other’ – believed a heavenly voice had permanently barred him from repentance, it wasn’t really God who closed that door. It was his own conviction that he was irredeemable.
“The moment he believed that, he stopped trying, and the belief became self-fulfilling. That’s the trap: ‘Can’t change’ is rarely the truth about a person. It’s usually the story they’ve come to believe about themselves – and that story does more damage than any real limitation ever could.”
The more you practice small acts of kindness, the more natural it becomes, because it starts to shape how you see yourself, and it usually feels good and makes people respond well to you, which makes you want to do it again. That’s what happened to Scrooge.
“It’s also something people pick up from example – kids who grow up watching kindness modeled, or communities that build regular opportunities to help others into everyday life, tend to produce more of it,” Cherniak concluded.

Screen time and cognitive skills often predict each other over time, but the pattern varies by child
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
22:00:37 UTC
07:00:37 KST

A new study provides evidence that the relationship between using screens to soothe upset children and the development of their cognitive skills is often a two-way street, though this pattern can vary from child to child. The research, published in Journal of Communication, suggests that for most children, screen time and cognitive development influence each other over time, while for a small group, screen use primarily drives cognitive outcomes.
Executive functions are mental skills that help us plan, focus attention, and juggle multiple tasks. Two key parts of this cognitive system are cognitive flexibility, which is the ability to shift thinking or adapt to new rules, and inhibitory control, which is the capacity to resist impulses and stop an automatic behavior. These skills grow rapidly during early childhood and form a foundation for academic and social success.
Parents sometimes use smartphones, tablets, or television to help calm their children when they are throwing a tantrum or struggling with strong feelings. This practice is known as media emotion regulation. Research has generally pointed to a relationship between heavy screen use and developmental challenges. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost earlier this year suggested that high screen time in infancy might indirectly lead to poorer emotional regulation later in childhood. Similarly, another study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that problematic media use in toddlers is linked to an increase in emotional and social difficulties a few years later.
But how exactly do these things influence each other over time? In communication and media research, there is an ongoing debate about what causes what. Some theories propose that media use directly causes changes in an individual. Other theories argue the reverse, proposing that a person’s individual traits and struggles cause them to seek out specific media. A third perspective proposes a cycle, where media use and individual traits continuously feed into each other.
“When we talk about issues related to children and media, usually the questions people are asking is about cause,” said lead author Jane Shawcroft, an assistant professor in the School of Communication at The Ohio State University. “‘Is TikTok causing mental health problems for my teen?’ ‘Will giving my child a tablet cause developmental issues?’”
“But cause is a tricky if not impossible thing to prove from a scientific perspective,” Shawcroft told PsyPost. “This study was really about trying to think carefully about one of the conditions for causality – that the cause has to come before the effect.”
Specifically, the research team wanted to understand this temporal ordering, or which event happens first, in the context of parents using media to soothe their children. “In this study we were trying to see if there was evidence that the answer to the question ‘does giving a child media to calm them cause changes in their cognitive development’ is different for different children,” Shawcroft said. The researchers suspected that if the pattern varies, looking at group averages might hide important differences in how children actually develop.
To explore this, the researchers analyzed data from Project M.E.D.I.A., a long-term study following child development. They focused on a group of 87 children whose parents provided information over several years, spanning from when the children were two and a half years old to seven and a half years old. Each year, parents completed surveys detailing how often they used media to help manage their child’s emotions, with responses converted to a scale from 0 to 100.
When the children were between five and seven years old, they completed computer-based tasks to measure their executive functions. To test inhibitory control, children played a game where they had to identify the direction of a middle arrow while ignoring surrounding arrows pointing in different directions. To test cognitive flexibility, they completed a card-sorting task that required them to sort pictures by one rule, such as color, and then suddenly switch to a new rule, such as shape.
The researchers also gathered information on the family’s background at the beginning of the study. This included household income, child temperament, parent stress, and parent depressive symptoms. Using a statistical approach designed to group individuals with similar developmental paths, the researchers looked at how each child’s media emotion regulation and executive functions predicted each other from year to year.
The analysis identified three distinct patterns of temporal ordering among the children. The vast majority of the children, 87.36 percent or 76 kids, fell into a group the researchers called the Bidirectional class. For these children, the process was a two-way street. How often parents used media to soothe them predicted their later executive function skills, and their executive function skills equally predicted how often parents would use media to soothe them in the future.
A much smaller group, making up 7 percent of the sample or six children, fell into the Media Emotion Regulation Driven class. In this group, parental use of media to regulate emotions strongly predicted the children’s later cognitive flexibility and inhibitory control. The reverse was not true, as the children’s cognitive skills had almost no predictive power over how much media their parents used to soothe them.
The third group, making up 6 percent of the sample or five children, showed a Diverging Temporal Ordering. For these kids, media use strongly predicted changes in cognitive flexibility, but the pattern flipped for inhibitory control, with inhibitory control predicting media use.
When the researchers looked at what family factors might predict which group a child belonged to, they found that a parent’s mental health played a role. Higher levels of parent depressive symptoms at the start of the study were linked to a higher probability of a child being in the Media Emotion Regulation Driven group. Higher parent depression was also linked to a lower probability of a child being in the Bidirectional group. Other factors like household income, parent stress, and child temperament did not have a statistically significant relationship with group membership.
“The relationship between using media to calm children and development is different for different children,” Shawcroft explained. “Most kids we found a bidirectional pattern – using media to calm them was related to their cognitive development, and their cognitive development in turn was related to how often their parents used media to calm them down.”
“But there were children who were exceptions and showed different patterns,” she added. “This means that from a parenting perspective, understanding how to support children in relationship to their technology use is going to be more about understanding your child and your family’s unique situation rather than a one-size-fits-all approach.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study relied on a relatively small group of 87 children, largely because collecting detailed behavioral data over a five-year span is difficult. The small number of children in the two minority classes means these specific group percentages should be treated as estimates that need further testing in larger groups.
“This study is a little weird because we weren’t looking at effect sizes or the direction of effects, just the underlying patterns in the order of effects,” Shawcroft noted. “This study doesn’t tell us if using media to calm children results in poorer cognitive development (although other studies do), or vice versa.”
It is also important to note that establishing the timeline of events is only one part of finding a cause-and-effect relationship. Just because one behavior happens before another does not mean it is the sole cause. The researchers point out that future work needs to explore other hidden variables that might influence both a family’s media habits and a child’s brain development.
Despite these constraints, the findings point toward a more personalized approach to technology and parenting. Rather than assuming screen time affects all children in the exact same way, pediatricians and parents might need to consider a family’s unique context. For some families, reducing the use of screens as a soothing tool might directly improve a child’s cognitive development. For most, however, a child’s developing brain and a family’s media habits are locked in a continuous loop, influencing one another year after year.
The study, “Media emotion regulation and executive functions: individual differences in temporal ordering among young children,” was authored by Jane Shawcroft, McCall A. Booth, Chris L. Porter, Megan Van Alfen, Megan Gale, Lara A. Maximiano, Elena K. Holmes, Sarah M. Coyne, Hailey G. Holmgren, and Blake L. Jones.

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 20, 2026

While You Were Sleeping: 5 stories you might have missed, Sept 20, 2026
Trump says he will create ‘AI Force’, name AI czar
US President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Sept 19 that he plans to appoint a new artificial intelligence adviser, known as an “AI czar”, and create an “AI force”, though he did not provide details about either initiative or how they would be implemented.
Fears are growing in Washington among lawmakers about the risks posed by AI technology on humans and property. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said that “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary.
If Trump follows through on the pledge, it would be his second AI czar. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served in the role before stepping down in the spring and moving into an external advisory position.
CNN, MS NOW, Politico denied access to White House grounds
US media outlets CNN and MS NOW said they were denied access to the White House grounds on Sept 19, a day after President Donald Trump announced a ban against them for reporting what he calls “fake news”.
The news outlets both denounced the move as a violation of the US constitution and vowed to keep reporting on the US government. Both are expected to take the bans to court to regain access to the presidential mansion.
“The White House belongs to the American people and the decisions made inside are funded with our tax dollars,” MS NOW, formerly known as MSNBC, said on X.
Thousands protest inaction over climate crisis in Switzerland
Several thousand people marched in the Swiss cities of Geneva and Lausanne on Sept 19 to protest government inaction in the face of global warming.
They were answering a call by a coalition of more than a hundred associations and political parties under the common banner: “No 50-degree summers!”
People of all ages took part in the marches, carrying placards with slogans such as “No Planet B” and “We’re cooked!”, AFP journalists noted.
The larger demonstration was at Lausanne, where organisers said at least 8,000 had taken part.
Man charged in US boy’s disappearance after 33 years
When 10-year-old George Burdynski Jr hopped on his bike on May 24, 1993, near his Maryland home, it was the last time his family saw him.
The disappearance of George, who was also known as Junior, shocked Prince George’s County in Maryland and prompted a large search by law enforcement, including the FBI. Volunteers also joined the search.
But the case languished for more than 33 years.
Now, investigators say they have arrested a 61-year-old man, Joseph Lynch, who has been charged with second-degree murder, rape and other sexual abuse charges in connection with George’s disappearance.
UN peacekeeping chief in Lebanon says smooth transition is critical before pull-out
The head of United Nations peacekeepers in Lebanon said on Sept 19 it was critical to ensure other UN agencies and Lebanese troops could assume the tasks carried out by the force before it begins withdrawing at the end of 2026.
Major-General Diodato Abagnara of Italy spoke to Reuters in southern Lebanon at a position operated by the UN peacekeeping force known as UNIFIL, which has been monitoring hostilities in southern Lebanon for nearly 50 years.
Since a new war erupted between Israel and Iran-backed Lebanese armed group Hezbollah in March, the force has also provided security escorts for humanitarian aid convoys to residents in a small cluster of predominantly Christian southern Lebanese towns now encircled by Israeli troops. Residents in much of the rest of southern Lebanon have been forcibly displaced by Israeli strikes and evacuation orders.

Lawsuits filed over Nazi-looted art displayed in museums in Los Angeles, Auschwitz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
21:52:53 UTC
06:52:53 KST

Lawsuits filed in California over Nazi-looted art displayed in museums in Los Angeles, Auschwitz
Jewish heirs of Holocaust victims and their representatives have filed two lawsuits in California staking their claims to Nazi-looted paintings that still hang on the walls of prominent museums in Los Angeles and Auschwitz.
The two lawsuits are the first to be filed after the recent passage of laws by California and Congress, which strengthen U.S.-based claims to artworks that were forcibly taken from Jewish families during World War II.
One lawsuit was filed in Los Angeles Superior Court on Monday by the Jewish Federation of Greater Los Angeles and its board chair Daniel Gryczman against Norton Simon Museum in Pasadena for the return of "Adam and Eve." These are two life-size oil-on-panel masterpieces created by Lucas Cranach the Elder in 1530.
The other lawsuit was filed in federal court in L.A. the same day by the daughters of the late Dinah Gottliebova Babbitt, a Holocaust survivor and California-based animator who was held in Auschwitz. It demanded the return of watercolors of fellow prisoners that the artist was forced to paint for Josef Mengele, a Nazi physician who had earned the nickname the "Angel of Death."
Spokespersons for both museums say the museums legally hold titles to the works and intend to continue displaying them to the public. The lawsuits don't specify the monetary value of the paintings.
The issue of Nazi-looted art is an emotional, legally and ethically charged topic that pits Jewish families that have suffered inter-generational trauma against museums that say they are trying to preserve a painful, yet important, chapter of history.
Between 1933 and 1945, the Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history, seizing over 600,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums. Decades later, many of these masterpieces reside in prominent museums around the world, making the push for their recovery more complex than a simple property dispute.
Rabbi Noah Farkas is president and CEO of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles, the organization to which Marei von Saher, sole heir of Dutch Jewish art dealer Jacques Goudstikker, has signed over her rights. The paintings were seized from Goudstikker's collection by Hermann Göring, Adolf Hitler's second-in-command, and changed hands several times before being sold in the 1960s to the Pasadena Museum of Modern Art, which was renamed the Norton Simon Museum in honor of its benefactor.
Farkas said the federation plans to use most of the net proceeds from the recovered art to provide much-needed help to the about 2,500 Holocaust survivors living in the L.A. area.
"These are incredibly beautiful European masterpieces stolen from a Jewish family to enrich the Nazi party and fund the war and death machine against the people," he said. "It's our honor to take on this role on behalf of the community and use most of the proceeds to help these elderly survivors live out the last years of their lives in dignity, comfort and peace – something their family members were denied during the Holocaust."
Marei von Saher, in a statement, said she is grateful to the Jewish organization for taking up her family's cause.
"This effort represents a meaningful step toward justice for Holocaust survivors and victims of Nazi era atrocities," she said.
Democratic California Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel, who represents the Woodland Hills neighborhood of L.A., wrote Assembly Bill 2867, signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom in September 2024, which requires that the state law must apply in lawsuits brought by California residents or their heirs to recover art seized during the Holocaust or during other acts of persecution. Gabriel, who co-chairs the California Legislative Jewish Caucus, introduced the legislation in response to a federal court ruling, which allowed the state-owned Thyssen-Bornemisza National Museum in Madrid to keep a multimillion-dollar Camille Pissarro impressionist masterpiece.
That painting had been taken by the Nazis from the Cassirer family in 1939. This case, which prompted this new law, is expected to be heard in federal court in California next month.
Gabriel said it's time for museums to "do some deep introspection on whether they want to be on the right side of history."
Norton Simon Museum released a statement pointing out that a federal court in 2018 unanimously determined that the museum had proper title to the Cranach paintings. In May 2019, the U.S. Supreme Court declined to get involved in the case, leaving in place lower court rulings.
They said the Cranach paintings, which originally belonged to the Stroganoff family, were put up for sale in 1931 by the Soviet Union in an illicit auction in Berlin where they were purchased by Goudstikker. After a complicated journey, the paintings were sold to the museum by a Stroganoff family descendant. The museum later restored and preserved the pieces.
"For nearly 50 years, they have been on view at the Norton Simon Museum and will continue to be accessible to the public for years to come," the statement said.
Pawel Sawicki, a spokesperson for the Auschwitz Memorial, said the watercolors of Roma victims that Gottliebova Babbitt was forced to paint by Mengele to document his horrendous experiments and racial research, "must remain in the Memorial" to document the man's crimes. He said these paintings must not be mischaracterized as "Nazi-looted art" because Gottliebova Babbitt painted them against her will as a prisoner and therefore didn't have ownership of the watercolors.
While he understands the family's sentiments, Sawicki said the portraits of Roma and Sinti victims are among the few remaining documents of Mengele's criminal experiments and should be treated as unique documents related to the history of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
"While fully respecting the rights of people who created some of the documents here, we are of the opinion that any loss in the collections of the Memorial will constitute irreparable harm," he said. "… The loss of even the smallest part of the documentation is an irreparable loss and blemish on the memory of the victims of Auschwitz."

Germans arrested for Louvre stunt in Mona Lisa hall

Germans arrested for Louvre stunt in Mona Lisa hall
PARIS - Two Germans were arrested on Sept 19 after they stuck two paintings on a wall of the hall that hosts the Mona Lisa in Paris’s Louvre museum, police sources said.
The two men used sticky tape to stick the two paintings – measuring 30cm by 40cm – in the hall where visitors flock to see Leonardo Da Vinci’s masterpiece.
One showed one of the two men wearing armour, while the other was a portrait of the two men accompanied by a woman.
Security officers at the museum detained the two men and called the police, who arrested them for minor damage to the wall. Interviewed by police, they said they had done it for fun.
The two men will be summoned to appear in court once the museum files a formal complaint for the damage, said the police sources.
The Mona Lisa itself, now behind a thick layer of protective glass, suffered no damage in the incident.
Museum officials are more than usually alert these days after a spate of heists at French museums and galleries, which have highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.
The Louvre itself was targeted last October when eight items of jewellery worth millions of dollars were stolen during a daylight heist.
Even though four suspects have been arrested, the stolen items have still not been found despite extensive searches by French investigators.
The burglary stunned the world, embarrassed France and revealed a series of security lapses, including the museum’s old-fashioned CCTV system.
Many of the museum’s security flaws had already been highlighted in a 2019 audit ordered by the museum, the findings of which were never acted on.
The Louvre welcomed around nine million visitors last year, far above its intended capacity, which has led to overcrowding problems.
In May, French President Emmanuel Macron announced a major overhaul of the museum, which will include a new space for the Mona Lisa and a new museum entrance. AFP

What China really means when it says it’s being ‘strategic’
Unknown

What China really means when it says it’s being ‘strategic’
Rather than geopolitical manoeuvring or calculation, this diplomatic label aims to convey seriousness, patience and a willingness to work for mutual long-term benefit
He called for an objective and rational “strategic” perception. That means the two sides should treat each other as partners rather than rivals, and as opportunities rather than threats.
In Chinese official and diplomatic language, the term “strategic” is routinely used to denote matters of high importance, long-term significance and central weight in the nation’s interests and development. When China defines a bilateral relationship as “strategic”, it signals that the relationship is viewed from a high level, beyond immediate disputes or short-term calculations. It implies a willingness to invest sustained political attention and effort, and a belief that the engagement can generate mutual benefits and positive externalities for the wider region or the world.

Human beings need meaning. We not only perceive the world around us, we also perceive value: we…
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
21:14:00 UTC
06:14:00 KST

Human beings need meaning. We not only perceive the world around us, we also perceive value: we reflect on our perceptions and judge certain things to be better for us than others. Everything that carries value we also take to be important, good, and meaningful. And only what is meaningful feels worthy of our pursuit or support.
We need meaning not just in the objects we find and the events we experience but in ourselves as well. The absence of meaning in life would seem to make everything we do unnecessary, including being alive at all. A life devoid of meaning is not one we would want to have. As such, meaning becomes a demand we make on life itself.

Trump says he will create ‘AI Force’, name AI czar
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump said in a social media post on Sept 19 that he plans to appoint a new artificial intelligence adviser, known as an “AI czar”, and create an “AI force”, though he did not provide details about either initiative or how they would be implemented.
Fears are growing in Washington among lawmakers about the risks posed by AI technology on humans and property. Earlier this month, former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said that “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Trump has repeatedly downplayed concerns about AI and argued that additional regulation is unnecessary.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, his social media platform. “Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System.”
If Trump follows through on the pledge, it would be his second AI czar. Venture capitalist David Sacks previously served in the role before stepping down in the spring and moving into an external advisory position.
Sacks has echoed Trump’s skepticism of new AI regulation. Speaking at a Politico event on Sept 16, he said AI developers should be responsible for ensuring the safety of their products and could be held liable if problems arise, adding that new federal rules are unnecessary.
The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Trump’s post.
Trump’s post comes ahead of his scheduled meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Sept 25. Washington and Beijing are competing for leadership in AI, which both governments view as vital to their economic and military strength. Trump and technology executives have argued that excessive regulation would slow US AI development and undermine American companies’ ability to compete with Chinese rivals, a claim that safety advocates often refute.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will meet with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng on Sept 20 at JPMorgan Chase headquarters in New York to discuss AI security, trade and other economic issues, a person familiar with the planning said on Sept 19. REUTERS

Ed Sheeran returns to stage after calls for boycott over removal of Macklemore
Protesters and police were expected to greet concertgoers in Philadelphia on Saturday for pop superstar Ed Sheeran's first show since he became embroiled in controversy set off after he was asked to remove Macklemore from his performance due to his pro-Palestine remarks.
Rapper Macklemore was booted from Sheeran's US Loop Tour on Monday after the owners of stadiums hosting upcoming shows told Sheeran he would have to choose between using their venues or having Macklemore as a supporting act.
The move comes after Macklemore called for a "Free Palestine" onstage in New Jersey earlier this month.
Sheeran, who has since faced backlash, has denied being behind the decision to remove Macklemore, saying his tour's promoter was responsible.
But four supporting acts soon quit the "Shape of You" singer's tour. They included Sheeran's backing band as well as performer Finneas, who rose to fame collaborating with his pop superstar sister Billie Eilish.
At a time when a growing number of artists are speaking out against the war on Gaza and West Bank Israeli settler violence, the 35-year-old British performer has maintained his apolitical stance.
"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care," he said on Instagram on Tuesday.
However, he said, "those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum."
The former busker-turned-superstar, accused by critics of failing to stand up to the stadium owners, has been targeted by boycott calls over the controversy.
On Saturday, a pro-Palestinian group urged artists, fans and crew members to stay away from Sheeran's concerts on three continents.
"We now extend our call for boycotting Ed Sheeran's entire world tour, including the upcoming Latin American dates, and the as-yet-unannounced European leg," the Palestinian Campaign for the Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel (PACBI) said in a statement.
"Clearly, there's some real discontent around how this whole situation is being managed, and he's definitely having to do some brand reputation management," said Gretchen Larsen, a professor specializing in the music industry at Durham University Business School in the UK.
Solo show?
No new opening acts or backing bands have been announced, and it was not known how Sheeran planned to carry out his show at Lincoln Financial Field in the eastern US city of Philadelphia on Saturday night.
A pro-Palestinian rally organised by local groups was scheduled to take place near the venue in the afternoon.
City police told AFP there would be an "appropriate police presence" to "help ensure the safety of concertgoers, employees and neighborhood residents."
On the resale market, tickets for the show have been changing hands at a slightly brisker pace since Monday when compared to previous dates on Sheeran's tour, according to tracking site TicketData.
"Some share of the audience isn't tuned in to anything political, or is completely indifferent to it, and has only just now become aware that Ed Sheeran is even playing their city. They're buying tickets with zero connection to the controversy," site founder Keith Pagello said.
The price of the cheapest tickets had fallen from $123 on Monday to $67 by Friday afternoon.
Pagello said the decline was not necessarily linked to the row, as it is common for concert ticket prices to drop as the event date approaches.

Turkey says it could help meet Saudi military needs under defence pact
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said on Saturday that Saudi Arabia may have military needs due to the ongoing attacks by Yemen's Houthis and that Turkey was ready to help under a trilateral defence pact that also includes Pakistan.
"We see there are very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia's territorial integrity and sovereignty. We have an alliance agreement in our pact. We are in serious solidarity on this point... They may have some military needs, especially on some technical issues. We would have no issues in meeting these," Fidan told broadcaster NTV.
The joint defence agreement, dubbed the "Mecca Joint Defence Agreement", signed last month stipulates that an armed attack on any one of the three countries will be regarded as an attack on all of them.
The Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, have been launching attacks on Saudi Arabia since declaring a naval blockade against Riyadh in July, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. The attacks have targeted Saudi cities, energy infrastructure and shipping, threatening global oil supplies and the main alternative Red Sea route for Gulf exports while traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains disrupted.
US President Donald Trump has rebuffed pleas from the Saudis for military support to fight the Houthis, who agreed a ceasefire with the United States last year after Washington bombed the group for two months.
Fidan said that it was unacceptable for Saudi Arabia to be made a part of the US-Iran war as it had no desire to join the conflict. He added, without elaborating, that proposals have been conveyed to all sides to end the fighting.
"There are many initiatives, but the sides need to accept these," he said. "There are new proposals, I hope they accept them. Otherwise, the crisis was tolerated until a certain point, but the economic reflections have started to exceed the point of being tolerable."
Turkey, which has NATO's second-largest army, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion and did not seek to replace any existing alliances.
Pakistan has said that there were no discussions about a military reaction from Islamabad under the Mecca agreement in response to the Houthis' attacks on Saudi Arabia, but added that Pakistan would act when the "time comes".
Earlier on Saturday, Yemen's Houthis said they attacked "sensitive" sites in the Saudi capital Riyadh with missiles and drones, hours after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen near the city's main airport.
Turkey has condemned the Houthi attacks and called for them to stop immediately.

Israel’s president pardons soldier who killed wounded Palestinian in 2016
Elor Azaria had shot a Palestinian who had already been incapacitated by Israeli troops, in controversial case.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog has expunged the criminal record of a former soldier convicted of manslaughter for killing a wounded Palestinian in Hebron a decade ago.
Herzog announced on Saturday that he had shortened the remaining erasure period on Elor Azaria’s record, effectively clearing it despite opposition from Israeli army Chief of Staff Lieutenant-General Eyal Zamir.

The military had opposed the move.
In a letter to the defence minister, Zamir and other senior officers said Azaria “has refrained from expressing remorse and taking responsibility for his actions, even a decade after his conviction”.
The president’s office said it had taken the military’s position into account but decided the circumstances justified allowing Azaria to “open a new chapter in his life”.
Azaria, an army medic at the time, was filmed shooting Abdel Fattah al-Sharif in the head in March 2016.
Al-Sharif had stabbed and wounded a soldier but had already been shot by Israeli troops and had lain on the ground for about 11 minutes before Azaria killed him.
Azaria was convicted by a military court in 2017 and sentenced to 18 months in prison, later reduced to 14 months. He was released in May 2018 after serving nine months.
Herzog’s office said the decision followed a request from Defence Minister Israel Katz in July and was based on “the passage of time, the completion of his sentence, and the remorse he has expressed”.
The statement added that the pardon was issued “in the spirit” of Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, and did not challenge the original legal proceedings.
Katz welcomed the pardon, writing on X that it “sends an important message to [Israeli army] soldiers and their families: We do not abandon our fighters”.
Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, called the decision “deeply moving” and urged Herzog to grant a similar pardon to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is on trial for corruption.
The 2016 shooting generated intense debate in Israel and drew international condemnation at the time.
The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs had condemned the shooting as an “extrajudicial execution” and a “war crime”, saying the video footage “demolished all the slogans chanted by the occupation leaders about the ethics of the Israeli army”.
The family of al-Sharif had dismissed the legal proceedings as a “farce” aimed at improving Israel’s international image rather than delivering justice.
The United Nations human rights office described the original sentence as “excessively lenient” and said it risked “reinforcing the culture of impunity”.
In 2024, the Joe Biden administration barred Azaria and his immediate family from entering the United States, citing an “extrajudicial killing”.

War update: 188 clashes on front line, Kostiantynivka sector sees heaviest fighting
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Facebook in an update on the battlefield situation as of 22:00, Ukrinform reports.
“A total of 188 combat clashes have taken place since the beginning of the day. The aggressor launched one missile strike, carried out 64 airstrikes using 199 guided aerial bombs, deployed 6,084 kamikaze drones for attacks, and conducted 2,006 strikes on the positions of our troops and populated areas,” the report says.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, two enemy assault operations were recorded since the beginning of the day. Russian forces carried out 74 attacks on Ukrainian positions and populated areas.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Russian forces attacked Ukrainian positions six times toward the settlements of Lyman, Artilne, Ternova, Mala Vovcha, Vilkhuvatka, and Shevyakivka.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces twice attempted to improve their positions by conducting assaults near Kurylivka and Kivsharivka.

In the Sloviansk sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces stopped three Russian attempts to advance near Yampil and Mykolaivka as well as toward Pyskunivka.
In the Kramatorsk sector, Russian forces conducted no assault operations.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces repelled 18 enemy assaults near Kostiantynivka and toward Osykove, Dovha Balka, Illinivka, Rusyn Yar, Mykolaipillia, Stepove, and Vilne. Two assault operations are still ongoing.
In the Pokrovsk sector, Russian forces launched 15 attacks, attempting to advance toward the settlements of Dobropillia, Vodianske, Bilytske, Novyi Donbas, Serhiivka, and Molodetske.
According to preliminary estimates, 29 Russian troops were killed and 17 wounded in the sector today. Ukrainian forces destroyed six vehicles, 11 pieces of special equipment and two personnel shelters. Five vehicles and two pieces of special equipment were damaged, along with four UAV control posts and 51 personnel shelters. A total of 84 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
No Russian offensive operations were recorded in the Oleksandrivka sector.
In the Huliaipole sector, Ukraine’s Defense Forces repelled one enemy attack toward the settlement of Kopani.
Russian forces conducted no offensive operations in the Dnipro River and Orikhiv sectors.
No significant changes in the situation were recorded in the other sectors of the feront, the General Staff said.
As reported by Ukrinform, total combat losses of Russian forces since the beginning of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine stood at approximately 1,516,430 personnel as of September 19, 2026.

guadagnino, lynch, and the movie directors who design interior spaces
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19

Int. Home – DAY… interior design by Movie Directors
At the end of September, film director Luca Guadagnino and designer Stefano Baisi will release a line with Zara Home that includes nearly 200 sumptuous pieces of interior décor, from squiggly couches that recall Italian Radical Design to tableware that feels snatched from an Italian villa. Through this collection, there is a chance to bring a bit of the energy of Queer, Call Me by Your Name, Challengers, or one of the director’s many other films into a domestic space.
This meeting between interior design and film is not a new one. The visually seductive worlds of David Lynch, Wes Anderson, and Wong Kar Wai have inspired the likes of hotels, home goods collections, and even train cars. For these directors, their cinematic worlds have homes both on and off the silver screen.
Baisi Guadagnino for Zara | campaign by David Sims
Baisi Guadagnino for Zara Home | campaign by Valerie Sadoun
Studio Luca Guadagnino, Zara Home, and the Dior Runway
A few years ago, when Luca Guadagnino was brought up in conversation, those in the know would share, ‘and you know he has an interior design studio!’ The Milan-based director has brought his aesthetic sense to runways, hotels, and villas through Studio Luca Guadagnino, where he began working with Baisi, who would later go on to collaborate with him on Queer, After the Hunt, and Jonathan Anderson’s S/S 2026 Dior runway in Paris. In Rome, monumental spaces within the Palazzo Talìa hotel were redesigned by his studio, complimenting the building’s rich history with contemporary styles.
Palazzo Talìa by Studio Luca Guadagnino | image courtesy of Palazzo Talìa
Baisi Guadagnino for Zara Home | campaign by Valerie Sadoun
David Lynch’s things and places for thinking and listening
‘Every film is going into a new world,’remarked the late American film director David Lynch at the 63rd Venice Film Festival. He talks about following one’s intuition as they navigate the world that is set out in front of them—a world of actors, costumes, dialogue, and sets. Lynch, whose films are characterized by rich colors and liminal spaces, has created a few interior spaces. In 2024, he created A Thinking Room within Milan’s Salone del Mobile. The club Silencio, created in Paris in 2011, features glittering gold walls and takes its name from the Club Silencio in his 2001 thriller, Mulholland Drive. On a smaller scale, the auteur also created a line of speakers with Bang & Olufsen in 2018 that feature his visual art.
interiors of David Lynch. A Thinking Room, curated by Antonio Monda, Salone Internazionale del Mobile, pavilions 5-7 | image courtesy of Salone del Mobile
interiors of David Lynch. A Thinking Room, curated by Antonio Monda, Salone Internazionale del Mobile, pavilions 5-7 | image courtesy of Salone del Mobile
Beoplay M5 and Beoplay P2, a collaboration between David Lynch and Bang & Olufsen | image courtesy of David Lynch & Bang & Olufsen
Bar Luce and the Cygnus Carriage of Wes Anderson
A Wes Anderson movie is so visually particular that it sparked a whole social media trend of creating short videos with symmetrical compositions, a hazy pastel color palette, and yellow, overlaid sans serif text. It makes sense that he would be tapped to create real-life spaces that bring that dreamy cinematic space to real places. At Fondazione Prada’s space in Milan, Bar Luce’s pinball machine and candy-colored seats welcome guests to experience his quaint world over a gelato or espresso macchiato.
Anderson, who staged almost an entire film aboard a train for The Darjeeling Limited, also redesigned the Cygnus carriage for the Belmond train, the British Pullman. In giving the history of the locomotive, Belmond writes that it’s, ‘a carriage built in the 1950s – [which] has its fair share of cinematic history, featuring in the 1972 film ‘Agatha’ starring Dustin Hoffman and Vanessa Redgrave. It is one of eleven on the British Pullman, whose carriages have hosted royalty, carried statesmen and survived World War II bomb raids over the years.’ A very Andersonian space!
Fondazione Prada, which has long championed the cinematic arts, created a sister space to Anderson’s Bar Luce in the form of Wong Kar Wai’s fine dining space, Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai. The Hong Kong director has long enchanted audiences with his rich, neon images. Think the romantic, intimate space of In the Mood for Love or the luxurious lights of his TV series, Blossoms Shanghai.
Wong Kar Wai’s fine dining space, Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai | image courtesy of Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai
Wong Kar Wai’s fine dining space, Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai | image courtesy of Mi Shang Prada Rong Zhai
Pedro Almodóvar and Roche Bobois
If there’s one thing that unites Pedro Almodóvar’s movies, it’s the primary color palette that runs through his films. There are some films, like The Room Next Door or The Skin I Live In, where he takes a more restrained approach. But in his other films, like Kika, Volver, or Parallel Mothers, this intense use of color in the sets brings the stories forward, making his films seem more like a dream than a retelling of reality. In 2025, the Spanish director created a line with interiors company Roche Bobois, famous for its Bubble Sofa, designed by Sacha Lakic, that brought Almodóvar’s eye-popping palette off the screen and into some of the company’s most iconic silhouettes.
Pedro Almodóvar’s collection for Roche Bobois | image courtesy of Roche Bobois
