Oldest part of population give the most gifts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:41 UTC
01:43:41 KST

One out of every 3.81 gift tax cases in Taiwan last year involved donors aged 80 or older, with older Taiwanese transferring a combined NT$86.9 billion (US$2.73 billion) in assets, accounting for more than one-third of the nation’s total gifted assets, Ministry of Finance data showed.
About 23,000 taxable gift cases nationwide were recorded last year, of which 6,026 involved donors aged 80 or above, accounting for 26.24 percent of the total, ministry data showed.
Those aged 75 to 79 accounted for 3,189 cases worth NT$46.8 billion; donors aged 70 to 74 recorded 3,955 cases worth NT$40.3 billion; and people aged 65 to 69 filed 3,193 cases, with gifted assets totaling NT$33.4 billion, the data showed.
Photo: Hsu Yi-ping, Taipei Times
Total gifted assets reached NT$260.6 billion last year, down slightly from NT$281 billion in 2024, they showed.
The figures indicate that retirees are the demographic most likely to transfer assets through gifting.
Life expectancy in Taiwan rose to 81.27 years last year, an increase of 0.5 years from a year earlier, Ministry of the Interior data showed.
Sinyi Realty Inc research manager Tseng Ching-der (曾敬德) said longer life expectancy appears to have extended the period during which elderly people tend to distribute assets to family members.
This longevity could be the reason that people aged 80 or older accounted for the largest number of gift filings, he said.
The annual gift tax exemption is capped at NT$2.44 million per person, meaning that donors might give assets to any number of recipients without incurring a gift tax, provided the cumulative value does not exceed the exemption threshold, he added.
As Taiwan becomes a super-aged society, the number of taxable estate cases and the value of taxable estates reached a nine-year high last year, finance ministry data showed.
In other developments, separate data showed that more than 91,300 people renounced their inheritance rights last year, the second-highest figure in the past nine years.
The number of inheritance renunciations exceeded 90,000 annually for three consecutive years from 2023 to last year, with 2023 hitting a record high with almost 92,300 cases, they showed.
From 2017 to last year, women consistently accounted for more inheritance renunciations than men.
In 2017, women made up about 56.3 percent of all inheritance renunciations, compared with 43.7 percent for men, a gap of 12.6 percentage points — the widest disparity during the nine-year period.
However, the gender gap in inheritance waivers narrowed significantly between 2022 and last year, shrinking to less than 10 percentage points in 2022, 2024 and last year, with last year recording the narrowest gap at 9.2 percentage points.
Colliers International owner-occupier services director Huang Shu-wei (黃舒衛) said the most common reason for renouncing an inheritance is that the dead person’s debts exceed the value of their assets.
By formally renouncing inheritance rights, heirs can sever liability for outstanding debts, he said.
Another common scenario involves heirs carrying substantial personal debts, he said.
As accepting an inheritance could expose the assets to creditors and trigger compulsory enforcement proceedings, renouncing the inheritance allows assets to pass directly to siblings or other eligible heirs under the law, preventing them from being claimed by outside creditors, he said.
Traditional views could play a role in some regions, where sons are expected to inherit land and property while daughters receive cash, contributing to a higher rate of inheritance renunciation among women, Tseng said.
The Ministry of the Interior estimated that the total value of unclaimed inherited land reached NT$99.2 billion last year, based on officially assessed land values.
More than 72,000 land parcels covering about 3,400 hectares remained without completed inheritance registration last year, the ministry said.

On Friday, the first day of the national team events, Taiwan won gold in the senior women’s 500kg and junior women’s 480kg events, with the men’s 600kg team taking bronze.

In the senior women’s 500kg event, Taiwan faced Germany in the final.

The ground was firm at the beginning, making it easier to attack, Hung said.

The president of the Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) yesterday said that politics — in the form of a welcoming ceremony involving Taiwan — had already entered into the Asian Games.
He did not sound pleased about it, speaking just hours before the official opening ceremony.
Some events at the Asian Games began several days ago to accommodate a packed schedule and more than 17,000 athletes and officials. Up to 5,000 are housed on a cruise ship.
Photo: AFP
“I don’t think, you know, the politicians or politics should be involved in sports,” said Sheikh Joaan bin Hamad Al Thani, speaking with media at the Asian Games.
He is a younger brother of the Emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani.
Sheikh Joaan was asked about an incident on Friday at the Asian Games in which Minister of Sports Lee Yang was temporarily barred from a welcoming ceremony and a flag-raising.
Photo: Reuter
Lee was later allowed to participate and the OCA attributed the incident to a misunderstanding.
“We don’t mix sports with politics and we already have,” Sheikh Joaan said. “We’re going to take — if something like this will happen, we have our way of taking care of it. And all the delegations know what the protocol is and what should be done, and what shouldn’t be done.”
Lee is a two-time Olympic gold medalist in badminton. He won gold twice in doubles — 2020 and 2024 — each time defeating a Chinese pair in the final.
Photo: Reuters
Taiwanese media reported that the OCA had issued an order barring Lee.
Taiwanese officials asked to see the order, but officials were unable to produce it, they reported.
“We chose to stick to our principles,” said Chen Shih-kwei, a vice president of Taiwan’s Olympic committee. “We asked the local organizing committee and the OCA to uphold the Olympic spirit so that we could attend all events equally and with dignity. We insisted on this, and then negotiations began. We stood firm on our dignity and principles.”
Lee later told Taiwanese reporters that “we are doing our best to safeguard our rights and do not want to be subjected to any form of suppression.”

Taiwan’s women lost their hockey opener against South Korea 3-1 on Friday and face China tomorrow.
In soft tennis, the men’s and women’s teams have reached the medals rounds.
In the women’s Group B, Taiwan beat Thailand, Mongolia and the Philippines, all 3-0. They face South Korea at the Nagoya City Higashiyama Park Tennis Center in the semi-finals today.
The men’s team beat Laos, India and Mongolia, also 3-0 in each, in Group C, and also face South Korea in the semis.
Taiwan had accumulated 30 medals in the sport at the Asian Games prior to this year.
In volleyball, the women’s side beat Kyrgyzstan 3-0 on Wednesday and Mongolia 3-0 on Thursday, but lost to Thailand 3-0 on Friday. They face Japan today in the quarters.

Union chairman jailed in China returns to Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

Taiwanese Tsai Chin-shu (蔡金樹), who had been imprisoned in China for engaging in activity that “endangers national security,” said on Facebook on Friday that he has returned to Taiwan.
Tsai, chairman of the Southern Taiwan Union of Cross-strait Relations Associations, had traveled frequently between Taiwan and China for years, and at one time ran a trading company in China’s Pingtan.
In July 2018, he traveled to Quanzhou, Fujian Province, to attend a cross-strait food trade fair and stayed at a hotel in Xiamen. He checked out the following day and then disappeared. His family had made repeated appeals to the authorities and sought help from Straits Exchange Foundation. It was not until September 2019 that China’s Taiwan Affairs Office confirmed at a press conference that Tsai was under investigation for allegedly “engaging in activities that endanger national security.”
Screen grab from Facebook
Chinese state broadcaster CCTV aired a report on a “Taiwan spy” case in October 2020, in which Tsai appeared on television confessing, saying that he regretted being used by Taiwan’s military intelligence agency to collect information from inside China.
Tsai was sentenced to four years in prison. After completing his sentence, he was barred from leaving China in May 2023 for four years as a deprivation of political rights. He was placed under house arrest on Gulangyu Island in Xiamen.
Regarding Tsai’s Facebook post on Friday saying that he has returned to Taiwan, people familiar with cross-strait affairs said that if his additional sentence was four years, the restriction on leaving China would normally have remained in effect from his release in May 2023.
However, if he has returned to Taiwan it would suggest that he might have been granted early parole.
The Mainland Affairs Council said it was aware of the circumstances surrounding the case, but declined to provide further details, citing the person’s privacy.

Nail polish overuse can lead to ‘green nail syndrome’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:38 UTC
01:43:38 KST

Prolonged use of nail polish, gel polish or artificial nails can create a damp environment that allows bacteria to grow beneath the nail, causing the grayish-green discoloration known as green nail syndrome, said dermatologist Wu Jen-chin (吳仁欽), advising people who frequently get their nails done to periodically give their nails time to rest and breathe.
Nails turning a grayish green might not be a fungal nail infection, Wu said.
One patient who wears gel polish regularly found one of their nails was discolored after having the gel removed and sought medical attention as they were unsure how long the discoloration had been there, he said.
Photo: Screen grab from Wu Jen-chin’s Facebook page
Prolonged use of nail polish, gel polish or artificial nails can create a warm, damp environment beneath the nail, eventually causing the nail to separate from the nail bed, a condition known as onycholysis, Wu said.
Once a gap forms and moisture accumulates, bacteria can infect the area and produce pigments that give the nail a grayish green color, known as green nail syndrome, he said.
Because the patient’s nails were covered by polish, there were no noticeable symptoms and the condition was only discovered after the polish was removed, he added.
Treating the condition requires the patient to keep their nails dry and avoid any nail polish or artificial nails, Wu said.
The patient should trim the part of the nail that has separated from the nail bed to give bacteria less space to accumulate, he said.
In addition, they should undergo local antibacterial treatment, especially for pseudomonas aeruginosa, which is the common cause of green nail syndrome, he said.
If the patient has a simultaneous fungal nail infection, it should be treated at the same time to prevent recurrence, he added.
The discoloration might not disappear immediately, as the nail has to grow naturally to replace the affected part, which can take several months, Wu said.
People who regularly get their nails done should periodically give their nails time to rest and breathe, he said.

Taiwan Travelogue
Non-Taiwanese living in Taiwan would benefit greatly from reading Yang Shuang-zi’s (楊?子) Taiwan Travelogue — and thanks to Lin King (金翎), they can read the translated version in English.
King won the US National Book Award for Translated Literature in 2024 and the International Booker Prize this year for her translated work.
Taiwan Travelogue navigates a story of colonialism, culture and exploration. Each chapter is titled after a Taiwanese dish or ingredient, reflecting the rich culinary tradition that many Taiwanese take great pride in.
However, the story should not only be read to enjoy the motif of cuisine or companionship of the characters. It is set in a period that still affects Taiwan today: Japanese colonization.
Taiwan underwent radical changes in the 20th century, from modernization under Japanese occupation to decades of cruel authoritarian martial law under the then-Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) government, finally blossoming into a young, self-ruling democracy.
Under immense top-down institutional pressure to Japanize and Sinicize, the diversity of languages and cultures in Taiwan survived.
Discourse around Taiwan today is dominated by political factionalism, a potential China contingency and other clickbait topics. These topics are usually what foreign media focus on — and it does not represent daily life in Taiwan faithfully.
Taiwan Travelogue is a refreshing novel, allowing the reader to step back in time to experience Taiwan through the lens of a young Japanese writer and foodie set in the 1930s.
Without proper linguistic and historical knowledge, it is not an easy read, nor should it be.
The English-language version of Taiwan Travelogue uses the Romanization of three languages: Mandarin, Japanese and Tai-gi (Taiwanese, also known as Hoklo).
This creates a dynamic where Taipei is referred to as Taihoku and silver noodle vermicelli is called bi-thai-bak. At first glance, the reader might not recognize what is being referenced. Critics might say that the decision not to use the more recognizable names disenfranchises the reader and makes it less accessible.
In fact, King keeps the context and language as close as possible to the original.
Throughout the book, footnotes from Yang and King support the reader in comprehending the context. I found myself referencing the map provided exclusively in the English-language version as the characters travel around the nation.
It is a multifaceted novel to digest. It challenges the reader with unfamiliarity, and familiarizing oneself with the unfamiliar is a good thing.
This is especially true as a guest in a foreign country.
While Taiwan Travelogue was not necessarily written as an educational resource, it most certainly doubles as a lovely novel and means of learning in greater depth about Taiwanese culture. Taiwanese identity and history are complicated. In no way will this book explain Taiwan in its entirety, but it is a good start.
Elliot Gross
Taipei
Taiwan’s domestic political situation is following recognizable political rhythms, while the international environment surrounding Taiwan is undergoing a major transformation. Within Taiwan, there are ongoing battles between the legislative and executive branches over the budget, and between cities and the central government over resources. Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

China did not lose face: President Xi Jinping (習近平) was an honored guest in India, was endorsed as the chair of BRICS for next year, and China is to host the next summit. Yet the carefully crafted 140-paragraph New Delhi Declaration (NDD), the longest BRICS declaration so far, reveals a subtle, but important shift. BRICS is moving from a loose grouping toward a more substantive platform for the global south, giving developing countries greater voice and bargaining space

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:34 UTC
01:43:34 KST

Continued from yesterday（延續自昨日）
https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/lang
Like espresso, regular coffee is consumed worldwide and plays an important role in many people’s daily routines. Millions of people rely on it for the energy they need to start their day or get through a tiring task. Coffee is typically served in larger portions than espresso, usually around 220 to 250 milliliters, and is often consumed with milk and sugar. However, the differences between the two do not stop there.
Photo: AdobeStock I 照片：AdobeStock
While espresso often uses a dark roast, regular coffee can range from light to medium or dark roasts. Also, because of the brewing method, regular coffee doesn’t have crema. Rather than forcing water through finely ground beans under high pressure, it uses a coarser grind and employs the pour-over or drip method. Both methods require about four to five minutes to allow for gradual extraction. This helps bring out the beans’ natural acidity and floral notes.
Pour-over coffee requires a paper filter and a dripper. Depending on how strong you want it, add one to two tablespoons of ground coffee per 200 milliliters of water. Begin by pouring hot water over the grounds in a slow, circular motion, starting from the center. Drip coffee is even simpler, relying on a machine to automate the brew. Either way, you will quickly taste the distinct characteristic that separates regular coffee from espresso.
和濃縮咖啡一樣，一般咖啡在全球廣泛被飲用，並在許多人的日常習慣中扮演重要角色。數百萬人仰賴咖啡來獲得開始一天或撐過疲憊工作所需的能量。一般咖啡的分量通常比濃縮咖啡大，約為兩百二十到兩百五十毫升，且常會加入牛奶和糖飲用。然而，兩者之間的差異並不止於此。
雖然濃縮咖啡通常使用深焙咖啡豆，但一般咖啡的烘焙程度可以從淺焙到中焙或深焙不等。此外，由於沖煮方式不同，一般咖啡並沒有咖啡脂。它不是在高壓下強行將水沖過磨成細粉的咖啡豆，而是使用較粗的研磨粉，並採用手沖或滴濾的方式。這兩種方法大約需要花四到五分鐘來讓咖啡逐漸萃取。這樣的過程有助於帶出咖啡豆天然的酸質與花香風味。
手沖咖啡需要使用濾紙和濾杯。依照你想要的濃度，每兩百毫升的水可加入一到兩湯匙的咖啡粉。先從中心開始，以緩慢的畫圓方式將熱水倒在咖啡粉上。滴濾咖啡則更簡單，透過機器自動沖煮咖啡。不論採用哪種方式，你很快就能品嚐出讓一般咖啡有別於濃縮咖啡的獨特特徵。
What Did You Learn?
1. Which of the following is true about the difference between espresso and regular coffee?
(A) Espresso uses darker beans, while regular coffee uses lighter roasts.
(B) Espresso relies on machines for speed, while regular coffee is made by hand.
(C) Espresso is served in larger amounts, while regular coffee is usually mixed with milk.
(D) Espresso is brewed under high pressure, while regular coffee is brewed more slowly over time.
2. According to the passage, who is MOST likely to enjoy a regular coffee instead of an espresso?
(A) Martha, who dislikes sour flavors in her drinks.
(B) Julie, who prefers drinks with a simple and familiar taste.
(C) Vincent, who finds bold and concentrated flavors too intense.
(D) Andy, who needs a quick drink before rushing to his next meeting.
答案：1. D 2. C
Words in Use
1. consume vt. 喝；吃
Gary usually consumes a cup of black coffee before starting work.
蓋瑞通常在開始工作前會喝一杯黑咖啡。
2. worldwide adv. 在世界各地
The news quickly spread worldwide through social media platforms.
這則消息透過社群媒體平臺迅速傳遍全球。
3. routine n. 日常工作，例行公事
Carmen follows a simple morning routine that helps her stay organized.
卡門遵循著有助於讓她保持井然有序的簡單早晨習慣。
4. coarse a. 粗糙的
The salt has a coarse texture, which makes it suitable for certain dishes.
這種鹽質地粗糙，適合用於某些料理。
5. drip n. 滴落；滴液
Many people prefer the drip method because it is simple and reliable.
許多人偏好滴漏法，因為它簡單又可靠。
Practical Phrases
1. do not stop / end there 不止於此
The problem does not stop there, since it affects other areas as well.
問題不止於此，因為還會影響其他層面。
2. range from A to B 範圍從 A 到 B 都有
Skills range from simple tasks to advanced techniques in this course.
這門課的技能從簡單任務到進階技巧都有。
3. allow for. . . 使……成為可能
The new system allows for faster communication between team members.
這個新系統讓團隊成員之間溝通可以更快速。
4. bring out. . . 帶出……，使……顯現出來
The spices bring out the flavor of the dish.
香料能帶出這道菜的風味。
5. depending on. . . 取決於……
Depending on how many times the tasks are done, the outcomes may differ slightly.
視任務執行的次數而定，結果可能會稍微有所差異。

Carney and the politics of selective principles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:34 UTC
01:43:34 KST

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney gave an impressive speech to the European Parliament on Thursday. Elegant, thoughtful and rich in historical imagery, it began with Goethe and Buchenwald, traveled through Vimy Ridge, and ended with Canada and Europe growing a transatlantic forest together.
Underneath the poetry was a sensible economic argument. Canada is too dependent on the US. The weaponization of trade has exposed the danger of relying excessively on one market.
Canada should diversify, and Europe — with its vast market, technological capabilities and broadly compatible political system — is an obvious partner.
Carney spoke of sovereignty, territorial integrity, democracy, human dignity and individual freedom. Economic integration, he warned, is being weaponized; tariffs and financial mechanisms are being used for coercion; and supply chains have become vulnerabilities. Canada and Europe should build resilience together because they share fundamental values.
However, only eight months ago, Carney was in Beijing announcing a new “strategic partnership” with China, explicitly presenting deeper engagement as part of Canada’s effort to diversify its trade and reduce excessive dependence on its largest trading partner.
There is nothing inherently wrong with Canada trading with China. However, if economic dependence creates vulnerability, and if governments should guard against countries that weaponize trade, China cannot somehow disappear from the analysis.
After Lithuania allowed a representative office bearing the name “Taiwanese” to open in Vilnius, Lithuanian goods began encountering difficulties entering China. The EU later brought a WTO case alleging discriminatory and coercive measures, including customs rejections and restrictions on products containing Lithuanian components. China subsequently imposed import bans on Lithuanian alcohol, beef and dairy products using phytosanitary justifications that, according to the European Commission, China failed to substantiate. Lithuanian exports to China fell dramatically.
Days before Carney’s in Europe speech, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) attended the European Conference for Freedom and Democracy in Ventotene, Italy. Her participation had been kept confidential beforehand. After it became known, the European Commission withdrew its logo from the conference and canceled the participation of its scheduled representative. European Parliament Vice President Pina Picierno publicly linked the commission’s decision to Chinese complaints, while the commission declined to confirm that Hsiao’s presence was the reason.
Days later, Carney stood before the European Parliament declaring that democracies must protect their sovereignty, resist coercion and defend their shared values. “Freedom must be earned ‘every single day,’” Carney said emphatically.
The problem is not that Canada should refuse to trade with China, nor that Europe should confront Beijing at every opportunity. Diplomacy requires pragmatism.
The problem arises when democratic values are presented as fundamental principles against one powerful country, but become more flexible when another powerful country applies pressure.
Carney is right that excessive dependence creates vulnerability, that democracies need resilience and that sovereignty means retaining the ability to make one’s own choices. However, those principles need to survive contact with Beijing as well as Washington, otherwise they are not really principles.
They are just very good speeches.
John Cheng is a retired businessman from Hong Kong living in Taiwan.

Kuai Kuai union is strike-ready
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:34 UTC
01:43:34 KST

Members of Kuai Kuai Co’s Jhongli Plant Union yesterday voted to authorize a strike if called for after the company’s closure of a major factory triggered sweeping layoff fears and dissatisfaction over wages.
The namesake manufacturer of the famous snacks — the green-bagged snacks workers often place on computers and servers as good luck charms — sold its factory in Taoyuan’s Jhongli District (中壢) on July 30 to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc (ASE) for redevelopment.
In response, 158 members of the Jhongli Plant Union yesterday passed a motion to consider striking in protest of the move to and demand that the company make written guarantees on severance packages and pay raises.
Photo courtesy of the union
The membership passed the proposition with 149 “yes” votes, two “no” votes and two abstentions, enabling the union to strike if its demands for wage hikes are not met.
A union spokesperson said the vote reflects worker dissatisfaction with the breakdown of negotiations on Wednesday, following the corporation’s refusal of demands in writing.
During a protest in Taipei on Monday, union president Liu Neng-fa (劉能發) said that Kuai Kuai Co did not inform workers of its land deal with the ASE group beforehand and they received only spoken guarantees that they would be relocated to a new facility in Hsinchu.
The sale of the property netted the company NT$5.6 billion (US$176.1 million), none of which benefits its workers, more than one-third of whom have worked for three decades or more for near-minimum pay, he said.
The company only revealed the factory’s relocation on Sept. 1 and announced a 5 percent increase in pay, which Liu said only kept pace with the government-announced legal changes to the minimum wage.
The union proposed that Kuai Kuai share part of its artificial intelligence windfalls with assembly-line workers, prioritizing those with seniority, and increase the monthly salaries of all workers by NT$10,000, Liu said.
The company said yesterday it respects the resolution passed at the union meeting, but regrets their decision.
It said it had held multiple rounds of discussions with the union to explain its position.
The company said it is continuing to negotiate the two proposals for compensation and preferential severance packages following the plant’s relocation with union representatives.
Barring any major changes, the two sides are expected to meet again this week to discuss the matter.
The Taoyuan Department of Labor said officials are monitoring the situation with an eye on arbitrating a mutually acceptable solution.
The company’s offer should respect the years of service of the workers and secure the livelihoods their labor had earned, it said.

Marchers seek to solve stray problem
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:33 UTC
01:43:33 KST

The Walk for Wildlife Association yesterday in Taipei held a march urging the government to incorporate ecological governance into free-roaming animal management schemes to curb conflicts between strays and wildlife.
Association president Lee Tsung-chen (李宗宸) said this year’s march has four demands:
First, push for legislation for free-roaming animal management to reduce ecological conflicts.
Photo courtesy of the Walk for Wildlife Association
Second, to establish a scientific evaluation mechanism based on conflicts between wildlife and stray animals.
Third, to improve the animal shelter and relocation system to reduce the number of stray animal.
Fourth, to establish a biodiversity governance mechanism with clearly defined authority and responsibility to bridge the ecological governance gap.
The fourth demand is the most important, as many free-roaming animal issues originated from poor management by humans, Lee said.
With the ecological impacts caused by strays and their own animal welfare in mind, stray management should shift from a trap-neuter-return approach to a trap-neuter-shelter-adopt approach, he said.
“Let dogs and cats return to environments with proper care by humans, reducing the threat they pose to wildlife,” Lee said.
Policy effectiveness should translate into improvement levels instead of “what has been done,” Lee said.
The government usually points to the number of stray animals they have captured or sterilized, but whether such approaches improved the situations of people, strays and wildlife remains questionable, he said.
Chuang Chao (莊喬), who took part in the march, said he lives near a graveyard in New Taipei City’s Sindian District (新店) and has long suffered from loud barking by packs of stray dogs that frequent the area, drawn by food that well-intentioned residents leave out.
The barking disrupted his sleep for days, Chuang said, adding that over the past few years, he has talked with about 10 people who had fed stray dogs in the region.
“I chatted with all of them and asked how many dogs they knew, whether they understood the dogs’ situations, and what their next step or plan is for the dogs,” Chuang said.
While there used to be almost 30 free-roaming dogs around the graveyard, it is down to about seven due to Chuang’s communication with those feeding the dogs, he said.
Chuang said sterilization and a feeding ban on strays could help address the issue of free-roaming animals.
“What matters most is to apply strategies tailored to local conditions and start by changing people’s behavior,” he said.
Another marcher, Anrou Hu (胡安柔), said she has long been concerned about wildlife conservation, adding that she used to keep cats, rabbits and green iguana as pets.
“It’s a shame that such household pets got involved in conflicts with people or other animals simply because they wandered off or were abandoned,” Hu said.
Wild at Heart executive director Chen Hsien-cheng (陳憲政) said he is concerned about wildlife habitat protection, particularly where human development undermines natural habitats.
Coastal energy development projects are threatening Taiwanese humpback dolphins, while water diversion engineering could dry up Taitung County’s Jhihben wetlands and drive away local waterbirds, Chen said.
Protected wildlife populations such as humpback dolphins could dwindle with disappearing habitats, he said, adding that such losses might be irreversible or require high restoration costs.
Proper ecological impact assessments should be done prior to development, he added.
March lead organizer Chuang Po-jun (莊博鈞) said other issues, such as roadkill and habitat fragmentation or degradation are as important as free-roaming animals in terms of wildlife protection. However, most people are less aware of threats posed by stray animals, he said.
“People knew that clearing a forest would destroy wildlife’s homes, but they might not imagine how much unattended cats or dogs could harm other animals in the wild,” he said, adding participants could explore many other ecological issues at the event’s stalls.
The association said about 3,000 people participated in the march.

Nuclear referendum debate to be televised
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:30 UTC
01:43:30 KST

Five televised forums or debates on a referendum about whether to abolish Taiwan’s policy of creating a “nuclear-free homeland” are to begin on Nov. 12, the Central Election Commission (CEC) announced on Friday.
The referendum asks whether voters support the government using nuclear power to boost Taiwan’s economy and abolishing its “nuclear-free homeland” policy, the CEC said.
The referendum question was put forward by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and supported by the Taiwan People’s Party.
Photo: Taipei Times
The two parties hold a majority of seats in the Legislature.
In order to ensure both sides have an opportunity to present their views, the CEC said it decided on Friday to hold five forums or debates on nationwide television.
The Legislative Yuan would represent the side supporting the referendum, while the Executive Yuan or those opposing it would represent the other side.
The five sessions are to be held during the following dates and times: 3pm on Nov. 12, 7pm on Nov. 14, 3pm on Nov. 16, 10am on Nov. 18 and 7pm on Nov. 20.
People seeking to represent either side at the forums or debates must first obtain CEC approval to establish an office under Article 20 of the Referendum Act (公民投票法).
Both sides must submit the names of their representatives to the CEC by Oct. 15.
The referendum would be held alongside Taiwan’s nine-in-one local elections on Nov. 28, when voters would elect city and county leaders, local councilors and other local officials.
The referendum would be Taiwan’s fourth on nuclear power since 2018.
Voters in 2018 backed removing a legal requirement to end nuclear power generation by last year.
However, in 2021 and last year they rejected referendums to complete Taiwan’s mothballed Fourth Nuclear Power Plant and extend the operation of the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant.

16:43:26 UTC

US President Donald Trump on Friday said he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington “permanent control” over Greenland’s security that would bar Russia and China from setting up bases in the Arctic territory.
Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
Denmark and Greenland — an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen — both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week.
Photo: AP
However, the terms of the deal remain uncertain, and Denmark maintains its sovereignty remains intact.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the deal as “an agreement which at the same time recognizes the sovereignty an territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination.”
“I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland,” Trump said on his Truth Social network. “From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval.”
The 80-year-old said it was an “‘Infinite Life’ Agreement, there is no end!” and that Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory.
Trump has repeatedly warned about Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland as a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic unfolds, and the US Department of State left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so.
“This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors,” a state department official said.
At the Davos economic forum in January, Trump reached a purported deal with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte over the future of Greenland, the terms of which have remained vague.
Frederiksen had said that she was “optimistic” that ongoing discussions with the US and Greenland since January could resolve the dispute.
She said she was “pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States,” adding that it was “good for NATO and Europe.”
Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the US “strengthens” the territory’s security.
Trump gave no details about how the deal would work, and it was not clear if it was linked to or substantially different from the Rutte deal.
Several media outlets have reported that the US wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.

Breadcrumb
Iran executes man accused of providing missile info to Israel
Iran's judiciary announced on Saturday the execution of a man accused of providing information about Iranian missile sites to Israeli intelligence.
"The death penalty was carried out against Hossein Pedaran, who had provided the Mossad with information on missile sites in Isfahan province" in central Iran, judicial authorities said, without saying when he was arrested or put on trial.
Pedaran had faced accusations of "espionage and intelligence collaboration" in favour of Israel.
The judiciary said his sentence had been upheld by the supreme court.
The case had not previously been reported by the media.
Iranian authorities have escalated arrests and executions both in connection with the Middle East war that began in February and the nationwide protests that peaked in January.
Throughout the war, numerous missile sites have been bombed. Supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed at the start of the war.
Isfahan province, which hosts Iranian nuclear sites, has been one of the hardest hit throughout the war.
In August, the judiciary announced the execution of two men accused of having "transmitted the coordinates of sensitive military and security sites" to Israel.
Iran carries out the second highest number of executions in the world after China, according to rights groups.

Who should bear responsibility for Nepal’s tragedy?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:25 UTC
01:43:25 KST

In the wake of Nepal’s devastating floods, which killed at least 1,300 people, Nepalese officials and others were quick to cite climate change as the primary cause. They were not wrong. The Hindu Kush Himalayas are warming roughly three times faster than the global average, even though Nepal produces only 0.1 percent of global greenhouse-gas emissions. However, climate change alone does not explain why so many people and so much vital infrastructure were directly exposed to a known hazard.
The catastrophic damage was as much the result of a failure to account for location and risk as it was an effect of climate disaster. Climate risks were privatized when infrastructure projects were approved and socialized when things went wrong. While businesses and political insiders benefited from hydropower concessions, road contracts and floodplain development, households and workers bore the consequences when those assets were swept away.
The warning signs were there. The 2021 Melamchi flood in Sindhupalchowk District began with heavy rain and an upstream blockage, then swept an enormous amount of sediment downstream, burying the headworks of Kathmandu’s flagship water project under 15 to 20 meters of debris. Five years later, water and debris tore through the Trishuli Valley, where infrastructure projects had been assessed one at a time rather than as part of a single system.
Four development failures made the disaster worse.
The first is slope destruction in the name of connectivity, which Nepalese have come to call “bulldozer terrorism.” Politically driven and poorly engineered road cuts have left nearby slopes twice as prone to landslides, which were then blamed on the monsoon.
Hydropower hubris is another failure. Although reviews of the impact of the 216MW Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project on the river had said that climate risks had not been adequately assessed, those warnings were ignored. So were the risks of building bazaars, customs yards and worker camps along historic riverbeds.
These dangers are compounded by the Himalayas’ growing instability as retreating glaciers leave behind glacial lakes and weakened rock layers. While climate change increases the risk of glacial collapse, the extent of the damage ultimately depends on what gets built and where.
Nepal does not need to stop building, but it does need to stop pushing development into its river corridors. New projects should face a worst-case flood test, and the most exposed communities should be relocated rather than rebuilt in the same flood-prone areas. As former British prime minister Gordon Brown has argued, Nepal must rethink where it puts schools and critical infrastructure. Its solar potential is far greater than its hydropower capacity, much of which was wiped out in a single morning.
Nepal’s development failures do not absolve the countries that are most responsible for global warming. Nepal’s petition for US$20 million in compensation is the first real emergency test of the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD), established at COP27 in Egypt in recognition of the fact that poor countries are increasingly stuck paying for climate damage they did not cause.
With about US$822 million pledged, the FRLD has nowhere near enough money to meet the demand. So far, developing countries have submitted 176 requests for US$2.8 billion. The first funding window, known as the Barbados Implementation Modalities, set aside just US$250 million for grants of US$5 million to US$20 million. Nepal’s request for US$20 million reflects the program’s ceiling, not the scale of the country’s losses. In fact, reconstruction is projected to cost up to US$5 billion — one-tenth of Nepal’s GDP.
The FRLD is slow. Its 11-step cycle may make sense for multiyear programs, but not for a country whose trade routes and payment infrastructure have just been destroyed. And as Liane Schalatek has observed, if the fund shields donor countries from liability, it could act as an alibi rather than a genuine burden-sharing mechanism.
Nepal’s government is asking the fund to act outside its normal funding cycle. This month, Prime Minister Balendra Shah plans to press the case before the UN General Assembly, while board members representing African, Asia-Pacific and least-developed countries have called for an emergency meeting.
Pre-arranged disaster-risk finance can help absorb the initial shock, but someone must ultimately pay for the damage caused by climate catastrophes. If the FRLD cannot pay when disaster strikes, countries have to fill the gap by borrowing, pushing them into the climate-debt trap. The 2022 floods in Pakistan, for example, killed more than 1,000 people and forced the country to borrow more to cover US$30 billion in reconstruction costs.
When climate-related disasters hit communities made vulnerable by reckless development along flood-prone rivers, the cost should not simply be passed on to displaced households or piled onto sovereign debt. Without stricter zoning laws and immediate grant financing in place when disaster strikes, developing countries such as Nepal remain hostage to a warming planet and a climate-financing system that delivers too little, too late.
Nischal Dhungel is a fellow at the Nepal Institute for Policy Research.
Copyright: Project Syndicate

Firefighters could be seen trying to extinguish the flames of a burnt-out fuel tank emblazoned with the logo of the Saudi Arabian oil giant Aramco near the airport.
FlightRadar24 reported “major problems” at the Riyadh King Khalid International Airport, listing it under its maximum disruption index.
Photo: AFP
The disruption follows an overnight air raid alert issued by Saudi authorities, the first since fighting in neighboring Yemen intensified this month.
Hours after the early morning alert, residents said on condition of anonymity that they heard what sounded like another round of explosions echoing through parts of the capital.
“In the direction of the airport, we saw black smoke and fire,” one resident said.
This is the first time since Yemen’s long-standing civil war resumed that it has threatened the Saudi Arabian capital, further shaking a global economy already under pressure by nearly seven months of war between the US and Iran.
“The area is under a hostile aerial threat,” according to a message received by Riyadh residents, urging them to stay indoors.
Journalists heard two explosions, before the Saudi Arabian civil defense agency lifted the alert half an hour later.
“I heard the alarm, then my windows shook,” a Riyadh resident said. “It was definitely scary. I was not expecting this.”
Another resident described the attack as “terrifying.”
“I was extremely anxious — especially because, unlike previous times, the ‘all-clear’ signal didn’t come right away,” they said.
Saudi Arabia has not commented on the threat mentioned in the warnings sent overnight to residents of several regions and has not identified where it originated from.
The incident comes days after Riyadh accused the Houthis of targeting Mecca on Wednesday, denouncing it as a “cowardly terrorist attack” on Islam’s holy city, which welcomes millions of pilgrims each year.
The Iran-backed Houthis strongly denied the accusation, calling it a “worn-out lie.”

Allies send joint letter to UN in support of Taiwan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:22 UTC
01:43:22 KST

Representatives to the UN from five of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies sent a joint letter to UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on Friday, calling for the country’s inclusion in the body.
Allies in the letter sent ahead of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly General Debate made three demands in support of Taiwan: inclusion, recognition and camaraderie.
They implored the UN to seek an appropriate way to facilitate Taiwan’s meaningful involvement in the world governing body, saying that UN Resolution 2758, which accepted the People’s Republic of China (PRC) as a member of the UN, does not exclude Taiwan.
Photo: AP
Beijing claims that the resolution “confirmed” its “one China” principle, while Taiwan says the resolution only addressed the issue of China’s representation at the UN and did not mention Taiwan, nor did it address its political status or establish China’s sovereignty over Taiwan.
Taiwan’s allies’ second demand was for the body to recognize the nation’s contribution to cross-strait peace through its efforts in maintaining the “status quo.”
Cross-strait peace is a crucial element in world peace and prosperity, they said.
Photo courtesy of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in New York via CNA
The third called on the UN to stick to its principles and work with member nations in preventing military conflict and promoting the peaceful resolution of disputes.
The joint letter was addressed to Guterres and accepted by Guterres’ Chef de Cabinet Earle Courtenay Rattray.
Permanent Representatives to the UN Ilana Seid of Palau, Menissa Rambally of Saint Lucia, John Silk of the Marshall Islands, Janine Coye-Felson of Belize, and Vynnette Frederick of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines wrote the joint letter.
In a separate statement, Lee Chih-chiang (李志強), who heads the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in New York, thanked Taiwan’s allies for taking action to express their strong support for the country’s participation in the UN.
The UN must find ways to include Taiwan, so that the country can contribute to initiatives such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals, Lee said.
The inclusion of Taiwan is crucial to the UN fulfilling its theme for the debate of the 81st General Assembly: “Restoring trust, managing transformation: A United Nations that delivers for all,” Lee added.
The General Assembly began on Monday last week, with the high-level General Debate running from Tuesday next week to Sept. 28, at the UN headquarters in New York City.

South Sudan joins ban list with first ASF outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:21 UTC
01:43:21 KST

The Central Emergency Operations Center for African Swine Fever (ASF) yesterday cautioned against importing food that contain pork following South Sudan’s first confirmed ASF case occurring last month.
The World Organisation for Animal Health reported the ASF case on its official Web site in the afternoon on Friday, the center said.
The case was detected on July 18 in samples collected from a pig farm in Yambio, South Sudan, the first ASF case in the African country, it said.
Photo: Taipei Times
Taiwan has no records of living pigs or pork products imported from South Sudan, as the Ministry of Agriculture has not confirmed South Sudan to be free of ASF, foot-and-mouth disease or classical swine fever — the three major swine diseases — the center said.
There are no direct flights or mail service between South Sudan and Taiwan either, it said.
The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Agency yesterday said it listed South Sudan as a high-risk ASF country yesterday, and one that has had ASF cases in the past three years.
The agency has asked all border quarantine authorities to tighten quarantine measures, it said, adding it would continue to clamp down on illegally imported pork products based on the “zero tolerance” principle.
The center called on the public not to carry pork products or import them by mail or express delivery from ASF epidemic countries or regions to Taiwan, particularly ahead of the upcoming Mid-Autumn Festival.
There were travelers detained at customs for illegally bringing mooncakes containing pork into Taiwan, it said.
Those who illegally import pork products to Taiwan would be fined NT$200,000 (US$6,287) for the first time and NT$1 million for each repeat offense, the center said.
Taiwan has maintained its self-declared ASF-free status since April 6, it said.
Taiwan is the only country in Asia that is free of the three major swine diseases, the center said, calling on people to abide by quarantine rules to safeguard Taiwan’s livestock industry.

EDITORIAL: Whose history is it, anyway?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:21 UTC
01:43:21 KST

Academia Historica director Chen Tsui-lien (陳翠蓮), speaking at the handover ceremony for her new role on Monday, said that when she accepted the position, she knew that her peaceful life as a history professor was a thing of the past, and that from now on she would have to “wear a helmet.”
A specialist in Taiwan’s post-World War II history and the 228 Incident, she has been accused of being politically divisive. A phrase she used in her acceptance speech set headlines alight this week, putting her in the sights of editorials in blue-leaning media.
She said opposition figures calling for a “dangwai (outside the party) alliance” were appropriating the language of the democratic movement that opposed to the past authoritarian Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) regime.
Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕), who had called for an “opposition alliance,” was particularly angered. She said that an opposition alliance was a perfectly appropriate aspect of democratic politics, and objected to the use of the term dangwai.
It is important to understand the political and historical context of the term. It runs to the very core of why Chen’s appointment is contentious, and why she will to need that helmet.
“Dangwai” refers to the opposition against the KMT regime during the period of martial law when opposition parties were forbidden. The movement gave rise to the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
When President William Lai (賴清德) originally approached Chen about taking on the role in June, he asked her why it is that, three decades into the democratic era, divisions run so deep, and why so many Taiwanese are still unaware of their own history, still believing the account written under the political indoctrination of the authoritarian era.
Her academic expertise aside, Chen brings personal experience to the tensions between historical subjectivity and indoctrination. In an article titled “Life Under Martial Law: The Miseducation of a Party-State Youth” published in The Reporter in July 2017, Chen related her experiences of growing up under martial law, how she had been indoctrinated by the education system into a form of personality cult of Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石) and how she had fully bought into the authoritarian regime’s version of history.
It was only following the 1979 Formosa Incident, also known as the Kaohsiung Incident, when authorities cracked down on members of the dangwai movement, leading to the murder of the mother and two daughters of democracy activist Lin Yi-hsiung (林義雄), that she began to doubt what she had been taught, she said.
Historical truth is crucial. Chen setting her goal as the promotion of Taiwanese history from a Taiwanese perspective is to be applauded. Unfortunately, her replacement of Lu’s term “opposition alliance” with “dangwai alliance” has opened her to accusations of partisanism, because it implicitly equates the targets of her criticism with any party that is not Lai’s DPP. While Chen criticizes the extreme partisanship of the KMT and the Taiwan People’s Party and their accusations of authoritarism against Lai and the DPP, her comment has given, in the opposition’s eyes, the very justifications that she wishes to dispel.
Editorials in blue-leaning newspapers are already making allusions to George Orwell’s Party slogan from the novel Nineteen Eighty-Four that “who controls the past controls the future. Who controls the present controls the past,” or accusing Chen of wanting to exclusively preside over the historical account of a political party.
Academia Historica was established in Nanjing, China, in 1947 and relocated to Taiwan in 1957. The official Web site says that it is “dedicated to researching and preserving the rich heritage of the nation’s and Taiwan’s history,” making a distinction between the two.
One of the editorials said that Academia Historica is the archive of the Republic of China, and not a “Taiwanese independence propaganda mill.” It asksed: When Chen thinks of “national history,” which country’s history is it, anyway?
None of this makes sense without understanding the unique nature of a country that has yet to adequately undergo the process of transitional justice. However, at least it is the question Lai posed when he approached her for the role.

Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. Beijing drone owners rush to sell them before ban
Unknown

2026-09-19

01:43:18 KST

Drone owners in Beijing flocked to designated buy-back sites this week, looking to sell their devices for as much as possible ahead of an impending citywide ban.
New rules in the Chinese capital ban not just the flying of uncrewed aerial vehicles, but the possession or storage of them, meaning owners have until Nov. 15 to get rid of their drones.
At several authorized buyer sites across the city, people were waiting for staff to appraise their drones and negotiate prices.
Photo: AFP
All sites had a visible police presence, indicating the sensitivity of the new laws.
At the flagship store for the world’s largest drone maker, DJI, in Beijing’s business district, about a dozen people queued on Thursday morning hoping to sell their drones back for a reasonable price.
Users can sell devices at approved buy-back points and receive a government subsidy of 30 percent of the resale value — up to a maximum of 3,000 yuan (US$447.9) — before Oct. 31, and of 15 percent until Nov. 14.
Alternatively, they can recycle them for a subsidy of 200 yuan, or ship them out of Beijing free of charge.
“I think [the ban] is reasonable. I can understand why the government wants to ensure safety and manage the airspace,” a drone owner surnamed Wu said.
“After all, Beijing is the capital,” said Wu, who bought his drone six years ago for about 6,000 yuan.
He was hoping to get at least 1,000 yuan for the sale, which was what he had been given as a preliminary estimate on the official reselling app.
Some were not satisfied.
Zhu, who called himself a drone hobbyist, said the buy-back scheme was “robbery.”
“It’s made me lose a lot of money. This is my private property,” he said, adding that he had sold five drones back, losing thousands on the original prices.
Airspace safety fears were raised in June when a light aircraft smashed into Beijing’s tallest building, killing the pilot and injuring 13 others — as well as briefly disrupting the flight path into one of the capital’s international airports.
The incident, which was heavily censored, seems to have unsettled Beijing authorities, happening just a few kilometers from the seat of the Chinese government.
Beijing cited a need to “safeguard the security of the capital” when it announced the complete ban on drone possession inside the city.
There were 3.285 million drones registered nationwide at the end of last year, China’s Civil Aviation Administration said, but it is not necessary to register drone ownership in most of the country.
Online, many Beijingers posted farewells to their drone collections.
“There’s nothing I can do, thanks for your company,” one user wrote on Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote. “I hope you can keep roaming the skies in the future.”

Drugmakers eye next phase of space research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:18 UTC
01:43:18 KST

As the International Space Station (ISS) nears the end of its operational life, drugmakers are laying the groundwork for commercial pharmaceutical research and manufacturing in low Earth orbit while working with regulators to establish rules for producing medicines in space.
Pharmaceutical, biotechnology and space company executives told reporters they are working to demonstrate that such manufacturing outside the bounds of Earth can be done reliably and inexpensively.
Researchers have long studied how microgravity allows for appropriate distribution of cells and particles in biological materials that is difficult to reproduce on Earth.
Photo: Reuters / NASA / Roscosmos / Handout
LambdaVision, for example, is using microgravity to design an artificial retinal implant in which proteins and polymers must be layered carefully onto a scaffold. It has completed nine ISS missions since 2018 and hopes to begin clinical trials in 2028.
BIOPRINTER
Auxilium Biotechnologies has successfully used its 3D bioprinter aboard the ISS to manufacture structures containing human liver, kidney and cartilage cells.
Auxilium vice president of engineering Isac Lazarovits said the company sees this as a step toward production of transplantable tissues in orbit.
Merck collaborated on ISS research that informed the development of a subcutaneous formulation of its top-selling cancer immunotherapy Keytruda, providing a faster, more convenient alternative to intravenous infusion.
Such work has largely depended on the ISS, where laboratory space, astronaut time and return flights are scarce, creating bottlenecks. Experiments can take months or years to repeat, slowing refinement of manufacturing techniques.
The ISS operates more as a “test kitchen,” ISS National Lab chief scientist Michael Roberts said. “It’s not an environment that was built for the ability to scale these experiments.”
That is changing as NASA prepares to retire the ISS by the end of the decade.
Next-generation commercial stations are being designed with scalability in mind, enabling companies to increase production volumes and potentially do so at significantly lower cost than on the ISS, Roberts said.
Ariel Ekblaw, chief executive officer of the Aurelia Institute, a space architecture research institute, agreed that growth of commercial orbital infrastructure could make routine pharmaceutical research and manufacturing more economically viable.
Auxilium has signed agreements with companies developing orbital platforms expected to operate after the ISS retires.
Starlab, Vast and Axiom Space are developing privately operated stations, while Varda Space Industries is building autonomous capsules designed to process materials in orbit and return them to Earth.
Companies say the new platforms could provide more frequent access, dedicated manufacturing equipment and greater commercial flexibility.
Orbital laboratories tailored to the industry’s needs could incorporate more automation, dedicated manufacturing areas, specialized crew training and more predictable launch and return schedules, a spokesperson for Bristol Myers Squibb told reporters.
Regulators have yet to establish a dedicated pathway to ensure products manufactured in orbit meet the same standards as those produced on land.
Max Haot, CEO of commercial space station developer Vast, said the lack of a defined regulatory process could be a more persistent obstacle than transportation.
The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and NASA signed a memorandum of understanding in 2018 covering biomedical research and product development during space missions, but have not created a framework for regulating and approving the fruits of such work.
The British Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Agency in March said it would work with the British Space Agency to develop guidance for medicines manufactured in space.
It expects to publish its roadmap later this year, potentially making it the first major regulator to outline a formal approval pathway.
The FDA did not respond to requests for comment.
RETURN LIMIT
Launching payloads has become easier as the commercial rocket industry has expanded, but returning them on predictable schedules remains a challenge.
Executives say return capacity is a larger bottleneck than launch availability because companies often cannot design the next experiment without results of the previous one.
Commercial stations could allow developers to run several experiments across different platforms rather than waiting months between individual missions, industry executives said.
Starlab’s chief scientist, Luis Zea, said it plans to allow companies to rent laboratory capacity and use shared equipment rather than build their own orbital infrastructure.
The ISS laid the groundwork for a future low Earth orbit economy by giving scientists continuous access to a microgravity laboratory and the ability to gather data over long periods, Roberts said.
“We’re looking forward to seeing at least an order of magnitude leap in those capabilities as we move to the commercial platforms,” he added.

====================================================================================================

AI could reverse political polarization with  probability-based centrism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:14 UTC
01:43:14 KST

Political polarization has become so extreme that when Democrats and Republicans find common ground on a single issue — like their shared hatred of AI data centers — it becomes major news.
Those data centers could also be mending the nation’s political divisions. The large language models people increasingly use are far from benign, but they are quietly — if unintentionally — promoting consensus in how and what the public learns about the world. For better or worse.
It seems impossible to think that such a thing could happen. Research and commentary dedicated to analyzing today’s fragmented media ecosystem have made it seem like people have reached the point of no return. Looking back at the roots of extreme political polarization underscores why the time might be ripe for a reversal of that trend.
Illustration: Tania Chou
An ever-shrinking overlap between the two major parties began in the 1970s, but it intensified in the 1990s and beyond. Why that happened is the subject of longstanding debate, but one particularly compelling explanation traces the shift back to evolutions in the media landscape during that same period.
The rise of radio and television broadcasting resulted in a handful of stations and networks catering to a mass audience in the 1950s and 1960s. That meant the average person got much of the same information, even if there might be slight variations between outlets.
That era had legendary anchors like Walter Cronkite, who presided over CBS Evening News, building a brand based on overt neutrality. Such was the faith in this kind of media figure that Cronkite typically closed his broadcasts with a catchphrase: “And that’s the way it is” — as if there was no other version of the truth. This was problematic in that it tended to oversimplify reality, banishing dissident voices to the margins. As an antidote to polarization, it proved quite effective.
That manufactured reality fell apart in the 1970s, with the rise of cable television. Congress effectively removed barriers to entry in 1984 with the Cable Act, which allowed the number of cable networks to explode. Instead of three or four broadcast networks, Americans could seek out channels that suited their particular political and cultural sensibilities. By 1998, the US had 174 different national cable networks — it was 82 just six years earlier — along with thousands of local stations.
The rise of the internet only accelerated these trends, giving everyone with access to a computer the ability to go down various rabbit holes. The resulting amplification of conspiracy theories and other fringe ideas was bad enough before social media effectively obliterated any vestiges of a national common ground. Different platforms gave rise to a collection of adversarial digital tribes living in their separate realities.
Consensus and moderation prevailed when citizens relied on a highly centralized and homogenous group of media outlets. When that system was replaced by a multiplicity of outlets and sources, polarization intensified to dangerous levels.
Enter AI. Critics have said that the technology’s chatbots and models could sow disinformation, fueling polarization. Yet there is some evidence to suggest a different outcome.
People rely on the Internet for information. In the past, someone might Google a particular topic and then spend a long time clicking through links, searching for results that interested them or perhaps resonated with their own biases. Or they might turn to their social media connections, amplifying their own prejudices.
AI has upended that system. Increasingly, people are looking at what has been described as a “zero-click” future, where someone posing a query instead accepts an AI summary rather than exploring the cacophony of the internet. Or AI is relied on more directly, as when people pose questions to chatbots, which many often trust as much as, if not more than, other humans.
These developments represent a return to the spirit, if not the reality, of broadcast networks and moderating voices. This is inevitable, given the way that AI works.
Models are trained on vast collections of information in order to generate words and phrases. As such, they are probability machines, producing the likeliest answer based on training data. This means that chatbots and AI-generated search results tend to move to the middle, distilling an otherwise invisible consensus about any given issue. Answers come across as a reassuring, neutral and believable summary that comes across as the objective truth. Something like a digital Walter Cronkite. Little wonder that, even as Americans tell pollsters that they do not trust the “media,” they increasingly turn to AI for information.
A hint of where we could be going was captured in a report on election disinformation from the Brennan Center for Justice. It found that AI chatbots, far from amplifying fringe theories of election fraud, did the opposite, gently pushing back on these claims and banishing them. A study published in the Journal of Computer-Mediated Communication found that individuals who interact with chatbots about political issues tended to moderate their views.
That is all well and good, but we should not forget that AI models have a built-in bias toward conventional wisdom, not minority or fringe points of view. The public has been so conditioned to associate “fringe” with bad that we might forget those views can lead to a more equitable society. Many civil rights that we now regard as essential began as ideas far outside the mainstream.
As our reliance on AI grows, a decades-long drift toward polarization might reverse. The resulting consensus could come at a cost: a new kind of groupthink that is no less dangerous for democracy than the polarization it replaces.
Stephen Mihm, associate dean and professor of history at the University of Georgia, is coauthor of Crisis Economics: A Crash Course in the Future of Finance.This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

Stabilize prices, protect livelihoods
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:12 UTC
01:43:12 KST

Escalating tensions in the Middle East have led to a rise in international oil prices, causing inflationary pressures to resurface. The Executive Yuan’s price stabilization task force has decided to extend tax reduction measures for key raw materials through the end of March next year and continue stabilizing oil, natural gas and petroleum prices. The government is right to intervene and stabilize prices at this time, because for ordinary households, the most immediate economic indicator is not GDP growth, but how much their money can buy.
The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics reported that the consumer price index last month rose 2.04 percent from a year earlier. While that figure might not seem alarming, the producer price index — a measure of prices received by producers — surged 16.75 percent, while import prices denominated in US dollars increased by an even steeper 20.45 percent. Rising upstream costs would eventually filter down to consumers, so stabilizing prices of energy and raw materials is building a firewall against higher living costs in the future.
As the saying goes, “first fill your belly, then worship Buddha” (先顧腹肚，再顧佛祖). Rice, cooking oil, salt, rent and utility bills are everyday realities faced by ordinary people. When wages fail to keep up with prices, real purchasing power shrinks. For low-income families, increases in the cost of a bento box, cooking gas and transportation fees can add up to a heavy financial burden.
Taiwan is simultaneously facing low birthrates, an aging population and high housing prices. Many young people worry that little would be left of their salaries after paying rent and living expenses. When even making ends meet requires careful budgeting, how can they be expected to plan for marriage and children? Stabilizing prices might look like economic policy, but it is also population and social policy.
Stabilizing prices also requires addressing wages. This year, the minimum monthly salary was NT$29,500, while the minimum hourly wage was NT$196. The review of next year’s minimum wage is also set to begin soon, with the monthly rate expected to surpass the NT$30,000 mark for the first time. Increasing the minimum wage is a necessary step, but the ability of small and medium-sized enterprises to absorb higher labor costs should also be taken into account. The government, employers and workers should engage in thorough dialogue to ensure that economic gains are fairly reflected in workers’ incomes while preventing the costs from immediately being passed on to consumers.
For vulnerable households hit hardest by rising prices, the government should provide targeted support through social welfare assistance and housing subsidies. Focusing resources on those who genuinely need them is the best way to ensure that every dollar of public spending is used to its maximum effect.
We might not be able to control international conflicts or fluctuating oil prices, but the government can strive to mitigate external shocks, stabilize domestic prices and safeguard the public’s purchasing power.
Maintaining stable prices means maintaining people’s livelihoods, and protecting people’s livelihoods is essential for social stability. Ensuring that people can live better and hold on to every dollar of their hard-earned money is the government’s most basic — and most important — task.
Chen Ching-yun is a former director of the Legislative Yuan’s Bureau of Legal Affairs.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Tensions between political parties dominate headlines and consume much of the attention of party leaders. Jockeying is underway for local elections this November and national elections in 2028. And the longstanding philosophical debate inside Taiwan over how best to protect Taiwan and promote the good life remains unresolved. Amidst all of this, Taiwan continues to function well. It

Unions urge increase to minimum wage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:11 UTC
01:43:11 KST

Ahead of a minimum wage review scheduled for this week, a study has recommended an increase at least equal to the annual consumer price index (CPI) growth rate to ensure workers receive a fair share of economic growth.
The Minimum Wage Review Committee, which would determine the size of next year’s minimum wage increase, is slated to convene on Thursday at the Ministry of Labor, bringing together representatives from labor, business, government and academia.
Local media reported that minimum wage is expected to be increased for the 11th consecutive year, with the monthly wage potentially surpassing NT$30,000. The current minimum wage is NT$29,500 per month and NT$196 per hour.
Photo: CNA
Under the Minimum Wage Act (最低工資法), the minimum wage research group is required to submit a report ahead of the review.
The report highlights a growing imbalance in the distribution of GDP.
In 2024, employee compensation accounted for 43.1 percent of GDP, down 1.25 percentage points from the year before, it said, adding that corporate operating profits rose sharply to 35.06 percent of GDP, up 16.29 percent year on year.
The Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics has raised its forecast for economic growth this year to 11.05 percent, putting the distribution of those gains at the center of negotiations between labor and management.
Under the Act, the indicators used to review adjustments to the minimum wage are divided into two categories: “required indicators” and “optional indicators.”
The “Minimum Wage Research Report and Adjustment Recommendations” estimates that the CPI would rise 2.07 percent year-on-year this year. Among the required indicators, the CPI for 17 key household necessities that have a particularly significant impact on low-income families rose an average 2.01 percent in the first seven months of this year. Egg prices jumped 11.58 percent, pork prices rose 4.84 percent and rice prices increased 2.9 percent, directly eroding consumers’ purchasing power, the report said.
For the lowest-income 20 percent of households, basic living expenses — including housing, utilities, food and medical care — account for as much as 65.58 percent of total consumption, it said.
The report recommends that any increase in the minimum wage should at least match the 2.07 percent CPI growth rate to protect workers’ purchasing power, while taking into account widening disparities in industry development and ensuring that workers receive a fair share of the benefits of economic growth.
The gap between labor and management over the size of the increase remains wide.
Third Wednesday Club chairman Lin Por-fong (林伯豐) said that an increase of “no more than 3 percent” would be more reasonable, drawing criticism from labor representatives, who called the proposal “insincere.”
Taiwan Confederation of Trade Unions president Tai Kuo-jung (戴國榮) said such an increase would give workers less than one-tenth of the gains from economic growth. The federation has called for a 7.77 percent increase, which would bring the monthly minimum wage to NT$31,792 and the hourly rate to NT$211.

Police refer tech worker over Thai woman’s death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
16:43:08 UTC
01:43:08 KST

The Taipei City Police Department’s Wanhua Precinct yesterday concluded an investigation into the alleged killing of a 36-year-old Thai woman and identified a 43-year-old Taiwanese man surnamed Wu (吳) as the suspect, and referred the case to the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office.
According to the investigation, Wu, who works for a tech company in Taichung, met the woman, known as Arth, while traveling in Thailand.
The two maintained a long-distance relationship, with each occasionally traveling to the other’s country to visit, police said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The couple’s relationship was foundering, and Arth flew to Taiwan on Sept. 2 to end the relationship, police said the investigation had found.
She raised the matter while the two were at the hotel where she was staying, after which she was not seen or heard from, police said.
Arth was scheduled to leave Taiwan on Monday, but her family was unable to contact her, and she did not return home, police said, adding that her family asked friends in Taiwan to report her missing to police.
Police said they reviewed video footage and found that Arth checked into a hotel near Ximending (西門町), while Wu visited her late on Sept. 12 and left in the early hours of Sept. 13 carrying a large suitcase.
The suitcase aroused suspicion, as large suitcases have been used to transport bodies in other homicide cases, police said.
Police detained Wu on Friday on suspicion of criminal activity. During questioning, Wu allegedly told police that he lost his temper after Arth ended their relationship and strangled her, police said.
The police said that Wu told them that because he works in administrative and logistics operations for a tech company in Taichung, he was able to hide her body in a freezer rented by the company.
Wanhua precinct officers took Wu to the company’s office in Taichung early yesterday morning and recovered Arth’s body from the freezer. After a forensic pathologist from the prosecutors’ office conducted an autopsy, police returned Wu to Taipei yesterday afternoon, remanding him to the prosecutors’ office on homicide charges.

Detroit Tigers infielder Lee Hao-yu on Friday set Taiwanese MLB records for home runs in a season and hits in a game as he helped his team rally past the Chicago White Sox 11-8.
The 23-year-old went four-for-five with three RBIs and two runs scored, tying the game at 8-8 with a two-run homer in the eighth inning.
The blast was his 10th homer of the season, while his four hits set a single-game MLB record for a Taiwanese.
Photo: AP
“When I actually saw it go out, I just blacked out,” Lee said in a post-game interview, recalling his reaction as the tying home run cleared the wall. “I don’t know what I said or did.”
The Tigers never gave up despite falling behind early, he said, crediting his teammates with responding to their manager’s call for quality at-bats.
Asked what fueled his energy on the field, Lee said: “I mean, I like to win. I don’t like to lose. I helped the team, that’s why I’m so happy.”
Lee’s 10th homer surpassed the previous Taiwanese MLB record of nine set by Yu Chang in 2021 and made him the first Taiwanese to reach double figures in an MLB season.
He also became the first Taiwanese to collect four hits in an MLB game.
Lin Tzu-wei and Chang had previously recorded three-hit games, while Lee had done so twice earlier this season.
Photo: Matt Marton / Imagn Images
Batting ninth and starting at third base, Lee grounded out in the third inning before singling to right field off White Sox starter David Sandlin in the fifth and later scoring.
Detroit, who fell behind 6-1 early and trailed 8-5 after five innings, cut the deficit to 8-6 in the sixth when Lee doubled to deep center field off reliever Chris Murphy. The two-out hit was his 16th double of the season.
In the eighth, Eduardo Valencia was hit by a pitch with one out before Lee sent a pitch from Sean Newcomb over the right-field wall. The homer ignited a five-run inning in which Dillon Dingler delivered the go-ahead RBI single and Riley Greene added a two-run home run.
Photo: AFP
Lee singled again in the ninth to complete his four-hit game, raising his season batting average to .264.

Unknown Publisher
