Three questions to ask to find out if its really love
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:31:09 UTC
20:31:09 KST

This post was originally published on this site.
Hello everybody,
This week we’re looking at the Buddhist philosophy of laziness with Tulku Lobsang Rinpoche. Paid members can find the full version here.
On Monday, I spoke with a reincarnated Lama.
That’s a sentence to invite an eyebrow raise and a bit of old-fashioned self-analysis. For one, it’s made me appreciate how lucky I am to do what I do. To speak with a Tibetan Buddhist master on Monday and a cognitive scientist on Friday is a rare and wonderful thing. But it’s also made me aware of just how little I know about philosophical schools outside my niche.
I’ve spent decades studying mostly the Greek to Roman to European to American philosophical tradition. Everything else is kind of an embarrassing darkness. It’s like having a house and living only in one room. This room has all the lights on, pictures on the walls, and all the fluffy pillows you’d like. But all the other rooms are hidden behind locked doors.
Well, this week I unlocked a door. I interviewed Buddhist master Tulku Lobsang Rinpoche with the intention of exploring the other rooms in the house, and it was a joy. I don’t know if it’s Rinpoche’s ability to teach so well or something structural to Buddhism itself, but everything is presented in neat, numbered packages: “Three roads to enlightenment,” “Three kinds of laziness,” or “Four kinds of liars.”
Buddhism is a content creator’s dream. Hook the audience, pull them along, and give them an actionable mnemonic to wear on their belts. And here I have selected one of the best. Today, we look at “the three elements of love.”
Go well,
Jonny
The loving cure-all
There’s a particularly saccharine quote I’m rather fond of: “If you love someone, set them free. If they come back, they’re yours; if they don’t, they never were.”
It might look good plastered all over Facebook, but it’s also got philosophical pedigree. It’s there in Plato, Aristotle, and Seneca, all the way up to Simone Weil, Erich Fromm, and Iris Murdoch. Of course, these names are all firmly inside my wheelhouse. They live as books on the shelf in that well-lit room of my house. It turns out that Buddhism has a similar but subtly different angle to offer.
Rinpoche argues that there is a difference between attachment and love. Attachment is when we cling to another person. We get possessive of them. We get jealous. We don’t give them space. But for Rinpoche, love is something else entirely. And he told me that the love of another involves three things.
First, there is kindness. Rinpoche frames all of these elements of love as “antidotes” to something that wears us down. Love is a force that cures the “three poisons” of Buddhism that often cause us to suffer. And kindness is seen as the antidote to anger. Because we get angry when we feel people are out to get us.
Imagine you’re in the shop and someone barges into you. You turn around, angrily thinking someone has wronged you. You’re ready to be furious at an aggressive lout. But then you see an embarrassed 7-year-old pushing a shopping cart. Your anger dissipates.
Anger is often about perceived offense, and kindness is what sees people not as obstacles or as enemies, but as allies. Kindness softens the way we look at others’ intentions. It assumes it was a mistake rather than malice, and asks what someone might be struggling with before grumpily assuming they are out to get us.
Second, there is compassion. Compassion is the antidote to attachment, because attachment is what holds people too tightly. Attachment is what keeps the bird in the cage.
Compassion, though, gives somebody space. It allows them to make mistakes, to be imperfect, and to try something new. In a lot of relationships, we become attached to a certain version of a person. It might be the person we first met at the start of a relationship or an idealized, disconnected image we hold of them in our heads. But compassion gives someone the room to change into somebody different from what we might have expected of them. Love allows the other to move forward on their own terms and not according to some rat’s maze we’ve constructed for them.
Third, there is bodhicitta. Rinpoche describes bodhicitta as the antidote to ignorance, and it’s a great way to understand the idea. Because it is ignorant to try to understand the world from only your point of view. It is ignorant to assume the limits of your mind are the limits of the world. As Francis Bacon put it, when you spend your life living in a cave, it’s poor philosophy to assume that is all there is. The limits of your cave are not the limits of the universe. My reading philosophy in one room is not the same as learning all philosophy.
Bodhicitta accepts this and seeks to see things not only from another point of view but, in love, from another person’s point of view. It tries to see the world with their eyes, to understand their needs, and to experience things from their position. For example, I will often get irritated at my wife for leaving things too late. It takes 30 minutes to get to a 2 p.m. meeting, so why is she still getting changed at 1:40 p.m.?! Bodhicitta is what puts me in her shoes — or, more precisely, into her bare feet as she frantically looks about for her shoes that our eldest has hidden under the kitchen sink.
And so, the question of love actually comes down to three different questions:
Do I see them in the best possible light?
Do I give them enough space?
And do I see the world from their position?
Because love is not about desperately clinging to somebody or seeking your own happiness in somebody else. It’s when you find your own joy in the joy of another. It’s when you make a home into the room that they live in.
IN A QUOTE
Jonny is the creator of the Mini Philosophy social network. He’s an internationally bestselling author of three books and the resident philosopher at Big Think. He’s known all over the world for making philosophy accessible, relatable, and fun.

Hungary's "punishment" for Ukraine: how Magyar aims to humiliate Kyiv and block its EU future
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
14:30:00 EEST
20:30:00 KST

Hungary's "punishment" for Ukraine: how Magyar aims to humiliate Kyiv and block its EU future
On 18 September, Ukraine hosted the inaugural Carpathian Initiative summit, which brought together leaders or senior officials from all the countries linked by the Carpathian mountain range: Ukraine, Poland, Slovakia, Romania, Serbia, Czechia and Austria. Only one country was missing – Hungary. To meet with presidents and prime ministers, Hungary sent... a deputy ambassador.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar did not simply ignore the event.
It appears that while preparations were still underway, Budapest attempted to humiliate Kyiv and provoke a reaction, while Ukrainian officials tried to defuse the conflict.
Unfortunately, these events reflect Hungary's new policy.
A demonstrative contempt for Ukraine is at its centre.
The main tool of this policy remains the artificial crisis in relations that was created under former prime minister Viktor Orbán. While Magyar's government publicly declares its intention to restore good-neighbourly relations with Ukraine, it is actually cementing the problems that have built up over time.
Magyar's government policy is also punishing the Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia, firstly by blocking their path towards EU membership, and secondly by creating obstacles to the passing of laws the minority needs.
The lack of political dialogue with Hungary means Kyiv has no realistic scenarios for resolving this crisis. The only hope is that European and US partners will be able to convince Magyar to change his policy.
Instead of thanks, a diplomatic slap in the face
Two weeks ago, experts, politicians and diplomats working on Ukrainian-Hungarian relations had an excellent reason to be optimistic.
The Ukrainian parliament became the first parliament in the world to officially condemn the repression of Hungarians during the Soviet era. This crime, known in Hungary as "málenkij robot" (from the Russian for "little work"), was committed after the end of World War II. Hundreds of thousands of Hungarians, most of them civilians, were deported to the Soviet Union for forced labour. Tens of thousands never returned home, dying in camps, on the way, or in other circumstances.
Residents of Zakarpattia were also affected by these actions, so condemning the Soviet repression was an entirely logical step for the Ukrainian parliament.
The timing of the decision regarding "málenkij robot" was no accident. Ruslan Stefanchuk, speaker of the Ukrainian parliament, was preparing to visit Budapest and wanted to create a diplomatic bargaining chip that could help thaw relations with Ukraine's neighbour.
But no one could have imagined what Hungary's response would be.
The speaker of the Hungarian parliament, Ágnes Forsthoffer, refused to meet with her Ukrainian counterpart while he was in the country. And so did every other Hungarian official. A few days later, Stefanchuk happened to be in Budapest again on his way home from a G7 meeting, and once again, no one was available to meet him.
Despite these actions by his counterparts, the Ukrainian speaker decided not to escalate the conflict. In a comment to European Pravda, his office emphasised that they were continuing to work on arranging a meeting. However, they also pointed out that Forsthoffer herself had invited her Ukrainian counterpart, only to later refuse to meet with him.
Stefanchuk’s spokesperson Vadym Kolodiichuk told European Pravda: "The Ukrainian and Hungarian teams are actively working on arranging the first meeting between the Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada and the Speaker of the National Assembly of Hungary, Ágnes Forsthoffer. We are grateful to the Hungarian side for their official invitation to visit Budapest. At the same time, we are ready to welcome Ágnes Forsthoffer in Kyiv or any other Ukrainian city, subject to mutual agreement."
Members of parliament who spoke with European Pravda off the record tended to be harsher in their assessments, describing the situation as a "slap in the face" from Budapest.
But what happened next is even more striking.
How Magyar is avoiding reaching agreements with Ukraine
A popular explanation in Budapest is that the two leaders, Zelenskyy and Magyar, should meet first.
European Pravda sources had also expressed hopes that the Hungarian prime minister would attend the Carpathian Initiative summit. The thinking was that this was why Forsthoffer, who has no authority over foreign policy, had been unwilling to meet.
These explanations are contrary to the rules of diplomacy. On the contrary, if a leaders’ meeting is to be successful, it needs to be prepared for in advance. The fundamental agreements are worked out first, and the leaders then meet to settle politically sensitive details. Given that decisions by the Verkhovna Rada will be required to resolve the crisis in relations with Hungary, a meeting between the parliamentary speakers would have been appropriate.
That said, Magyar does often act contrary to established rules and conventional logic.
But the main problem is that he isn’t just avoiding meetings with Ukraine.
The Carpathian Initiative summit provided a vivid example.
European Pravda is aware that negotiations with Budapest over Magyar’s attendance at the summit had been going on for quite some time. Several sources claim that only two days before the summit began, the Hungarian prime minister’s office had still not said whether he would be travelling to Ukraine. Then an upcoming trip to the Hungarian city of Pécs was announced on Magyar’s Facebook page that would have been impossible to fit in if he had been visiting Ukraine as scheduled.
All previous attempts to arrange a meeting also failed.
Since the beginning of the summer, Magyar has rejected numerous proposals from Kyiv for a meeting – in Budapest, Brussels, Lviv and elsewhere. Twice, Zelenskyy has caught up with Magyar in person at multilateral international events – the EU and NATO summits. Magyar promised to agree to a full-fledged meeting, but then nothing came of it.
This rather undermines Budapest’s official explanation that the speaker, Ágnes Forsthoffer, was reluctant to meet because she wanted to give priority to Magyar.
It looks more like Budapest is avoiding any political dialogue with Ukraine.
It also looks as if they are trying to humiliate the Ukrainian government.
Forsthoffer is generally not very active in foreign policy, and up until this week she had not held a single meeting with speakers of other countries’ parliaments in Budapest. So technically it could have been argued that that was the reason for her reluctance to meet with Stefanchuk, despite Ukraine’s gesture ahead of his visit.
But two days before the Carpathian summit, a signal came from Budapest: no, this had been a targeted refusal specifically aimed at Ukraine. To prove the point, the speaker of Moldova’s parliament, Igor Grosu, was invited to Budapest to meet with Forsthoffer.
Moldova is not a priority partner for Hungary. Inviting Grosu was apparently intended as a signal or even a slap in the face for Ukraine.
Hungary is the only EU member state that is advocating for Moldova and Ukraine to be decoupled as they progress towards EU membership. It has proposed several times that the EU open the next negotiating clusters for Moldova while freezing the process for Ukraine.
European Pravda sources say that Kyiv got the message.
A veto without conditions
The biggest problem is that Hungary is blocking EU membership for Ukraine without clearly stating what Kyiv needs to do for the veto to be lifted.
The blockade is just there, and no one knows how to bring it to an end.
That is precisely why meetings between senior officials – whether parliamentary speakers or heads of government – are necessary: so that the two sides can understand each other’s positions and find a way out of the crisis. Hungary is doing everything it can to prevent such a dialogue from taking place.
Moreover, even in the EU negotiations, Hungary avoids being specific about what it demands of Ukraine. All we hear is that Ukraine has to "show progress" in implementing agreements on minority rights. Yet we are currently on track for reviewing legislative changes according to a schedule that was agreed on with the Hungarians. For example, in September we submitted a draft on implementing the agreements in the field of education to the European Commission and the Hungarian side.
In other words, Ukraine is fulfilling its commitments, whereas Hungary, which promised back in June to unblock all the clusters, is breaking that promise.
The veto remains in place, just as it was under Orbán, with no explanations and no dialogue whatsoever.
That’s the most shocking part.
Last spring Hungary got rid of Viktor Orbán, who had been moving further into Russia’s orbit (while his foreign minister, Péter Szijjártó, was openly carrying out the Kremlin’s wishes and leaking information from closed EU meetings to Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov).
Magyar, who replaced him, emphasises his opposition to Russia...
But when it comes to Ukraine, his actions often differ little from those of his predecessor.
The shadow of Orbán over the new government
What is Péter Magyar’s true objective? That question remains unanswered. The explanations offered by Hungarian politicians and diplomats do not seem convincing.
In Budapest they claim that Magyar is constrained by public opinion, which is largely negative towards Ukraine. It’s true that after years of Orbán’s propaganda machine, anti-Ukraine prejudices have become entrenched among many Hungarians, and it will take years to overcome them.
But that doesn’t explain the logic behind these actions. Is Magyar really planning to wait five, seven or even 10 years before the next negotiating clusters are opened? Or is this just a convenient excuse?
What’s more, Hungary has already enabled two clusters to be opened for Ukraine (Cluster 1 in June and Cluster 6 in July) without any political or reputational losses ensuing for the government – in fact Magyar’s approval ratings went up. Nor has this been a particularly noticeable topic in Hungary’s domestic political debates or a source of criticism within the country.
Ukraine has its own version of events, which was recently outlined by Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry. "Even after losing power, Orbán’s team continues to undermine the normalisation of relations between Hungary and Ukraine," he said.
Indeed, the Hungarian leadership may have changed, but Orbán’s people are still influential.
Hungary’s ambassador to the EU is still Bálint Ódor, who was appointed by openly pro-Russian minister Péter Szijjártó. So it’s not surprising that Hungary’s representation in Brussels should continue Orbán’s longstanding policy with respect to Ukraine: block, block and block. There have been no changes at the Hungarian embassy in Kyiv. Nor has the Hungarian Foreign Ministry replaced the diplomats responsible for Ukraine.
Despite this, Péter Magyar personally bears political responsibility for the course that has been set.
It was he who chose a policy that, in effect, aims to "punish" Hungarians in Ukraine.
You don’t need to be a Hungarian expert on Ukrainian affairs to understand that ostentatious slaps in the face and gestures of contempt towards the Ukrainian parliament is not going to help secure the adoption of the minority rights legislation that Ukraine is planning to approve as part of its pre-accession agreements.
And ultimately, how does it benefit the Hungarian minority in Zakarpattia if Péter Magyar continues to block Ukraine’s path towards EU membership?
How to resolve the crisis in relations
There is only one avenue of influence over Magyar that could realistically produce results: pressure from Western partners.
After Orbán, who was pretty much seen as "absolute evil", Péter Magyar was initially viewed positively in the EU. But as time has passed, more and more questions have been raised about him. His dismissive policy towards Ukraine, his seemingly arbitrary blocking of Ukraine’s EU aspirations and his deliberate gestures of disrespect should all change how Western partners view the Hungarian government.
There is hope that this will be understood in Berlin and Warsaw – the two European capitals that matter most to Magyar – as well as in the EU institutions in Brussels, and in Washington.
The United States remains highly influential with the Hungarian leadership, particularly following the passing of the Lindsey Graham bill, which will penalise buyers of Russian energy – one of which is Hungary. It is no coincidence that one of Magyar’s close advisers, National Assembly member Márton Hajdu, rushed to Washington this week.
At the same time, Péter Magyar’s policy on Ukraine is damaging to Donald Trump’s peace initiatives.
All proposals for ending the war include EU membership for Ukraine as one of the key elements of the postwar order and security guarantees. Yet Magyar is doing all he can to make this impossible.
The reasons for his actions remain unclear. Is the Hungarian prime minister simply making mistakes because of his inexperience? Is he, contrary to logic, genuinely afraid of how voters will react? Is the influence of Orbán’s "deep state" the decisive factor? Or is there some other explanation? It’s impossible to say.
What is clear is that Magyar’s policy on Ukraine is harmful to Ukraine, Hungarians, Europe and the United States alike.
This needs to end at some point. But without help from Western partners, it will be difficult to find a way out of the deadlock.
Ukraine also needs to be careful not to make mistakes of its own along the way.
Kyiv’s initial reaction to Hungary’s deliberate insults may be a desire to respond in kind – to block progress on minority rights legislation, for example.
But that would amount to Ukraine shooting itself in the foot.
Magyar’s current policy notwithstanding, Ukraine will still have to fulfil its commitments on minority rights as it moves towards EU membership – otherwise, Romania and Bulgaria could join Hungary in raising objections. Kyiv’s strategy, therefore, should be to implement the agreements in such a way as to leave Hungary without legitimate grounds for its objections once other Western capitals begin to apply pressure.
If this path is chosen, rebuilding trust will become possible, step by step. For example, negotiating the gradual opening of additional clusters alongside progress on the relevant legislation.
But given the deep crisis of trust, this process needs to be coordinated. Contact and meetings are necessary, including at the highest level.
The problem is that one side is opposed to finding a way out of the crisis. That side is Péter Magyar’s government.
Sergiy Sydorenko
Editor, European Pravda

Lockheed gets $76.6M for next-gen of Trident II nuclear missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:29:32 UTC
20:29:32 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed Martin a $76.6 million contract modification for continued design work on the next-generation Trident II D5LE2 nuclear missile.
- The program aims to keep the submarine-launched missile in service through roughly 2084, arming the future Columbia-class and Dreadnought-class submarines.
The U.S. Navy has added $76.6 million to a Lockheed Martin contract for continued design work on the next generation of the Trident II D5 nuclear missile, part of a long-term effort meant to keep the submarine-launched weapon in service into the 2080s.
The modification adds to an existing contract with Strategic Systems Programs, the Navy office that manages the country’s submarine-launched nuclear deterrent, and covers advanced design and development work under the Trident II D5 Life Extension 2 program, known as D5LE2. Lockheed Martin’s Titusville, Florida division will lead the effort, though the work itself is spread across more than a dozen locations, with Denver, Colorado handling 51 percent, followed by smaller shares in Elkton, Maryland; Montville, New Jersey; Greeneville, Tennessee; and Cape Canaveral, Florida, among others. The Navy is obligating the full $76.6 million now from fiscal 2026 weapons procurement funds, with work scheduled to run through Sept. 30, 2030. The award was not competitively bid, a legal option the Navy can use for specialized defense work, and only one company submitted a proposal after the opportunity was posted publicly.
Trident II D5 missiles form the sea-based leg of the U.S. nuclear triad, the three-part system of submarines, land-based missiles and bomber aircraft that has underpinned American nuclear deterrence for decades. The missile first entered service in 1990 and went through its first major refresh, called D5LE, in 2017. This second life extension effort is meant to keep the weapon effective for decades beyond that, with the Navy targeting continued service through roughly 2084, nearly a century after the missile’s original design.
The current Trident II D5 weighs about 130,000 pounds (59,000 kilograms), can fly roughly 4,000 nautical miles (7,400 km), and reaches speeds reported to exceed Mach 20. It currently arms the Navy’s Ohio-class submarines and Britain’s Royal Navy Vanguard-class boats, both of which are approaching retirement. The D5LE2 version being developed now is intended to carry over onto the submarines replacing them, the Navy’s incoming Columbia-class and the Royal Navy’s future Dreadnought-class, making this a joint U.S.-U.K. modernization effort rather than a purely American one.
The program has moved forward in stages. The Navy first awarded Lockheed a $383 million contract in January 2025 to begin D5LE2 design and development, followed by an $850 million contract modification announced in April 2026 to continue that work. Lockheed is separately building a roughly 225,000-square-foot (20,900-square-meter) production facility in Titusville expected to open in 2027, while the Navy is constructing its own 130,000-square-foot Engineering Test Facility at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, one of 28 facility projects the Naval Ordnance Test Unit plans to complete between 2024 and 2032 to support the missile’s development and testing.
Even as the newer version moves through design work, the current fleet of missiles remains active. The Navy conducted four unarmed Trident II D5LE test flights from an Ohio-class submarine off the coast of Florida in September 2025, a demonstration officials said confirmed the continued readiness of the sea-based deterrent while the next generation is still years from completion.

Enduring the tragedy of loss, Israeli families of suicide victims struggle to find a path to life
Unknown

2026-09-19
11:24:37 UTC
20:24:37 KST

One might think that losing loved ones because they committed suicide would be the worst possible misfortune – more horrible than if they died in war, a terror attack, a road accident, or from disease.
But Ofra Hermesh – one of the founders of Path to Life (Bishvil Hahayim, a play on words that also means “For Life”) whose son Assaf took his own life 31 years ago in a field near their Herzliya home – disagrees.
The voluntary organization she established with her psychiatrist husband Haggai aims at giving emotional support to bereaved families like theirs and to preventing others from taking their lives.
“Losing a loved one, especially one’s child, is horrific no matter how it happened. One will always live in the shadow of such tragedies,” Hermesh told In Jerusalem in an interview.
“Assaf was our eldest son, and we have three daughters. He started to speak early, and he was very verbal and had an impressive memory in kindergarten – but he couldn’t hold a pencil. We worried about how he would manage in first grade, because he didn’t have fine motor skills.”
“He didn’t like to write. In higher grades, he was in a regular class where all were gifted, but looking back, it was a mistake, because his classmates had a lot of motivation, but he didn’t have the motivation to work hard.”
She recalled that in high school, he wasn’t very skilled at sports, though he took a preparatory course for induction into the IDF and took part in an armored corps course near Eilat.
“He didn’t complain much, except that he didn’t want to be so far from home. In the last week of his 19 years of life, he was at home when there was a mobilization exercise. He got a phone message that the IDF was looking for him and that if he didn’t return immediately, he would be put in jail for a month,” Hermesh shared.
“He was so scared of authority. Haggai and I didn’t know, because we were on vacation. We came back and saw he wasn’t in his room, but his army boots were. Later, an IDF representative told us he had shot himself in a nearby field. He was buried in the Bnei Zion cemetery near Ra’anana.”
FOR 29 YEARS, she visited Assaf’s grave every week on Friday, but she stopped two years ago and now visits much less. “I don’t feel I need to do it. Some families don’t go at all.”
Young people, bemoaned Hermesh, “see everything in terms of black or white. He didn’t understand the significance of death. He was impulsive, but he didn’t confide in anyone. And since he was a soldier, we got emotional support from the IDF. I felt lost. My husband said that Assaf’s suicide was his worst failure as a psychiatrist.”
'There are still stigmas about suicide victims and their families today'
Assaf’s parents attended support groups. “I really needed them; the meetings helped. But if a family of someone who is not a soldier is in that catastrophic situation, no organization supports them,” she added.
They immediately felt stigmatized: “I was sure that people were talking about me behind my back, that they were crossing to the opposite sidewalk so as not to have to talk to me. Our family and some friends were with us, but many who knew us didn’t know what to say. There are still stigmas about suicide victims and their families today.”
Fortunately, their daughters, who were aged 10, 13, and 16, “returned to life. They are all married, and we have seven grandchildren who bring light into our lives,” Hermesh said happily.
“When they were younger, the girls didn’t want a photo of Assaf in the living room, so we put one and some of his things in our bedroom. His room isn’t an untouched monument. It’s my computer room, and I’m giving this interview from there.”
Bishvil Hahayim was officially founded in 2000, but Hermesh and her colleagues worked for several years beforehand to create an organization that would help families and prevent these calamities. Its budget comes from projects and contributions from Israel and abroad, and it would gladly take more volunteers.
“Eight years ago, the Social Welfare Ministry held a tender and chose two non-governmental organizations involved in preventing deaths from suicide, traffic accidents, and murder, and helping families left behind. We were one of the two. Studies show that such family members are at an eight-fold risk of committing suicide themselves,” said Hermesh.
“We give therapy in groups – to families, to individuals, and to siblings.”
‘Is something wrong? Can I help?’
DR. MAYA IOHAN-BARAK, a clinical psychologist and a board member of the organization, is also deputy head of the psychology service at Schneider Children’s Medical Center in Petah Tikva.
“Prevention begins when we teach young children of all ages, from kindergarten through high school, a strategy to get help, to express how they feel, and to learn about emotional strength. This helps them identify who is under stress so they can be helped,” said Iohan-Barak.
“They may keep to themselves, stop being social, or have a short fuse. Changes in a person’s behavior or emotional state should make family or friends stop and ask, ‘Is something wrong? Can I help?’”
“When one encounters someone who seems at risk, ask him or her directly if they were thinking of suicide. Don’t be judgmental, make fun of them, or berate them by saying: ‘Don’t talk like that; it’s ridiculous.’ It doesn’t plant the idea in their heads. There are all kinds of statements that give signs, such as ‘Soon I won’t be here’ or ‘My life is worthless,’” Iohan-Barak continued.
It’s best to be in touch with them and get help from a personal physician, public health fund, their school, or workplace: “There aren’t enough therapists, but one can always find help.”
Suicide is more common among recent immigrants or even second-generation immigrants from the former Soviet Union and Ethiopia. Females attempt suicide more often than males, but males actually carry out their plans more than women. The elderly who are depressed, lonely, or sick have the highest rate of all, Iohan-Barak said.
Scandinavia, the US, Europe, and Russia have higher suicide rates than in Israel, where there are between 500 and 550 per year and more than 10,000 attempted suicides.
There are misconceptions about suicide that the organization’s staff encounter, including that people who talk about it don’t really think about doing it. But even though there is much emotional stress and anxiety in Israel, “one can be optimistic that people can be helped. There’s more legitimacy to go for treatment, especially among men who were reluctant in the past.”
Research has taught that early prevention is vital. There were survivors of the Nova music festival on October 7, nearly three years ago, who later committed suicide, and some who lived in kibbutzim and moshavim along the Gaza border – a small number – who took their own lives as well, said Iohan-Barak.
She is nevertheless more hopeful than when the organization was launched, because “we have managed to break more glass ceilings and prevent many tragedies. Still, we can’t rest on our laurels.”
Suicide prevention does not only begin the moment a person comes to treatment
MICHAL ARCOSIN, Bishvil Hahayim’s director-general as of a few months ago, has over 15 years of management experience across the business, public, and social sectors, and is a doctoral student in public policy. She holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in government and public policy and is a certified family mediator.
“I learned about the organization from IDF veterans suffering from post-trauma,” she shared.
Asked what’s still missing from Israel’s suicide-prevention system, she said: “It’s not the responsibility of just the health system, but also of the family, workplace, schools, and community to identify people at risk as early as possible. We want to reach more people in the haredi sector, especially overburdened women, the Arab sector, and lone soldiers who made aliyah by themselves.”
The story takes on new importance in the current period, after years of war, loss, trauma, and uncertainty that have left their mark on many parts of Israeli society, she said.
“Today, it’s particularly important to ask how an entire society can identify distress earlier, reduce the stigma surrounding seeking help, and give families, communities, workplaces, and professionals tools that can help and sometimes even save lives.”
Through the story of the association, it seems that suicide prevention does not only begin the moment a person comes to treatment. It begins much earlier – in its ability to identify change, ask, listen, know how to respond, and not be afraid to talk about suicide in a direct, responsible, and knowledge-based manner.
The organization operates in workplaces, public institutions, local authorities, government ministries, and the education and health systems through lectures, training, resilience workshops, and various programs.
Raising awareness has a dual role. On the one hand, it allows for a space for families who have experienced suicide, reducing the silence and stigma surrounding the circumstances of death and allowing them to receive recognition, support, and legitimacy to talk about their loss.
On the other hand, awareness is also a tool for prevention. The more people who know how to identify signs of distress, are not afraid to ask questions, understand how to approach the person they care about, and know where to turn for help, the greater the possibility of identifying distress earlier and intervening before the end point, Arcosin said.
Bishvil Hahayim’s support centers are in the center and the South of the country. Another organization, the Elah Center, runs the centers in the north and the Jerusalem area. Help is given according to predefined criteria: that the loss occurred in the past five years, and that it was a first-degree relative.
The NGO has worked with government ministries, especially the suicide prevention unit in the Health Ministry, and the Knesset. But the outgoing Knesset hasn’t been very active on the issue, said Arcosin.
If there were one thing she wishes that every Israeli knew about suicide, it would be that “it can happen in any home, rich or poor, living in the periphery or the city, religious or not, Jewish or Muslim or Christian. We encourage conversation so it becomes known. It is the country’s responsibility because it can suddenly happen anywhere.”

'Zoti': Fun vibe in Tel Aviv - restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:24:27 UTC
20:24:27 KST

I was running late for my restaurant reservation at Zoti, a new Mediterranean chef restaurant opposite the boardwalk in Tel Aviv. When I arrived with my husband at 8:30 p.m. (late for us to eat dinner, but we were going with the Tel Aviv flow), we were met by a red velvet rope at the entrance and a man who looked like a bouncer.
When we walked in, we saw a space that looked like a cross between an Arabian palace and an upscale cave, and there were plenty of free tables. By the time we left around 10:30, every seat was taken, the DJ was going strong, and there were dancers with fire that made it more than just another restaurant. I was the only woman not wearing high heels and makeup.
It’s loud here, so it might not be the best place for a first date, but we’ve been married for so long that not being able to talk to each other is really not a big deal. The vibe is fun and very Tel Avivian. If you haven’t gotten to go abroad, this could be your chance to pretend to be overseas. Tel Aviv is really almost like being in a foreign country.
Cocktails are pricey but worth every shekel
The service here is excellent (and not just for journalists). Napkins were changed at least five times during the meal, and the servers all seemed to really care that we had a good meal. They were also familiar with the menu and had excellent suggestions.
The cocktails are pricey but worth every shekel (NIS 72-78). The bar’s unique design is a surprise I’ll leave for you to discover. Just remember to look up!
The chef here, also one of the partners, is Daniel Marciano, a young Jerusalemite who is also a partner in several restaurants in the capital.
Several of the dishes seem to be Jerusalem-inspired yet with a unique twist. For example, one of the appetizers we had was nems, a Vietnamese dish of crispy deep-fried spring rolls with chicken and vegetables. Here, there were nems made with brain that had a kick from cilantro, harissa, preserved lemon, and schug (NIS 118). It may be the only nems in the world made with brain.
We also tried the crispy hamachi (NIS 89), which were balls of crispy rice topped with yellowtail sashimi and a sauce made of yellow tomatoes, basil oil, and pesto aioli. Another winner.
A DJ, a live dummer, and a fire dancer
By now, the DJ had ramped up the volume, accompanied by a live drummer and a woman dancing with fire.
For our main dishes, we shared lamb chops (NIS 248) and a sirloin steak that was thinly sliced and cooked perfectly medium-rare, accompanied by a fried potato gratin (NIS 198). Both were excellent, and among the best pieces of meat I’ve had in recent months.
We were pretty full by the time we got to dessert, but it may have been the most unique dessert I’ve ever had. Called simply “Zoti” (NIS 154), it was a sparkling wine bottle made of chocolate, filled with chocolate mousse and vanilla ice cream. It was a huge dessert, easily enough for four people, and the bottle was incredibly realistic. When the server poured melted chocolate over the bottle, it broke open. A fun ending to a special evening.
This is not an inexpensive evening, but I think it’s in line with Tel Aviv prices. So, if you have a special occasion coming up, make the pilgrimage to Zoti in Tel Aviv. You will be glad you did.
Zoti
6 Kaufmann
Hours: Opens Sun.-Thurs. from 7 p.m. and Saturday from 9:30 p.m. Closes around midnight.
Reservations: seats.zotitlv.com/index.html
Kashrut: Rabbanut Tel Aviv
The writer was a guest of the restaurant.

Trying açaí at Oakberry Jerusalem: A not-so-sweet treat with sweet company - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:24:26 UTC
20:24:26 KST

Full disclosure: I had never had açaí before in my life. So when Oakberry Açaí opened its Jerusalem location on Agrippas Street, I made sure to bring an expert with me: my friend and colleague Goldie, who actually knows what she’s talking about when it comes to this stuff.
Before even trying the food, the location alone makes the trip worth it.
We ended up spending most of our visit just sitting, chatting, and people-watching, and that alone made for a genuinely lovely afternoon. Sometimes the best part of trying something new isn’t the thing itself; it’s who you’re sitting with when you try it.
As for the açaí: going in blind, it really wasn’t for me. I’m a known sweet tooth, and I don’t know if it was just this place or açaí in general, but in my amateur, first-timer opinion, açaí tastes like medicine. Tart, earthy, and not exactly what I was expecting from something so hyped up on social media. I will say, though, the toppings saved it. Oakberry has options like granola, fresh fruit, and a drizzle of something sweet on top. Those I enjoyed without hesitation.
If you love that distinct açaí tang, you’ll probably walk away thrilled
In Goldie’s much more informed opinion as a certified enjoyer of açaí... yeah, it could’ve been sweeter. But she did finish her cup, and I do know that not everyone needs the amount of sugar I do to get through the day.
This is very much a “know yourself” situation. If you love that distinct açaí tang, you’ll probably walk away thrilled. If you’re more of a milkshake-and-cookies person like me, temper your expectations on the bowl itself.
But again, what made the visit worth it was the bustling energy and movement of the city that Agrippas offers. Goldie and I stayed far longer than we planned to, and neither of us minded one bit.
So, would I recommend Oakberry? For the açaí itself, I’ll defer to Goldie’s expertise. For the experience of sitting there with good company on a nice day in Jerusalem? Absolutely, without hesitation.

Lockheed’s F-35 support deal grows by $871 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:24:12 UTC
20:24:12 KST

- The U.S. Navy awarded Lockheed Martin an $871.2 million contract modification to fund equipment for new F-35 operational sites worldwide.
- The award builds on a $2.29 billion base contract from June 2026 covering site activation and sustainment as the global F-35 fleet keeps growing.
Before an F-35 fighter jet can land at a new base and start flying real missions, someone has to build the entire support system around it first: spare parts stocked on shelves, specialized tools laid out, technicians trained, and computer systems wired into the global network that keeps the jet running. That unglamorous but essential groundwork is what the U.S. Navy just paid Lockheed Martin another $871.2 million to keep doing.
The money comes as a modification to an existing contract with Naval Air Systems Command, and it doesn’t buy any new jets. Instead, it increases how much support equipment Lockheed can supply as the Pentagon and its allies keep opening new places for the F-35 to operate, whether that’s a land base in a partner country or a fresh set of jets joining a Navy carrier air wing. The work will happen mostly at Lockheed’s facility in El Segundo, California, with a smaller share in Fort Worth, Texas, and it’s expected to run through February 2031.
The Navy structured this as a ceiling increase, meaning the money becomes available only as specific orders get placed over time, not as a lump sum handed over today. It’s a bit like raising the limit on a corporate credit card rather than writing a check. The Navy also didn’t put this work out for competitive bidding, and there’s a straightforward reason why: Lockheed built the F-35, owns the technical blueprints, and is really the only company that knows how to properly stand up a new operating site for it. That’s standard practice for this particular slice of the program.
To understand why this kind of contract keeps coming up, it helps to picture what “opening a new F-35 base” actually involves. It’s not like adding a new gate at an airport. Every location needs its own stockpile of spare parts, ground equipment built specifically for the jet, maintenance tools, and IT systems that plug into the F-35’s worldwide logistics network. Skip any of that, and a squadron of brand-new stealth fighters could end up sitting on the tarmac with nowhere to get serviced. This contract exists to make sure that never happens, whether the new site belongs to the U.S. Air Force, the Marine Corps, the Navy, or one of the many other countries that now fly the jet.
Lockheed said back in January 2026 that the worldwide F-35 fleet had grown to roughly 1,300 aircraft spread across a dozen nations, and by March that number had climbed past 1,325 built. New jets keep rolling off the line, new squadrons keep forming, and each one needs its own version of the setup work this contract funds. That’s really the whole story behind why the Pentagon keeps writing checks like this one: it’s not glamorous, but it’s the plumbing that makes a global fighter jet fleet actually function day to day.
This particular award builds directly on a much larger one. Back in June 2026, the Navy handed Lockheed a $2.29 billion contract covering the same broad category of work, site activation, temporary contractor support while a base gets fully staffed, fleet management, and ongoing reliability improvements. That contract runs through the end of 2028, and this week’s $871 million modification essentially tops up the amount of support equipment available under it. Think of the original deal as the overall budget for opening new F-35 locations everywhere over the next couple of years, and this modification as extra headroom within that budget specifically for hardware.
What’s still unclear, at least from the public paperwork, is exactly which bases or countries this new money is earmarked for. The Navy hasn’t said whether it’s tied to a specific ally bringing its F-35s online, a new U.S. squadron standing up, or simply general capacity to handle whatever comes next as the program keeps growing. Given how quickly the F-35 fleet has expanded over the past year, though, it’s a safe bet this won’t be the last contract of its kind.

Chinese art exhibitions draw Kenyan audiences as cultural ties deepen
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:20:57 CST
20:20:57 KST

NAIROBI, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- Two Chinese art exhibitions concluded Saturday at the National Museums of Kenya in Nairobi after a two-week run, providing a platform for cultural exchange between Kenya and China.
The dual exhibitions featured Chinese mythology through paintings, ceramics, sculptures and embroidery, alongside artworks highlighting China's rural revitalization, cultural heritage and community development.
Ketan Desai, a visitor from Eldoret in western Kenya, said the paintings are "very elegant and unique," adding that some illustrated China's history and development.
"I enjoyed viewing these pieces of art because they enlightened us about Chinese culture," he said.
Michael Kong'a, an interior design major at the University of Nairobi, visited the exhibitions after learning about the event from acquaintances.
"I am impressed by the paintings on display. The canvas, choice of colors and lighting are quite inspiring for me as an interior designer. Chinese art is beautiful and simple," Kong'a said.
Dozens of schoolchildren, accompanied by teachers and parents, toured the gallery ahead of the exhibition's closing.
During the exhibition, China's Sichuan Fine Arts Institute donated more than 30 artworks from its collection to the National Museums of Kenya, with Zhang Liang, a curator at the institute, presenting the works.
The donation will remain at the museum as a lasting reminder of the friendship between China and Kenya and help promote greater understanding of Chinese art and culture, according to Zhang. ■

Death toll from blast, militant attack in NW Pakistan rises to 31
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
19:20:54 CST
20:20:54 KST

This photo taken with a mobile phone shows Pakistani soldiers standing guard at the bomb attack site in Kohat of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, Pakistan, Sept. 18, 2026. As many as 31 people, including 16 police officers, were killed and over 100 others injured in a twin suicide attack inside a police residential compound in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province on Friday, police said on Saturday. (Str/Xinhua)
ISLAMABAD, Sept. 19 (Xinhua) -- The death toll from a suicide bombing and subsequent militant attack in Pakistan's northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province has risen to 31, including 17 policemen, six civilians and eight terrorists, rescue workers said Saturday.
More than 130 policemen and civilians were injured and shifted to various hospitals, Bilal Faizi, spokesperson for the state-owned Rescue 1122 service in the province, told Xinhua.
The incident occurred at about 1:15 p.m. local time (0815 GMT) in Kohat district on Friday, when a bomber rammed an explosives-laden vehicle into a mosque adjacent to the gate of the Police Lines compound before detonating it, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Inspector General of Police Zulfiqar Hameed told the media.
Following the blast, seven armed terrorists infiltrated the Police Lines premises, and one of them blew himself up near a building housing offices of the Special Branch of police, Hameed said.
Two terrorists were killed shortly after entering the premises, while four others infiltrated the building, he added.
In a statement issued Saturday, police said the clearance operation against the terrorists lasted about 21 hours, and during the operation, two terrorists were holed up on the first floor of the building and were killed in a clearance operation conducted early in the morning on the premises.
One more was killed in an exchange of fire, while another was badly burned and detonated his explosive vest, it added.
Ittihadul Mujahideen Pakistan, a faction of the militant group led by Hafiz Gul Bahadur, claimed responsibility for the attack.
The country's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and President Asif Ali Zardari condemned the attack and expressed grief over the loss of life.
The prime minister directed authorities to expedite rescue operations and provide all possible facilities to those affected. ■

Jiaojiang District in China's Zhejiang develops large yellow croaker industry

An aerial drone photo taken on Sept. 16, 2026 shows a large yellow croaker farm in Jiaojiang District of Taizhou City, east China's Zhejiang Province. In recent years, Jiaojiang District of Taizhou City has been developing its large yellow croaker industry by establishing standards for the geographical indication product, expanding aquaculture farms, promoting the integration of fishery and tourism, and developing related tourist attractions.
Jiaojiang currently has eight large yellow croaker farms covering about 4,900 mu (about 327 hectares). In 2025, the district's annual output of Dachen large yellow croaker exceeded 10,000 tonnes, while the annual output value of the entire industrial chain reached 1.1 billion yuan (about 164.2 million U.S. dollars). In 2025, the district's annual output of Dachen large yellow croaker exceeded 10,000 tonnes, while the annual output value of the entire industrial chain reached 1.1 billion yuan (about 164.2 million U.S. dollars). (Xinhua/Jiang Han)

Israeli army seals last route to West Bank, 47 Palestinian families isolated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:19:00 UTC
20:19:00 KST

The Israeli military has closed the last access route to a small Palestinian village in the northern West Bank, leaving 47 families isolated and struggling to obtain food, water and feed for their livestock, residents said.
The closure of the route to Khirbet Ras al-Ahmar, southeast of Tubas in the Jordan Valley, entered its fifth consecutive day Saturday after Israeli forces dug a trench across the last remaining track into the community, resident Thaer Basharat told Anadolu.
The rough road was already difficult to navigate and was mainly used by livestock and agricultural tractors. Its closure has left residents with no practical way to transport large quantities of essential supplies into the village.
"The 47 families in the village rely on livestock farming and are now unable to bring in their basic necessities or sheep feed," Basharat said.
Residents say the latest measure follows more than two months of closures affecting other dirt roads leading to the community.
They say restrictions have steadily tightened over several years, with the latest closure effectively turning the village into an enclosed area surrounded by trenches, earth mounds and military-controlled zones.
The community is home to roughly 40 to 47 families, with residents depending largely on livestock herding and limited agriculture for their livelihoods.
The loss of vehicle access has made obtaining animal feed particularly difficult. Residents also face challenges transporting water, food and other necessities, while moving livestock and agricultural equipment has become increasingly difficult.
Livelihoods under growing pressure
Basharat said the community previously relied on about 360,000 dunams of grazing land, but that roughly 90% had either been seized or placed off-limits.
The figure could not be independently verified, but residents have for years reported losing access to traditional grazing areas because of military restrictions, land seizures, settlement activity and new infrastructure.
The restrictions have increased the financial pressure on families who depend on livestock. With less access to grazing land, herders have had to rely more heavily on purchased animal feed, while road closures make transporting supplies more difficult.
Residents fear the worsening conditions could eventually force families to abandon the community.
"The Israeli pressure aims to forcibly displace the entire community from the village," Basharat said.
Khirbet Ras al-Ahmar is located in Area C of the West Bank, where Israel exercises civil and security control under the interim arrangements established by the Oslo Accords.
The community has faced repeated restrictions on construction and infrastructure, as well as demolitions and temporary evacuations linked to Israeli military activity.
The latest closure is linked to construction of a military barrier project known as the "Crimson Thread," which is being built along parts of the eastern edge of the West Bank.
The first major section stretches roughly 20 to 22 kilometers through the northern Jordan Valley. The project includes a military patrol road, trenches, earth embankments and other barriers.
Construction has cut through Palestinian agricultural land and infrastructure, according to Palestinian residents, rights groups and Israeli media reports.
The Times of Israel reported in July that trenches associated with the project had been dug through Palestinian farmland around Ras al-Ahmar and had damaged water pipelines. The project has also affected agricultural plots and other infrastructure in the area.
The Palestinian news agency WAFA reported in August that Israeli forces had filled in three artesian wells and damaged about 300 meters of a water pipeline in Ras al-Ahmar. Three livestock shelters were also demolished, according to the report.
For residents, the loss of access to water and grazing land has compounded the impact of the road closures.
The Jordan Valley is one of the West Bank's most important agricultural regions, supporting farming and livestock communities that depend on access to land and water.
The situation in Ras al-Ahmar is part of a wider deterioration in conditions for Palestinian communities across the West Bank since the Gaza war began in October 2023.
Movement restrictions, military operations, settler attacks, demolitions and land-access restrictions have increased in several parts of the territory.
Israeli human rights organization B'Tselem and other monitoring groups have documented the displacement of Palestinian herding communities, particularly in parts of the Jordan Valley and the southern West Bank.
Palestinian residents and officials say the cumulative restrictions are making it increasingly difficult for rural communities to remain on their land, particularly those whose livelihoods depend on grazing livestock.
Israeli authorities have rejected claims that their policies are intended to forcibly displace Palestinians, saying restrictions and demolitions are connected to security concerns and Israeli regulations governing construction and land use in Area C.
But for residents of Ras al-Ahmar, the immediate consequences are increasingly severe.
With the last vehicle route blocked, families are struggling to bring in essential supplies, livestock feed and water. Residents can still move on foot in some areas, but that provides little practical help for transporting heavy loads or supporting livestock.
The closure comes as work on the Crimson Thread barrier continues across the northern Jordan Valley.
Residents and Palestinian officials say the project is further restricting access to agricultural land and grazing areas and threatening the livelihoods of communities that have lived in the region for generations.
The wider dispute over the Jordan Valley has long centered on land, water and movement. The latest road closure has brought those issues into sharper focus for the families of Ras al-Ahmar.

Russia reportedly buries its drone factory underground
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:18:31 UTC
20:18:31 KST

- Ukrainian analyst Dnipro Osint said Russia has built about 42,000 square meters of underground production space for Shahed/Geran drones at Alabuga.
- The claim follows confirmed satellite evidence of new production halls, a 340-hectare site expansion, and defensive towers built around the facility in 2026.
Russia has begun building underground production space for its Shahed and Geran attack drones at the Alabuga industrial zone in Tatarstan, according to Ukrainian open-source intelligence analyst Dnipro Osint, who estimated roughly 42,000 square meters of underground area has already been constructed there.
Dnipro Osint said the shift underground appears to have followed earlier Ukrainian strikes on the Alabuga site, and that Russia has been expanding the underground infrastructure quickly since then.
The analyst placed the activity at coordinates 55.808719°, 52.026664°, within the broader Alabuga Special Economic Zone near the city of Yelabuga, roughly 1,200 km (750 miles) from the Ukrainian border. This specific underground construction claim comes from a single open-source analyst and has not yet been independently confirmed through separate satellite imagery analysis.
Alabuga is Russia’s primary production site for the Geran-2, a Russian-built version of Iran’s Shahed-136 one-way attack drone that Russian forces fire at Ukrainian cities on a near-nightly basis. The facility has grown substantially over the past year. Satellite imagery cited by Radio Liberty showed the zone’s footprint expanded by 340 hectares between May 2025 and May 2026, with new hangars, dormitories for foreign workers, and a roughly 450-hectare construction area added south of the M-12 highway. Ukrainian analysts reported on Sept. 14 that five additional production halls had gone up in the southern part of the site, based on satellite images similarly sourced from Dnipro Osint.
Russia has also added physical protection around the plant. Satellite images from July and August analyzed by Spencer Faragasso of the Institute for Science and International Security showed a two-ring system of lattice towers under construction around Alabuga’s production buildings, an arrangement meant to complicate future drone or missile strikes on the site.
Dnipro Osint said the combined effect of these changes, underground construction, dispersed production buildings and added physical defenses, is making Russia’s drone manufacturing base progressively harder and more expensive to target. The site relies heavily on foreign labor recruited through the Alabuga Polytechnic College and other channels; the United Kingdom sanctioned 35 entities and individuals in May 2026 over recruitment tied to the facility, and the site remains under separate U.S. and European Union sanctions.

South Korea rejects US pressure for deployments to Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:18:19 UTC
20:18:19 KST

Breadcrumb
South Korea rejects US pressure for deployments to Hormuz
South Korea is rejecting pressure from the US to deploy its navy to the Strait of Hormuz, with President Lee Jae Myung saying on Friday he would not involve his country in the ongoing US-Iran war.
"There won't be [a] deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly," he told a press conference, adding that "we won't deploy military assets in any form to that end".
Lee did caveat the comments, saying that South Korea was reviewing playing a role in ensuring free navigation in the region.
"[It] is also clear we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people," he said.
Lee's comments come as commercial shipping around the Middle East, specifically in the Gulf and Red Sea, comes under increasing strain from both Iran and the Houthis as a means of exerting pressure on the global economy in response to the U/S-Israeli war launched in February.
This has directly affected South Korea, which imported 70% of its oil from the Gulf prior to the outbreak of the war, alongside significant portions of LNG.
It also comes amid threats from US President Donald Trump, who asked the country in August to "give us a hand" with Iran, later saying he would scale back military drills after South Korea said no.
He also questioned why South Korea would say no, given that tens of thousands of US troops are stationed in the country.
"We have 39,000 soldiers over there guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbour. And you're not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran? That’s strange," he said.
Trump and members of his administration have also criticised European allies for not getting involved in the war.
The US has 28,500 troops stationed in South Korea, one of the longest continuous US military deployments, having been there since 1957.
Since the start of the war, the US has redeployed some forces out of the country, most importantly Patriot and THAAD batteries needed to intercept Iranian ballistic missiles.
Alongside Lee's comments, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
South Korea's foreign ministry said that Cho had explained to Rubio that the country would make a contribution to restoring freedom of navigation, though it didn't elaborate what this would look like.

‘We escaped barefoot’: Yemen families flee fresh Houthi offensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:10:00 UTC
20:10:00 KST

When a terrifying bombardment erupted around their camp in Yemen this week as the country’s long-running civil war flared again, Rawya Hassan and her family fled for their lives, running barefoot and leaving their animals and belongings behind.
The family had already been forced from their village by the war years earlier. Now they were fleeing the fighting once again, joining an estimated 115,000 people who aid agencies say have been displaced by a rapid advance by the Houthi group.
“We are under terror, under the rockets, under the missiles,” Hassan said as she made bread in a makeshift clay oven at the small al-Bireen camp, where the family has sought refuge among shacks and acacia trees.
Fighting between the Iran-backed Houthis and forces aligned with the Saudi-backed government largely subsided after a 2022 truce. But violence has erupted again amid the spillover from the wider conflict between Iran and the United States.
As the Houthis seized the port city of Mocha and the southern stretch of Yemen’s Red Sea coast last week, a wave of displaced people fled into government-held areas and across the sea to Djibouti.
Among them were Hassan, 48, and her seven children, who ended up in a remote district of Taiz province, an area of steep, dry foothills between the coast and Yemen’s central highlands.
The family was originally from the village of al-Tuweir but fled fighting in the area eight years ago for a camp in the nearby al-Kadha district. Now even that place of shelter is gone, and they must start afresh.
“We escaped barefoot. We didn’t even know where our children were. We had nothing with us, no covers, no mattresses, no food, no drink, nothing,” she said, describing shells falling and warplanes or drones circling overhead.
Her older sister, Rawda, was with the children. After a long walk, they reunited the next day at al-Bireen camp, where they are now entirely dependent on aid.
Rawda, an orange scarf wrapped around her head, said the family does not know where to go next. From the camp, a dirt path leads into the hills, while a nearby road runs between the Houthi-held coastline and another frontline at the city of Taiz.
Larger numbers of people fled along Yemen’s Indian Ocean coastline, traveling from the Bab el-Mandeb Strait at the mouth of the Red Sea toward Aden. Many arrived at camps outside the city, where white tents stood in rows across windswept sand.
Um Mohammed said her family escaped from Mocha when the Houthis advanced last week. It was the latest blow the family had suffered after her son was killed earlier in the war.
When they reached al-Firdaws camp, the family was given only thin mattresses and old blankets for the tent where they now shelter, she said.
Small children played nearby as women hauled large buckets of water from tanks delivered by pickup truck and aid workers distributed food rations.
“They put us in the middle of the sand. We have suffered a lot,” she said, boiling water in a kettle over a small twig fire and adding that they had lost their livestock, clothes and blankets while fleeing.
The fighting in Yemen has erupted into full-scale war along several fronts, with the Houthis using drones and ballistic missiles while Saudi Arabia pounds areas held by the Iran-backed group with warplanes. There is no immediate sign the violence will ease.
The U.N. migration agency IOM said Friday that at least 112,000 people had been displaced inside Yemen over the previous two weeks, while nearly 3,000 more had fled to Djibouti, crossing the Gulf of Aden in overcrowded boats.

Hungarians and Slovaks share breakfast on Danube bridge that survived war and division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:08:45 UTC
20:08:45 KST

Hungarians and Slovaks share breakfast on Danube bridge that survived war and division
ESZTERGOM, Hungary/STUROVO, Slovakia, Sept 19 - A historic bridge linking Hungary and Slovakia became an unlikely breakfast venue on Saturday, as locals gathered on the Danube crossing to celebrate friendship between the two neighbouring communities.
The Maria Valeria Bridge, which connects Esztergom in Hungary and Sturovo in Slovakia, has twice been destroyed and rebuilt since it first opened in 1895.
In late 1944, as World War Two drew to a close, retreating German troops blew up its three middle sections. The bridge then lay neglected for nearly 60 years, forcing people to cross the border by ferry during decades of communist rule. It reopened in its original glory in 2001.
On Saturday, dozens of tables were laid out along the bridge for a community breakfast of croissants, ham, cheese and coffee. Participants from both towns were paired based on their interests and languages, encouraging new cross-border friendships.
"I think the people of Esztergom and Parkany could mix a bit more," organiser Norbert Nagy said.
Ethnic Hungarians make up about 9% of Slovakia's 5.5 million people, and many live in Sturovo, known in Hungarian as Parkany.
"I met a really lovely and kind person here this morning on the bridge, so it was a great experience for me," said Mark Zelenak, who arrived from Esztergom.
Hungary and Slovakia have shared open borders since both joined Europe's Schengen zone in 2007, although political tensions have occasionally surfaced over Slovakia's ethnic Hungarian minority.
But Laszlo Valacsay, who also took part in the breakfast, said such tensions were often stirred by politicians, while local people lived peacefully side by side.
"It was always generated, but not by the people, by us, who live here..no, no," he said. REUTERS

Officials warn online threats carry federal consequences

“This case should serve as notice that if you threaten people or groups online, hiding behind your keyboard will not protect you from the consequences of your actions,” Benson said.

AI error nearly led US to seize Chinese ship: ‘Almost started a war’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
11:03:20 UTC
20:03:20 KST

A faulty intelligence report produced with the help of artificial intelligence and circulated throughout the U.S. military during the war in Iran nearly led the United States to launch a military operation against a Chinese vessel — and could have sparked a confrontation between the two powers, CNN reported Friday, citing people familiar with the incident.
According to the report, the episode took place last spring, when an intelligence assessment reaching U.S. military officials concluded that a Chinese vessel in the Middle East was carrying components linked to a nuclear weapons development program. The information immediately raised serious concerns, prompting the military to begin preparing to intercept the ship.
Four sources who spoke with CNN said preparations had reached an advanced stage: Armed U.S. personnel were preparing to board the vessel and military aircraft were already in the air.
Only shortly before the planned operation did officials decide to scrutinize the intelligence report more closely. They then discovered it had been prepared with the help of artificial intelligence and that a chatbot used by the analyst had incorrectly identified the material the ship was carrying.
CNN said it was unable to determine what the vessel’s cargo actually contained.
One source described the report as “entirely false,” adding: “It almost started a war.”
According to CNN, U.S. action against a Chinese vessel could have triggered a serious escalation and potentially an armed confrontation between Washington and Beijing. The network said the episode illustrates a more immediate danger than the extreme scenarios senior technology executives have warned about in recent weeks: not AI “going out of control,” but humans making potentially momentous decisions based on false information it generates.
The report was prepared by an analyst at Special Operations Command. According to CNN, the analyst entered intelligence about the ship’s cargo manifest into a chatbot, using information originating from U.S. Special Operations Command Pacific, which is headquartered in Hawaii.
It was unclear whether the analyst used a commercial chatbot or a system developed for the U.S. government. The system combined information from open sources with classified signals intelligence stored in government databases and reached the incorrect conclusion about the cargo.
The analyst then used artificial intelligence again, this time to turn the findings into the standard format of an official intelligence report — the kind of document military decision-makers are accustomed to treating as a reliable source — and circulated it.
A former senior U.S. official familiar with the artificial intelligence systems used by defense and intelligence agencies said internal government tools are not necessarily fundamentally different from commercial AI products.
U.S. Special Operations Command Pacific and the Pentagon did not respond to CNN’s requests for comment.
The episode comes as the U.S. military and intelligence community accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence across nearly every aspect of their work, from analyzing vast quantities of intelligence and selecting targets to budgeting, logistics and supply chain management.
The goal is to allow the military to make decisions more quickly, in part because of concerns that the United States could fall behind China and other rivals in the use of the technology.
In January, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled the Pentagon’s “AI Acceleration Strategy,” aimed at removing barriers and rapidly expanding the use of the technology so it would be available to roughly 3 million military personnel and civilian employees across all classification levels.
The plan included projects to integrate AI into battlefield management, intelligence and decision-making.
At the program’s launch, Hegseth said the United States would “unleash experimentation, eliminate bureaucratic barriers, focus our investments” to ensure U.S. leadership in military artificial intelligence.
But U.S. officials said implementation of AI systems is taking place in a decentralized way, with different parts of the military and intelligence community using different tools under inconsistent instructions and safety standards.
They said there is currently no single set of rules defining how AI-generated information must be verified before it is used in operational decision-making.
Concern is particularly acute when it comes to target selection.
A person familiar with military policy told CNN that the use of AI in targeting is “definitely something that is ramping up,” but said clear guidelines still do not exist to ensure that keeping a human in the decision-making process will actually prevent civilian casualties or friendly fire.
The AI “hallucination” — the term used when an AI system produces information that sounds credible but is false — that led to the Chinese ship episode was not an isolated case, according to one source.
Several veteran intelligence officials said the technology is increasing pressure on analysts to produce and distribute intelligence quickly, raising the risk of mistakes. They said younger analysts who have grown accustomed to using such tools may also be more inclined to trust them without sufficient scrutiny.
“AI allows you to get to a bad idea faster,” one source said.
Another sensitive China incident: F-35 parts reached Hong Kong
Alongside the faulty intelligence report, U.S. authorities have opened an investigation into another sensitive security incident involving China: A shipment of parts from an F-35 stealth fighter, which was being sent from Australia to the United States for repairs, was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, Politico reported Friday.
According to three people familiar with the matter, the components were being shipped on behalf of aircraft manufacturer Lockheed Martin through an intermediary, but during their journey across the Pacific the shipment arrived in Hong Kong instead of the United States.
It remains unclear why the shipment’s route was changed or who currently has possession of the parts, according to the report.
The Pentagon confirmed there was an issue involving a shipment of unserviceable F-35 components.
The F-35 program office said it was working with U.S. authorities and industry partners “to recover the components, investigate the incident and implement safeguards to prevent a recurrence.”
The incident has prompted an investigation on Capitol Hill and a series of briefings for congressional committees dealing with national security.
According to the sources, State Department and Pentagon officials began briefing congressional staff on the matter in June, with additional briefings expected in the coming weeks.
The main concern centers on the type of components included in the shipment.
Two of the sources said the parts included an F-35 cockpit canopy containing technology related to the aircraft’s stealth capabilities that is available only to the United States and its allies.
The canopy is a transparent acrylic shell covering the cockpit and is coated with a thin, transparent layer of radar-absorbing material designed to reduce the aircraft’s radar signature and make it more difficult for enemy systems to detect.
U.S. officials are concerned that if such a component fell into the hands of an adversary, it could be closely examined and parts of the technology could potentially be reverse-engineered.
The fact that the shipment reached Hong Kong has heightened concerns that China could gain access to the components.
Beijing has long been accused of trying to obtain information about sensitive U.S. weapons programs, including the F-35.
“It’s no secret that China has been aggressively trying to get F-35 data through electronic espionage, among other means,” J.J. Gertler, a former House Armed Services Committee staffer and military aviation analyst at the Congressional Research Service, told Politico.
Gertler said that even if Beijing already possesses specifications or other information about the parts, having access to an actual component could allow it to verify and improve the information it already has.
Lockheed Martin said it could not comment on the status of shipments for security reasons but stressed that it complies with all U.S. regulations governing the transfer of aircraft components.
The company added that its personnel handle every shipment “with the utmost diligence and safeguards” to protect the security of the F-35 program and participating allies.
The F-35 program is one of the largest and most expensive weapons programs in U.S. history. Along with supply chain problems and spare-parts shortages, it has for years struggled with high maintenance costs and difficulties meeting readiness targets for the aircraft fleet.
The episode also highlights a longstanding problem in the F-35 program’s vast and complex supply chain, which relies on maintenance and repair facilities in multiple countries as well as commercial shipping companies.
Countries participating in the program use a shared global pool of spare parts, which remain Pentagon property until they are installed on aircraft but are, in practice, managed largely by contractors.
A 2023 report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that more than 1 million F-35 spare parts, worth tens of millions of dollars, had been classified as lost over roughly five years.
The watchdog criticized the Pentagon’s limited ability to track the parts, in part because much of the relevant information is held by contractors that manage the supply system.
