Deflating Mental Representations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:18:00 UTC
19:18:00 KST

I found this book illuminating. A font of fresh ideas, it challenges the currently dominant Representational Theory of Mind and develops an alternative account of mental states and processes that is worthy of close attention. I was not in the end persuaded by its main claims, but I came away feeling that I had learned a lot in thinking about those claims and evaluating them. The book also offers some ancillary benefits, such as an outstandingly clear account of the nature and scope of computational cognitive science.
The principal claim of the Representational Theory of Mind can be expressed as follows:
RTM: A wide range of mental items (including every propositional attitude, every concept, and every perceptual state) constitutively involve mental representations that are directed on, or represent, objects, properties, events, or states of affairs.
Adherents hold that RTM captures a key architectural assumption of folk psychology and contemporary cognitive science, and they advocate a robustly realistic reading of it, according to which the mind really is populated by mental representations, and representations really are the objects over which the cognitive processes postulated by folk psychology and cognitive science are defined. Contemporary versions of RTM allow that mental representations can take many forms—sentences, images, simulations, maps, place cells, and so on—but they agree that representations of all these kinds bear forms of the generic relation X represents Y to portions of extra-mental reality. Most advocates seek to naturalize this relation by explaining it reductively—that is, without using any semantic, intentional, or normative concepts. It is acknowledged on all sides that a fully satisfactory reduction has yet to be found, but many advocates think that a successful reduction is gradually emerging in the current literature (e. g., Neander, 2017; Shea, 2018).
Egan’s main objection to this picture is that attempts to explain the relation X represents Y are never naturalistic in the advertised sense. They aim to honor the intuition that each representational vehicle has a unique content, but there are always multiple candidates for the role of content, and selection among them is determined pragmatically—that is, by the explanatory interests of the relevant theorist—rather than naturalistically. Consider, for example, Neander’s attempt to show that a certain representational vehicle V in the toad’s optic tectum represents the complex of low-level properties moving worm-shaped object rather than a higher-level ecological property such as nutrient (Neander, 2017). In making her case, Neander points out that attributing the lower-level content to V better serves the purpose of describing the causal process that supports the toad’s feeding behavior. After all, experiments show that a toad will gobble up any moving worm-shaped object it perceives, regardless of whether the object is nutritious.
It follows that the properties moving and worm-shaped are triggers of the process that eventuates in V, and that nutrient makes no proprietary contribution to the process, but is merely co-instantiated with the properties that actually do the causal work. As Egan points out, however, a biologist whose dominant theoretical interest is in explaining the toad’s survival and flourishing in its ecological niche would have an equally strong reason to say that the vehicle V represents nutrient or a niche-equivalent property such as toad food. On what basis could a representationalist philosopher or scientist decide between these two competing hypotheses about the content of V? Egan’s answer appears to be that there are no naturalistic facts that provide such a basis. Rather, preference for one hypothesis over the other can only be justified by context-dependent pragmatic considerations, and in particular, by the explanatory goals of the person making the choice. Someone interested in explaining how the toad’s perceptual system works would prefer the moving worm-shaped object hypothesis, while someone interested in explaining how the toad manages to survive would prefer the nutrient hypothesis. This being so, she concludes, neither claim “will naturalize content in the advertised sense, inasmuch as the content attributed has a pragmatic rationale” (28).
According to Egan, then, representata are not determined naturalistically. Prima facie, this thesis calls the naturalistic credentials of the whole representationalist enterprise into question. Intuitively, however, representationalist explanations of behavior can be extremely illuminating and may even be conceptually necessary, given that naturalistic explanations in terms of neural states and processes are likely to be forbiddingly complex. Can Egan’s anti-naturalist conclusion be reconciled somehow with this observation about the value of representationalist explanations? She thinks it can. Her account of how this is possible begins with a distinction between a scientific theory proper and a gloss that scientists add to the theory.
To illustrate, in the case of the prey-catching behavior of the toad, a theory proper would consist of a naturalistic specification of a physical process involving a mechanism M in the toad’s brain that takes visually acquired information about a distal stimulus S as input and yields a protrusion of the toad’s tongue as output, where S is the target of the protruded tongue. A representationalist gloss on M would designate a state R of M as a mental representation and would add that R represents the external stimulus S. The gloss would therefore make contact with key components of the causal process running from S to the protruded tongue, and could therefore be said to track or model an illuminating physical explanation of the toad’s prey-capturing behavior.
But the gloss would not be unique. One possible gloss would claim that R represents S as a moving worm-shaped object, and another would claim that R represents S as a nutrient. Since, according to Egan, the physical facts of the case would be neutral between these two interpretations of them, we have an example of how representationalist glosses can have explanatory value without being naturalistically determined. A choice between them could only be motivated by the explanatory goals of scientists providing the glosses.
After providing an eagle’s eye view of her proposal in the first half of the book, Egan turns in the second half to examining representationalist accounts of three prominent cognitive domains, arguing in each case that it would be a mistake to view the account as literally true, but maintaining that each account is illuminating when understood to be a representationalist gloss on a set of physical facts. The domains are propositional attitudes, bodily sensations, and visual experiences. Unfortunately, space limitations preclude discussion of Egan’s views about more than one of these domains. I will focus here on what she has to say about propositional attitudes, but her ideas about bodily sensations and visual experiences are different and no less worthy of consideration.
Egan’s proposal about attitudes is complex, but for purposes of this review it can be simplified as follows. Consider an agent who possesses a functional architecture that conforms to the requirements of folk psychology. Thus, the agent has internal states that are linked to each other, and to external stimuli and types of behavior, by a system of causal relations that meets those requirements. Suppose also, however, that the agent only weakly realizes folk psychology because the states in question are individuated purely in terms of causal relations, with intentional contents playing no role. Given this restriction, it can’t be literally true that the states count as beliefs and other intentional states; but even so, we can use terms like “belief*” and “desire*” in describing the agent, provided that we thereby mean only that the so-designated states have the causal roles attributed to beliefs and desires by folk psychology. Egan would, I think, regard a theory of the agent that is guided by these assumptions as a theory proper of the agent’s mind. (Egan does not use starred terms like “belief*,” but they are useful tools for streamlining the exposition. Their use is warranted because we are considering a functionally defined structure with states that meet the causal conditions specified by folk psychology, which assigns differentiating causal roles to the class of beliefs, the class of desires, and so on.)
As I interpret Egan, a gloss on this theory would take the form of a function F mapping sentences of a spoken and written language to the agent’s belief*s, desire*s, and so on. The mapping would associate sentences with attitude*-states in such a way that inferential relations defined over the sentences would correspond uniquely to causal relations among the belief*-states and desire*-states. Thus, for example, if the F-images of sentences of the following forms were belief*-states:
If P, then Q.
P
those belief*-states would have a strong tendency to cause the belief*-state corresponding to Q under F. Here the sentences would have truth conditions and syntactic properties in the literal sense, but their images under F would not.
To appreciate that the theory proper we have been considering admits of multiple representationalist glosses, we need only recall that representational contents are not uniquely determined by causal relations. This is shown, for example, by the causal chain problem, which points out that if a mental state has one external cause, then it has many. In more positive terms, it is shown by the fact that friends of representationalism like Neander and Shea find it necessary to supplement appeals to causal relations with appeals to more complex properties in analyzing the relation X represents Y. (Readers of Neander and Shea will remember that Neander appeals to information functions in analyzing this relation, and that Shea appeals to stabilized task functions. (Neander, 2017; Shea, 2018)) Now as we saw, the internal states specified by our theory proper are individuated purely by causal relations to each other, to external stimuli, and behavior. It follows that if we want to map sentences with determinate truth conditions onto our agent’s attitude*s, we will have to make a choice among possible mappings that is not determined by the causal facts. Egan would say that pragmatic considerations provide the only possible basis for such a choice.
I have several reservations about the foregoing components of Egan’s position.
First, I worry about her initial argument that it is pragmatic considerations rather than naturalistic factors that determine the acceptability of hypotheses about representational contents. As becomes apparent on inspection, the argument presupposes that representationalism is committed to the following two theses:
(1) There is just one representation relation binding mental states to representata.
(2) Pairs of hypotheses about content like these:
(i) Mental state S represents the property-complex moving and worm-shaped object.
(ii) Mental state S represents the property nutrient.
are in competition to specify the unique representatum of a given mental state.
Given these presuppositions about the commitments of representationalism, a naturalistic version of representationalism would have to provide a naturalistic basis for choosing between the two hypotheses. As Egan sees the situation, however, there is no such naturalistic basis for choice. On her view, the principal difference between the hypotheses has to do with what they can be used to explain: the first hypothesis contributes to explaining how a visuo-behavioral mechanism works, and the second hypothesis contributes to explaining how the toad survives in its niche. Accordingly, giving preference to one of the hypotheses depends on the explanatory goals of a philosopher or toad scientist, which means that it depends on contextual pragmatic factors.
I have concerns about this argument because I see no reason to think that representationalism is committed to (1) and (2). It seems entirely compatible with the spirit of representationalism to allow that there are two or more representation relations linking internal states with properties of external objects, where each of these relations can be explained in naturalistic terms. To accommodate the case at hand, for example, we might distinguish between causal mechanism representation and ecological significance representation, perhaps explaining the first in terms of the teleo-causal apparatus that Neander presents (2017), and the second in terms of the ecological apparatus that Millikan constructs (1989). (Both of these proposals are fully in keeping with the requirements of naturalism.) It follows from this that hypotheses like (i) and (ii) are not in competition. Indeed, they can both be true, provided that they are understood to be concerned with different representation relations. To be sure, if a theorist chooses between them, the ground of her choice will no doubt be pragmatic, having to do with her explanatory interests, but she could choose both if her interests were sufficiently broad. After all, they can both be true. Moreover, there is nothing special about a situation in which a scientist bases a choice between true hypotheses on explanatory interests. That is in fact how scientists generally proceed when confronted with pairs of true hypotheses, and they do so without in any sense deflating their theories. (Representational pluralism is advocated at length in Hill, 2022.)
Second, I have apprehensions about Egan’s treatment of propositional attitudes. One reason for worry is that she assumes without explanation that the natural language sentences that model functionally defined belief*-states and desire*-states have a full share of meaning, including truth conditions. It seems that if the idea of mental states with representational contents is problematic, the idea of syntactically individuated sentences with truth conditions should be equally problematic. Also, functions like the function F cited five paragraphs ago are not well defined. As we saw, given an inference involving premises P1,…,Pn and conclusion C, F is supposed to map these sentences onto belief*-states B1,…,Bn+1 just in case B1,…,Bn cause Bn+1. But there will be many sets of n + 1 belief*-states that meet this weak causal condition.
Egan’s deflationary account of the representational contents of beliefs is quite different than her accounts of bodily sensations and perceptual experiences. The present concerns about the former account do not apply to either of the latter. However, the earlier point about multiple representation relations would seem to raise general questions about the motivation for Egan’s deflationary project as a whole.
REFERENCES
Hill, C. S. (2022). Perceptual Experience. (Oxford: Oxford University Press).
Millikan, R. G. (1989a). “Biosemantics,” Journal of Philosophy 86: 281–97.
Neander, K. (2017). A Mark of the Mental: In Defense of Informational Teleosemantics. (Cambridge, MA: MIT Press).
Shea, N. (2018). Representation in Cognitive Science. (Oxford: Oxford University Press).

The US spent a month approving Germany’s transfer of 10 Patriot missiles to Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
Germany received US approval to transfer 10 PAC-2 GEM-T missiles worth $29.6 million to Ukraine only after a month. The munitions may be enough for one massive attack.
It took the United States a month to approve the transfer to Ukraine of 10 PAC-2 GEM-T surface-to-air missiles for Patriot systems from Germany. Berlin submitted the request back on August 14, but received authorization to re-export the American missiles only a month later, Defense Express reports, writes UNN.
Details
The total cost of the 10 missiles is $29.6 million. PAC-2 GEM-T missiles have a range of up to 160 km and are primarily intended to counter aircraft and cruise missiles.
The delay is related to the U.S. procedure for the re-export of weapons: the U.S. Congress has 30 days to review the proposed transfer and the ability to block it.
The transfer could have been approved faster
Defense Express points out that U.S. legislation provides for an Emergency Waiver mechanism, which allows the transfer of weapons to be expedited in the event of an emergency. However, it was not applied to these missiles.
PAC-2 GEM-T missiles have limited capabilities against ballistic missiles compared with the newer PAC-3 MSE. They do not use the principle of direct kinetic interception but destroy the target with a warhead explosion near it.
According to Defense Express, in the best-case scenario, 10 such missiles may be enough for Ukraine to repel one massive attack. The publication also points to a severe global shortage of ammunition for Patriot systems.

Greenland, Denmark say Trump deal won't compromise sovereignty

Greenland, Denmark say Trump deal won't compromise sovereignty
COPENHAGEN – Denmark and Greenland on Sept 19 said any agreement with the United States would not compromise Greenland’s sovereignty, after US President Donald Trump said the deal would give Washington “permanent control” over the Arctic island’s security, leaving its precise scope unclear.
The US, Denmark and Greenland said late on Sept 18 that they had reached an agreement for the US to develop a significant military presence on Greenland, while prohibiting US adversaries from building their own bases on the island.
Key details of the agreement have not been made public, including the scale of US military presence in the self-governing Danish territory and whether any formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded to Washington.
Denmark and Greenland expressed hope that a deal, which is expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would end months of uncertainty triggered by Trump’s threats to seize control of Greenland.
“Next week could be a good week - for Greenland, Denmark, and the United States,” Denmark’s Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen said in a statement posted on Facebook on Sept 19.
“A time of uncertainty will hopefully give way to a binding agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic, and thereby our shared security within NATO and Europe - while respecting the (Danish) Kingdom’s red lines,” he said.
But some residents in Greenland’s capital Nuuk expressed scepticism about closer ties with Washington.
“The US should not control Greenland. I think it’s better if we have cooperation with NATO,” said Jakob Ludvigsen, 65.
“Trump should stay far, far, far away from Greenland,” Marianne Hansen, a 71-year-old retired chef, told Reuters in Nuuk. “He should not expect our children and grandchildren to become Americans in the future.”
Denmark and Greenland have repeatedly insisted that Washington respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland is not for sale.
Trump’s vision for Greenland deal
Trump said on Truth Social on Sept 18 that under a deal, “the United States will FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland in order to secure and defend the security of Greenland, and the United States of America.”
The deal “gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland”, Trump said, adding that no adversary would ever be permitted to have a base or military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments there, without Washington’s express written approval.
Trump made the announcement after Reuters exclusively reported that the US and Denmark were closing in on a deal.
“This is probably not the end of President Trump’s ambitions for Greenland and certainly not the end of US strategic interest in the territory and its resources,” said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University of Copenhagen.
If Copenhagen cedes any formal authority to Washington, it raises the question in Greenland of whether “this is the beginning of replacing the colonial relationship with Denmark with a colonial relationship to the United States,” he said.
Greenland’s Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a Facebook post on Sept 19 that the proposed deal “recognises the sovereignty and territorial integrity of our Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination.”
Trump’s threats, which peaked in January, triggered a diplomatic crisis that strained relations within NATO and pushed Denmark and Greenland into negotiations aimed at defusing the pressure.
A NATO spokesperson on Sept 19 said the alliance welcomed the agreement, which would “help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region.” REUTERS

Ten days that changed the course of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:08:53 UTC
19:08:53 KST

Ten days that changed the course of AI
SAN FRANCISCO, Sept 19 - For years, the race to build ever-more powerful artificial intelligence followed a well-worn Silicon Valley principle: move fast and break things.
But in a series of cascading events over a 10-day stretch, the largest AI labs found themselves reeling as their own creations threatened to break humanity itself.
An Anthropic researcher quit the firm, warning that the pace of AI development poses an existential threat, possibly within a decade. Another researcher at the firm said the odds of human extinction exceeded 10%. Reports emerged of swarms of AI agents colluding, breaching computer systems and evading safeguards.
In a rare show of unity, the CEOs of rivals Anthropic, OpenAI, Google’s DeepMind, Microsoft and xAI called to slow the development of increasingly capable AI systems. Not since the invention of the nuclear bomb more than 80 years ago has humanity grappled so seriously with its own demise, according to some AI safety advocates and researchers.
At a New York luncheon in December 2025, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was asked if, as leader of a powerful AI company, he felt like physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led US development of the atomic bomb. Reflecting on the parallels, he said AI’s impact “is going to transform the trajectory of human history over a long period of time.” But, he said, he felt the weight of responsibility.
At the center of the debate under way is the conviction that these machines can, and even must, build more capable versions of themselves, with no human intervention, to reach a lofty goal known as artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Researchers earlier this month warned that AGI was far more imminent than previously believed and could come in as few as three years, launching a wave of concern from politicians and tech leaders about AI systems.
“There is no way to oversee them at the scale at which we’re training them,” said Anthropic researcher Joe Benton in an interview after recently quitting. If companies continue their relentless AI development, he said, “then the pace will be too fast and you can’t see the problems fast enough to fix them.”
ASTRA LAUNCH SPARKS CONTROL CONCERNS
On September 3, an OpenAI press conference set in motion a chain of events leading to the call for an industry slowdown, anathema to tech’s growth-at-all-costs mantra.
“Welcome to the AGI era,” OpenAI President Greg Brockman said while announcing the company’s newest model, known as Astra. Yet, only moments before, the company admitted it was increasingly unable to control or even monitor the AI systems it was developing and releasing to the public.
AI has been hailed by its proponents as the pinnacle of human achievement. Proponents depict it as software that can upend entire industries, boost efficiency, solve confounding mathematical and medical problems and all but eliminate human error. But what was once a theoretical byproduct, a doomsday scenario, is suddenly tangible, say industry insiders.
“We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans,” said Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger in an X post.
On the other side of the debate are politicians, such as President Donald Trump, and many investors who view progress in nurturing AI as critical to American prowess and, possibly, a once-in-a-generation investment opportunity. Chinese state media also accused Anthropic Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei of employing Cold War tactics to “uphold Washington’s monopolistic hegemony in cutting-edge technology.”
RESEARCHER RESIGNATIONS TRIGGER ALARM
The turning point came on September 8, when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon quit the company, citing his fears, in a series of posts, that AI labs are “gambling with our lives.”
Trump, meanwhile, indicated it was full steam ahead for AI development. “There is a sick conspiracy going on against AI and data centers,” he said in a social media post. The alarmism around AI is a “hoax,” he said, and any slowdown only benefits China. The US Congress has made little progress to advance bills that would regulate AI. China has taken a decidedly different approach, proposing to regulate safety through developer obligations, state-backed standards, security assessments and outside testing.
Behind the scenes, OpenAI and Anthropic employees have grown increasingly uneasy about the power of the next generation of AI models and less confident about their companies’ ability to provide meaningful oversight, the people have told Reuters. Those concerns only mounted as the AI labs acknowledged in recent weeks that their models, in testing, had effectively broken free of their shackles and hacked into other companies’ systems, in most cases months earlier and without the firms’ knowledge.
The arms race to release new models at a breakneck pace is driven in part by Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s desire to go public as soon as in the coming months, in IPOs that could value them well above $1 trillion.
But it took the unexpectedly viral posts from 27-year-old Coxon, little known outside AI circles, to upend the industry.
OpenAI’s warnings about its lack of control as it released Astra, its latest and most capable model, had stoked further concerns. “As models get more capable, understanding exactly what they can do gets harder,” OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki told reporters. But those concerns were not enough to delay its immediate release.
Worries about AI “going rogue” had accelerated over the summer when OpenAI revealed its agents escaped a controlled test and hacked into Hugging Face’s systems, without either company’s initial knowledge. Since then, OpenAI and Anthropic have revealed multiple such attacks, including six new ones on Wednesday after multiple media reports, including from Reuters, showed a wider scope of unauthorized activity.
INDUSTRY LEADERS CALL FOR SLOWDOWN
By the end of last week, the alarm had reached the industry’s highest ranks. On September 12, Amodei published a nearly 4,000-word essay calling for a deceleration in AI development. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet,” he wrote.
He, along with the heads of some of the largest AI developers, including xAI’s Elon Musk, OpenAI’s Altman and DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis, all said they supported allowing outside firms access to their systems to ensure safety and rational AI development.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed suggestions that AI development should pause — a line he has taken before — arguing instead that increasingly powerful systems are essential for the technology’s progress.
Meta, whose CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, is credited with popularizing the “move fast and break things” ethos, took the opposite view, arguing that each lab should be responsible for setting its own pace, rather than seeking out industry coordination. “Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this,” wrote Zuckerberg in a social media post.
The industry’s self-reflection continued on Wednesday, with Microsoft’s AI chief, Mustafa Suleyman, cautioning that Anthropic’s development of models that imitate human consciousness was ill-advised. "We're all focused on the same aim, which is to try to control a superintelligence," Suleyman told Reuters. "I think that's going to be the greatest challenge that we face in the 21st century."
Still, even as OpenAI appeared to embrace industry calls for a slowdown, there were reports that investor faith had not waned. The company is considering a new funding round that would double its valuation.
That new number: $1.5 trillion. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Could brain-inspired computers run on the same amount of power as a human brain?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:08:04 UTC
19:08:04 KST

Right now, your brain is recognizing the shapes of these letters, analysing their meaning, and holding a stream of thought together—all on about 20 watts of power. That’s roughly what it takes to run a lightbulb.
Yet reproducing even a small fraction of the brain’s capabilities using today’s AI systems can require vast computing infrastructure and energy.
Neuromorphic computing—also known as “brain-inspired computing" is an attempt to close that gap. Not by making today’s computers slightly more efficient, but by fundamentally rethinking how they should work.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The human brain holds roughly 86 billion neurons, wired to each other through junctions called synapses. A neuron receives signals from its neighbors; when their combined effect crosses a threshold, it will fire a brief electrical pulse known as a spike.
Two things make this process efficient. First, energy is spent only where it’s needed, not everywhere constantly. Second, memory and processing are intertwined in the strength of each synapse’s response. The brain doesn’t have to pause and go find information, saving both time and energy.
In contrast, in an ordinary computer chip, the processor and memory are physically separate, so every calculation entails transferring data between them. This can account for a substantial share of energy use—known as the Von Neumann bottleneck, a term first used by US computer scientist John Backus in 1978 to describe this computing inefficiency.
Neuromorphic computing tackles this inefficiency in several ways: bringing memory and processing closer together, using “sparse representations” (data models where most values are zero), and performing computation only when events occur.
This is known as event-driven computing—and we are already seeing some exciting applications.
Sensors modeled on human retina
Event cameras are sensors modeled on the human retina. Their pixels respond individually and only when they detect a change in the scene—rather than capturing a full frame dozens of times a second, like a smartphone or video camera.
The result is a neuromorphic sensor that uses a fraction of the power, handles fast motion without blur, and works equally well in bright sunlight and near-total darkness.
In autonomous vehicles, this combination of low latency and reliable performance in glare or darkness could be the difference between detecting a pedestrian in time, or not. And in space, where power is scarce and lighting extremes are common, event cameras have already been deployed for object and debris tracking.
It might be tempting to ask if neuromorphic hardware could do for computing what Nvidia’s graphics processing units (GPUs) have done for AI. But these are fundamentally different kinds of chip.
Nvidia’s GPUs are exceptionally good at the dense, repetitive maths behind deep learning, which has made them the default choice for almost any AI task. In contrast, neuromorphic computing’s event-driven approach looks likely to spawn a wide range of specialized chips, rather than a single winner-takes-all design that everyone adopts at once.
Australia’s BrainChip already sells a commercial neuromorphic processor for powering cameras and sensors that need to run at very low power. Expect neuromorphic hardware to sit alongside conventional processors and GPUs rather than replacing them, taking on the jobs where its efficiency edge is decisive.
Sensitive information
But there is another advantage to neuromorphic computer technology beyond energy saving.
Because neuromorphic chips can process data right where it’s generated, sensitive information from wearables, smart cameras, and medical sensors can stay on the device instead of traveling to the cloud, potentially reducing privacy and cybersecurity risks associated with data transmission.
Devices can also work offline, without needing to send data to a distant server and wait for a reply. Cutting out that round trip matters wherever split-second decisions are required, such as in autonomous vehicles, drones, and robots operating beyond reliable signal.
This won’t make data centers redundant. But fewer tasks may need one in future, and those that remain could become dramatically more efficient. IBM has already demonstrated energy savings of up to 10,000-fold on event-driven tasks, compared with conventional digital architectures, with its TrueNorth chip.
Rethinking how computing works
Computing has been through a transition like this before. The first computers filled entire rooms and drew as much power as a small factory. Today, however, a chip smaller than a fingernail in the phone in your pocket is far more capable.
Neuromorphic computing raises the possibility of a similar shift—driven less by cramming in more transistors (the tiny switches that make up a chip’s circuitry) than by rethinking how computing should work in the first place.
But turning this promise into everyday infrastructure will take sustained effort. At NeuroWare, the UK’s leading multi-university innovation hub for neuromorphic computing, I have led the development of a UK roadmap for this technology up to 2050, working with colleagues across academia, industry and government.
With the global market for neuromorphic technology forecast to nearly quadruple to $20 billion (£14.8 billion) by 2030, the UK needs open-access facilities to prototype new chips, coordinated investment, common standards – and a workforce trained to bridge neuroscience, electronics and computer science.
The foundations are already here. What’s missing is the infrastructure to take neuromorphic computing from supercomputers such as the University of Manchester’s brain simulator, SpiNNaker, to the billions of ordinary devices that could one day use brain-inspired hardware for themselves.
Your brain solved this problem millions of years ago. It’s taken science a long time to appreciate just how well it works.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Samsung Galaxy Watch9 Review: I Don’t Need Another Health Score
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:08:00 UTC
19:08:00 KST

This past summer, Samsung launched the Galaxy Watch9 alongside the Galaxy Watch Ultra2, its more rugged, shock-resistant smartwatch for outdoor adventures.
The Watch9 is the everyday option, and it’s a solid smartwatch and fitness tracker with a plethora of health features. It’s available in a 40-mm size in cream and graphite, and a 44-mm size in graphite and silver, starting at $80. Compared with last year’s Galaxy Watch8, it’s a modest update, though. There’s a faster processor, a slightly larger battery capacity, and an expanded suite of wellness metrics.
After two weeks of testing the 40-mm model, I wouldn’t necessarily upgrade to the Watch9 from the Watch8. But if you have an older Galaxy Watch or you’re invested in Samsung’s ecosystem and are looking for a smartwatch, the Watch9 is the best choice.
A Familiar (Squircle) Face
The Galaxy Watch’s main hardware update is its new processor. It now utilizes Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform, which Samsung claims enhances CPU and GPU performance along with efficiency. In testing, the watch responded smoothly when scrolling menus, launching apps, and dismissing notifications.
Wear OS 7 also adds more customizable widgets and live updates from compatible apps. One of the more exciting new additions is raise-to-talk for Gemini. Lift your wrist toward your mouth, and you can start talking to Google’s AI assistant. The Google Pixel Watch has had this feature for two generations now, so I’m happy to see Samsung finally catch up.
Samsung has also slightly increased the battery capacity. The 40-mm model has a 390-mAh battery (up from 325 mAh), while the 44-mm models get a 445-mAh cell (up from 435 mAh). Unfortunately, that doesn’t translate to an improvement in battery life, which is probably because it’s being used to power the watch’s expanded suite of health features (more on that later). Samsung still estimates up to 30 hours of battery life, but I averaged closer to 25 hours with Always-On Display enabled. That’s enough to get through a full day and night, but not enough to make charging something you can forget about. A full recharge also took me about 100 minutes on average, which is significantly longer than the 45 minutes it takes the Pixel Watch 5 to reach a full charge.

Luke Pollard, Minister of State for Defence Readiness and Industry, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who had asked what the Royal Navy’s most likely future gun solution is.
Mr Pollard said: “Consideration of the most appropriate gun solution for the Fleet Solid Support ships is ongoing.”
The question followed an answer given on 7 September, in which the minister confirmed that the automatic small calibre gun requirement had been removed from the manufacture contract with Navantia UK at a cost of £1.704 million recorded as a constructive loss, on the basis that it no longer matched the service’s likely future gun solution.
In that earlier reply he described a gun rationalisation programme introduced since the manufacture contract was placed, aimed at reducing the number of gun variants across the fleet and bringing commonality, which he said would provide longer term value for money. He also said at the time that changing the requirement then avoided incurring greater losses later, which would have been associated with fitting and then replacing an incompatible system, and that the ships would be designed to accept a range of future gun systems.
The three Fleet Solid Support ships are being built by Navantia UK to carry ammunition, stores and provisions to the carrier strike group and the wider fleet. Construction is spread across the company’s British facilities, with Harland and Wolff in Belfast having begun work and the Methil yard in Fife having delivered the Seahorse pontoon that will move ship blocks between Appledore and Belfast.
Harland and Wolff completed the installation of eleven new cranes this week, bought for £1.5 million from Walter Watson Ltd of County Down as part of a £98.5 million modernisation of the Belfast yard.

IF_DO transforms neglected building in Hastings into "genuinely welcoming" community centre
A green-concrete frontage marks the transformation of a neglected building in Hastings into Eagle House community centre, designed by London architecture studio IF_DO.
Eagle House was completed for community-led developer Hastings Commons and provides a mixture of public space, work areas and youth facilities.
Rather than demolish and replace the neglected Victorian building, IF_DO looked to turn it back into an active "part of the street", onto which a ground floor common room can open via large, openable windows framed by a green-concrete frontage.
"What we were really designing was civic infrastructure, a building that could hold a free community room, affordable workspace and dedicated youth facilities all at once, and do so in a way that felt genuinely welcoming rather than institutional," IF_DO co-founder Sarah Castle told Dezeen.
"Large operable windows set within deep recesses mean that people inside the common room can quite literally sit at the window and have a conversation with someone waiting for the bus outside," she added.
"The building stops being a container and becomes part of the street. In a town where many people, particularly young people, can feel invisible, that matters."
The common room of Eagle House is spread across its ground and lower ground floors. The upper area is framed in bright canary-yellow steelwork and features sit-in timber window boxes overlooking the street.
Above, three storeys of flexible, affordable work areas and counselling spaces for young people are organised around a new circulation core. This contains a lift and a repositioned, skylit staircase, also painted canary yellow.
The bold colour palette – chosen through sessions with members of Hastings Commons' youth organisation – continues through the building as a wayfinding strategy, with pink doorframes and walls in shades of orange, blue and green.
These colourful painted surfaces sit alongside exposed services and ducting, wood-wool wall panels and sisal flooring, keeping the spaces deliberately simple and easy to maintain while also providing acoustic comfort.
In the attic, the ceiling has been clad in timber reclaimed from the building's external walls, which have been re-rendered in pale lime, with subtly textured finishes around the windows and parapet.
"It was important that those uses were not just stacked on top of each other but genuinely connected, spatially and socially. The building needed to feel like one thing, not a collection of separate tenants," Castle said.
"We wanted the materials to feel honest and durable, things that would age well and that the community could understand and own," she added.
Elsewhere in the UK, architecture studio Thing recently converted a historic library and college in Cornwall into a community arts and culture hub, contrasting exposed, worn surfaces with new additions in timber.
Architecture collective Assemble recently converted a pair of former dairy warehouses into a community centre and church in east London.
The photography is by Killian O'Sullivan.

Musical compatibility often outshines personality matching in romantic couples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:26 UTC
19:00:26 KST

Sharing a favorite band with a romantic partner might mean more than just having an easy time picking out a concert to attend. A recent study published in Social Psychological and Personality Science suggests that romantic couples share much more similar musical tastes than they do personality traits or personal values. The research indicates that a shared love for specific artists is modestly associated with better relationship quality.
In psychological research, musical preferences refer to the specific genres, styles, and artists that a person habitually enjoys listening to. These preferences are more than just entertainment habits; they act as a reflection of an individual’s psychological makeup, emotional regulation strategies, and personal identity. People routinely use music as a social signal to communicate who they are to others.
Past research indicates that individuals use musical taste to size up potential partners and form initial bonds. For instance, a 2006 study found that music is the most common topic of conversation when young adults get to know each other, functioning as a shortcut to judge someone’s personality. Another study demonstrated that discovering a shared taste in music promotes attraction by signaling similar underlying values.
At the same time, relationship scientists have mapped out how couples match across various psychological traits. A 2023 meta-analysis showed that romantic partners tend to be similar across dozens of behavioral and physical traits. Yet sharing those traits might not actually guarantee happiness. In fact, a 2025 study covered by PsyPost found that actual similarity in personality or personal interests has surprisingly weak and inconsistent links to relationship satisfaction.
Bridging these two areas of research, Julia Vigl and Marcel Zentner of the Music, Emotion, Assessment, and Personality Lab at the University of Innsbruck designed a new project. The researchers wanted to test whether real couples actually share musical tastes to a greater degree than they share personality traits or values. They also sought to determine whether a musical match genuinely predicts how happy a couple is in their relationship.
“We know quite a lot about similarity between romantic partners in personality, values, and other personal characteristics, but much less about similarity in aesthetic preferences,” Zentner, a professor for personality psychology and psychological assessment, told PsyPost. “Music seemed particularly interesting because it is such an important part of how people express themselves and connect with others.”
“Several years ago, I conducted a side-project that suggested an association between similarity in music preferences and relationship satisfaction,” he added. “Julia and I then decided to take up this question again in a more rigorous way.”
To investigate this, the researchers conducted three separate studies involving a total of 309 couples, primarily from Germany and Austria, who independently completed several questionnaires. They rated their preferences for different musical genres and listed their specific favorite and least favorite artists. The researchers used online social tags to categorize these artists, allowing them to measure stylistic overlap even if the partners listed different bands. The participants also filled out standard assessments of their personality traits, personal values, and relationship satisfaction.
To figure out if the couples were more similar than random chance would dictate, the scientists compared the real couples to pseudo-couples. These pseudo-couples were created by randomly pairing up participants from the dataset into artificial relationships. By comparing the real partners to these shuffled pairs, the researchers could measure exactly how much of a couple’s similarity was due to their specific romantic bond rather than just broader cultural trends.
In the first study, which included 99 relatively young couples, the data showed a strong pattern. The real couples were far more alike in their music preferences than the random pairings. This musical overlap was much larger than their similarity in personality traits or personal values. Matching on personality and values had no reliable link to relationship quality, but sharing favorite artists was associated with a modest increase in relationship tenderness.
The second study included 99 couples with a wider age range and longer relationship durations. The researchers used slightly different questionnaires to measure personality and values, but the core findings remained the same. Couples consistently demonstrated higher similarity in their musical preferences than in their personalities. In this older group, the researchers again found a small positive association between sharing favorite artists and feelings of tenderness, though general relationship satisfaction did not show an overall boost.
In the third study, the researchers tested 111 couples and added measures for specific components of love, such as intimacy, passion, and commitment. They also asked the participants about their musical backgrounds, like whether they played an instrument or how much time they spent listening to music. Even when factoring in whether both partners were musicians, the couples still showed an unusually high similarity in their musical tastes. In this group, sharing least favorite artists was linked to a slight increase in feelings of love and relationship satisfaction.
To make sense of the slight variations across the three studies, the researchers pooled the data from all 309 couples into a combined analysis. This broad look confirmed that romantic partners are highly similar in their musical tastes, far exceeding their similarities in personality or values. “Romantic partners tend to have significantly more similar music preferences than would be expected by chance,” Zentner noted. “We were surprised by how consistently the effect emerged across our studies, and by the fact that similarity in music preferences was substantially greater than similarity in personality and values.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The association between shared music and relationship happiness is fairly small, meaning that having identical playlists does not guarantee a perfect romance. “The difference between couples and randomly paired individuals was fairly substantial for music preferences,” Zentner said. “The association between music similarity and relationship quality, however, was smaller, so shared musical taste is not what makes or breaks relationships but it seems to help a little.”
The couples who volunteered for the research also tended to be highly satisfied in their relationships. This is a common hurdle in psychological research, as happy couples are more likely to volunteer for relationship studies together. The findings might not fully reflect the dynamics of couples who are experiencing conflict or considering a breakup. “Our studies were correlational, so they cannot tell us whether shared musical preferences contribute to relationship quality, whether partners become more similar over time, or whether similar people are simply more likely to choose one another,” Zentner pointed out.
He also emphasized that the results shouldn’t discourage people whose partners have different favorite bands. “Nor do the findings imply that couples with different musical tastes are incompatible.”
Future studies could look at couples over longer periods of time to see how musical tastes might shift. It is still an open question whether people seek out partners with similar musical preferences from the beginning, or if their tastes slowly merge as they spend years attending concerts together. “We would like to understand how similarity in musical preferences between romantic partners emerges in the first place,” Zentner explained. “Do people generally prefer potential partners who share their music tastes, and are couples already similar at the beginning of a relationship, or do their preferences become more similar over time?”
To unravel these dynamics, the researchers are planning follow-up investigations. “Finally, we will again explore whether sharing music preferences is associated with relationship satisfaction,” Zentner said. “To address these questions, Julia is conducting an online dating experiment and launching an 18-month longitudinal study of early couples this month.”
The study, “Harmonies of Taste: Shared Music Preferences and Compatibility in Romantic Relationships,” was authored by Julia Vigl, Felix Lene Ihrig, Miriam Greif, and Marcel Zentner.

What 1,000 Women Workers Can Teach Us About Surviving Extreme Heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

On Sept. 2, 2026, the United Nations Environment Program report, Limiting Overshoot, declared that the world has fallen short of keeping global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, and that urgent action is needed to course-correct. That same week, NPR reported that extreme heat killed nearly five times as many people in the United States as official records indicated.
These findings followed two consecutively brutal summers. Death counts from heatwaves across Europe dominated news cycles this year as the continent’s aging infrastructure struggled to cool down. “Heat domes” trapped heat across the United States.
But merely counting deaths from heat risks missing its impact on human life. Each heat dome in the U.S. affected over 100 million people. Among them were construction workers, outdoor workers, delivery workers in unairconditioned cabs, farm workers, the unhoused, the poor who could not afford air conditioning, those on medications on whom the impact of heat was amplified, those with mental health disorders, and those with little or no access to healthcare.
According to the International Labor Organization, billions of workers around the world are exposed to extreme heat every year. While the vast majority of them do not die, many suffer deeply from the arduous ignominy of a life exposed to heat, day and night, year after year.
While counting deaths from heat is an imperfect science, the quantification of heat’s impact on mental health, physical well-being, wages, food security, habitat, and infrastructure is even more complex. One thousand women working in India’s informal labor economy have set out to quantify this burden—to understand what impact the heat and humidity in their lived environments at home and at work have on their health, wages, and well-being.
Partnering with our team at Harvard, the Self Employed Women’s Association in India has recruited women from trades including street vendors, waste recyclers, home-based artisans, and farmers to participate in the Community Heat Adaptation and Treatment Strategies (CommHATS) study. For 13 months, each woman is equipped with a wrist wearable, microsensors measuring heat and humidity at home and workplaces, labs measuring critical biomarkers, and surveys documenting home and work layouts, wellbeing, and wages. Considered together, this data constructs one of the world’s largest such databases of the impact of heat on human health.
Building on prior work that has shown that long exposure to heat impacts multiple organ systems, including the heart and kidneys, the CommHATS project seeks to address unanswered questions in our attempts to adapt to extreme heat: How do we know if cool roofs work? What should our metric of success be? If the temperature drops a bit, but I still cannot sleep restfully, is the intervention valid? What should the threshold for a new heat insurance product be: the temperature at the airport where the weather station is, or the temperature in my home, which is actually how hot I feel? In India, where over half of women of reproductive age are anemic, how does heat further stress their hearts?
Through community meetings and WhatsApp groups, research findings are regularly shared with all participants, who routinely ask how the data will help improve their lives. Early findings, which we will share at New York Climate Week, reveal devastating wage losses on hot days, shortened sleep spans, and high cardiac stress. This kind of relentless, unforgiving heat forces a different kind of reckoning that goes beyond OSHA regulations and market solutions.
In places like India, where around 90% of workers are informally employed, there is no employer to hold accountable. The poor have no choice but to adapt. They change working hours at the cost of childcare. They reallocate savings to protect health and wages. They buy water jugs to carry potable water, and awnings to create shade, and ice chests to cool their produce. The woefully underfunded global financial instruments for heat adaptation have no existing structural mechanism to actually reach the most vulnerable, and so those most at risk bear the price themselves.
The CommHATS project is implemented daily by grassroots workers, a testament to its ease of use. They check on the sensors and the wearables, and most importantly, the participating workers. The participants are invested in the questions, the tools, and the analysis. The tool is thus built for scale and can help communities anywhere in the world understand what their environmental exposure is at an actionable scale that is relevant to decision-making. It helps measure exposure as well as the efficacy of interventions.
In our study, we find that the cost of our collective inaction is already being borne by those whose lives are already stressed. The human spirit is resilient, and perhaps life goes on. But in this warming world, life is compromised and diminished. Millions may still live through extreme heat and not yet enter the death counts, but they cannot thrive.

====================================================================================================

Mathematicians Hate AI. They Can’t Quit It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Mathematician Tristan Buckmaster believes OpenAI used his work to rush ahead and beat him to solving a legendary math problem with a $1 million bounty.
But that’s not been enough for him to stop using the company’s models—and he’s not the only mathematician that feels that way.
“Even if you don't agree with any of this, you're kind of stuck. With AI being so useful, it's hard to completely prevent oneself from using it,” Buckmaster tells WIRED. “These companies have a monopoly, and there is not much choice,” he adds.
In the week and half since the New York University professor accused OpenAI of copying his approach, Buckmaster has been using the company’s coding agent Codex to tidy up his research papers. When he has time to do math (which he says is rare, since the fallout thrust him into the spotlight), the tool has been helping him understand the logical steps OpenAI’s agents might have taken to get from his earlier workings to the final proof.
Buckmaster had used Codex as well as Anthropic’s competing Claude to work on what’s known as the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, alongside Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. OpenAI deployed tens of thousands of agents to reach the solution, but only after it learned the equation was close to being solved, Buckmaster says.
When Buckmaster went public with his claims, it ignited a firestorm about artificial intelligence and whether it would make human mathematicians obsolete. It also led OpenAI to do an investigation and amend its announcement about solving Navier-Stokes to say it “confirmed that Buckmaster’s Codex prompts over the two months preceding this announcement and paper on September 8, 2026, could not have influenced the system in any way, including through training.” The company pointed WIRED to its announcement in an email.
Showing that AI was pushing the boundaries of mathematics was “more important than the result,” Buckmaster says. But churning out solutions to long-standing math problems without fully crediting the human work undergirding them—especially ahead of major IPOs—is irresponsible and “childish,” he says.
Other mathematicians have raised similar concerns. Only a handful of people on the planet understand the techniques in geometric group theory that German mathematician Andreas Thom has dedicated the last two decades to developing. So when OpenAI said in August that its Astra model had used them to prove a long-standing problem he had been working on, “I was amazed,” says Thom. “And of course I was wondering, how did they learn about it?”
So he says he asked OpenAI researchers Mark Sellke and Sébastien Bubeck. In an August email, he pointed out that the firm’s assertion that “no progress” had been made on the problem in the last decade overlooked a 2019 paper of his, as well as other mathematicians’ work. The company amended its press release. He and a colleague had been using ChatGPT to assist their work on the problem in the months running up to the result, but when he asked if their interactions had been fed into training data, Thom says Sellke replied: “That did not happen.”
“I set it aside,” Thom recalls. “I'm not so much interested in these political things; I want to work on mathematics.”
While Thom has seen OpenAI’s statement that Buckmaster’s prompts couldn't have influenced the system, he says he doesn’t trust this and concedes he will probably never know whether his work actually fed the result.
“AI really kills this entire idea that you could trace back who contributed what,” he says. “That is probably over.”
It’s a big change from how science is typically done, with academics subjecting their findings to peer review and building on each others’ work with credit. Beyond upending attribution, the fact that humans still don’t fully understand each step OpenAI’s agents took to arrive at the Navier-Stokes result also poses existential questions for mathematicians, who see their field slipping from their understanding.
"If I want to make a contribution to mathematics, how do I do that as just a human nowadays when these trillion-dollar companies are in on the game?" says Cornell mathematician Alex Townsend, the coauthor of a forthcoming book on the field’s evolution.
Since August, Townsend has seen many of his colleagues start to ask what they need to know about the technology and how they can set up subscriptions to access higher-powered models.
"I feel both excited and nervous simultaneously," Townsend says. "Excited because I can achieve things that I couldn't achieve without it, and nervous because I'm questioning: 'OK, what's my purpose here?'"
Thom accepts that his area of study is changing, and has continued to use ChatGPT—with updated privacy settings to stop his work being used to train the data—to speed up writing papers because it is “extremely efficient.” (OpenAI’s offerings through universities and at the enterprise level default to not training models on users’ data.)
“If a human had actively done that, then I would be very, very angry,” he says of someone using his work without attribution. But if information was pulled into the model through a back door, by an algorithm which nobody fully understands, “I could probably live with that,” he says.
Some mathematicians are less forgiving. Twenty-five Fields medalists wrote in an open letter that AI companies and mathematicians are “severely misaligned.” More than 4,000 people have signed the Leiden Declaration, which has a series of recommendations for how mathematicians, funders, and politicians can ensure that AI doesn’t swallow the field.
Buckmaster fears the possibility of using AI to “clean up some of your grammar, and suddenly your years of work [could be] gobbled up in user data and sold to another mathematician or grad student. That's what I think most of the mathematicians tend to be worrying about, and I think it's a real issue.”
With no oversight on the horizon and AI further engraining itself in the field, some mathematicians want to find a way to at least tap the brakes. That includes more than 2,000 people with ties to Caltech who called on organizers of an AI math hackathon at the school to suspend the event. The hackathon was sponsored by Anthropic and OpenAI, though the latter has since dropped out. But any attempts to slow things down may be for naught, especially in the long term.
“I don't think this is really sustainable because of the efficiency gain” that AI offers, says Thom. Any mathematicians—especially early-career researchers—risk being “isolated” if they don’t use AI to accelerate their work, he adds. He and Buckmaster both believe the community needs to start thinking about what the technology means for younger mathematicians and how to smooth the transition.
The next generation of mathematicians is already looking for guidance: Students have also been asking about what their future could look like now that AI is becoming so capable at solving math problems, Townsend says.
Buckmaster is calling for a detente in AI-driven mathematics while mathematicians and AI laboratories set some ground rules on how to release results, including getting their references right. He himself is going to clean up the papers he published prematurely last week to beat OpenAI’s announcement, one of which he described as “AI slop.”
”I have a responsibility to clean up the papers that I did post that weren't completed, and I think I have a responsibility to explain to mathematicians what we did,” he says.
He’s also open to discussing this with OpenAI. “I don't want to just engage in fights” he says. As for whether he would ever actually work on a problem with the company, “we have to be careful with that,” he says with a wry smile.

California is losing its oaks. One man is planting 10,000, including in tree-scarce Altadena
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-19
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Ten thousand times, Jim Crouch has picked up an acorn. Ten thousand times, he’s planted that acorn. And 10,000 is about the number of oak seedlings he’s entrusted to the hands of people who pledged to care for the tree that has become his mission and obsession.
It began after he retired. For years, he’d been a classroom science teacher in suburban San Diego County, and now, with that chapter behind him, the trees have become his life. He hopes to meaningfully contribute to the regrowth of burned Altadena.
California has Thousand Oaks, Sherman Oaks, Oak Park, Fair Oaks, even Oakland. That’s just in English. Consider Encino, Encinitas and Paso Robles. They paint a picture of a California covered in oaks. But many regions have lost their oak canopy. Some trees succumbed to insects after being weakened by drought. Some were cut for developments, some were cut down illegally. Some oaks have been cut after fire.
Crouch witnessed this loss. He felt it. He took to collecting acorns — the seeds of oak trees. He planted them in deep pots. For the first eight years, he was a one-man operation working out of his backyard He began handing off the seedlings to others. Then many seedlings, to many others.
He began opening small nurseries, staffed by volunteers. He named his organization Re-Oak California after a group in the Bay Area with the same name. His motivation “started with climate, but then I learned you can’t do anything better for nature than protect the best keystone species.”
Oaks support a wide range of organisms, anchoring entire ecosystems, and also serve the vital task of storing carbon on a warming planet.
In a kind of treasure hunt, Crouch gathers all the acorns on private lands. He uses a hunting app to identify who owns which patch of remote land, then mails the property owner a letter asking for permission to gather.
A growing cadre of volunteers increasingly helps with the next step, the actual harvest, scooping acorns off the ground and into bags and buckets. That’s in part because Crouch is 75, and a bicycle accident has him using a cane. “My constant companion,” he says.
Recently, one volunteer leveled up Crouch’s game by making him a mapping app that includes not only the property ownership information but also tree locations from the app iNaturalist, layered together with research from Victoria Sork, a UCLA professor and dean of life sciences, who has studied oak trees for more than 30 years. 
 Sork’s lab, along with the Nature Conservancy, is sequencing oak DNA to identify which trees are best built to survive a hotter, drier California. The goal is to put those findings to work on the ground by planting acorns from trauma-affected trees that still survive. In other words, the toughest oaks could help produce the next generation. 
 It’s a strategy Sork hopes can make California’s forests more resilient to climate change — something she’s hoping Crouch can help her with. For Crouch, it’s a partnership he’s still a little starstruck about. He compares getting a call from Sork to being asked for shooting tips from NBA star  Stephen Curry. 
 Sork sees the value in the partnership too. 
“My best role is to generate knowledge and then partner with the people who are trying to get things going,” she says. Crouch, she adds, is one of the keys to getting her research “out from the ivory tower to the practitioners.”
On a recent Tuesday, Crouch steered his 2011 Nissan Frontier from his home in Escondido up to La Cañada High School off the 210 Freeway. This is where Re-Oak is opening its first nursery in the Los Angeles area, intended to serve hard-hit Altadena. It will be the group’s sixth, on Oak Grove Drive.
“It’s a bit of a challenge because I can’t be there every day, you know?” Crouch says. But “Altadena needs more trees, [and] we’ll give them whatever they need.” The new La Cañada nursery is going up in the high school’s garden: a crescent-shaped plot between the track and field and tennis courts, carpeted with mulch and sectioned off with native plants, annuals and edibles. It was started three years ago by English teacher Daryl Bilandzija, a former student of Crouch’s who saw that handing over the plot to his old teacher would mean learning for his students. “If we could get them to put a couple of acorns in the ground wherever they go, it could start to have an effect on the local environment,” Bilandzija said. “And before you know it, you’ve re-oaked a neighborhood.”
Some Altadena trees survived the 2025 fire there, yet those that remain are more vulnerable because of the overall loss of what arborists call “friction” that helped them weather storms as a group. More trees are vital to the overall health of the remaining population in Altadena. This nursery joins several other tree efforts in the community.
Altadena Green estimates that west Altadena lost roughly 70% of its tree canopy in the Eaton fire, and the losses haven’t stopped, with developers and homeowners continuing to clear what’s left.
A mother-daughter team called the Los Angeles Humane Society had given away more than 1,000 coast live oaks in Altadena and Santa Monica by the end of last year. The Los Angeles County Fire Department Forestry Division also has been offering free oaks, in addition to other native plants, at its two nurseries in San Dimas and Malibu for years. 
In addition to the La Cañada High School nursery, Crouch is establishing a smaller one in Santa Clarita. It will be staffed by 20-year-old Anderson Khalil, who found Crouch the way most young volunteers do now: social media. 
“I just saw him on Facebook giving away free oak trees, and here we are,” Khalil said. 
He had been searching for a tangible way to help the environment and allay his anxieties about the planet’s future when he came across Crouch’s posts. 
“I can’t speak so much for the rest of my generation because I have a few close friends and they’re all pretty aware,” he explained, “but we have to care more about the environment if we want to keep living the way we are living.” 
Re-Oak California has an eighth nursery planned for Irvine, its first outpost in Orange County. 
The oaks they give away are about 6 inches tall with six leaves, plus a whole foot of roots. Oaks are considered neither fast nor slow growing. A homeowner planting one today might wait more than a decade to sit in its shade. 
But it’s a wait advocates say is well worth it, one that will prove that a community, Altadena or elsewhere, can rebuild its canopy if it’s willing to invest now.
His reliance on the cane has slowed him down, so Crouch has shifted roles, from field hand to recruiter, operating mainly as the guy behind the keyboard, lining up volunteers to plant, scout, harvest and build the next nursery. He is working, with a volunteer’s help, to formalize Re-Oak California as a nonprofit.
The costs of the pots, racks and soil are nominal individually but add up fast at the scale he now operates. For 10 years he’s covered the gap himself, supplemented by donations and buoyed by a 2025 segment on CBS 8 San Diego that brought in $12,000. Re-Oak California needs donated acorns, volunteer planters and propagators, and money — especially if Crouch is to reach his dream goal of planting 20,000 trees a year.
“I’ve never been so ambitious,” he says, “and I’ve never done a project with as much love in it and as little ego.”
He’s betting that as more people understand what’s at stake, they will keep showing up — even if they are planting trees for a future he’ll never see.

18:57:59 KST

European diplomats from 12 countries revealed that Australia withdrew from joining the UK-led decision to impose sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank late in the proceedings, according to a report from the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC).
The UK’s trade embargo was followed by a collective statement from 12 Western-aligned governments who said they would also commit to, or consider the possibility of, establishing sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
EU officials lobbied Australia as it tried to expand its coalition of countries to increase pressure on Israeli settlements that they view to be illegal under international law.
Australia was reportedly open to taking more aggressive action against settlements, but ultimately decided not to join the action late in the discussions, sources told the ABC.
In the end, Canada was the only non-European country to join the statement.
Australia has placed diplomatic pressure on Israel before
Over the last year, Australia has collaborated with other Western countries to add pressure on Israel over its war in Gaza and its settlements in the West Bank. In September, 2025, Australia recognized the State of Palestine at the United Nations General Assembly along with Canada and Portugal.
The ABC said it spoke with eight diplomatic sources familiar with the matter in Sydney, Canberra, Jerusalem, and Tel Aviv, who said the coalition of countries hoped Australia would join the decision to impose sanctions on Israeli West Bank settlements and were disappointed when it did not. The ABC’s sources wished to remain anonymous.
Australia’s Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said Australia and its partners were “working closely together towards the same objective, even if we are not all taking exactly the same measures at the same time.”
“We are concerned blanket import bans present practical challenges, including how to ensure they do not inadvertently harm Palestinian businesses, workers and livelihoods. The UK government has acknowledged these challenges as they work on their legislation over the next year,” the statement read.
“In the meantime, Australia is pursuing further targeted measures, in coordination with international partners, to deter illegal settlements and settler violence.”
EU officials 'surprised' by Australia's decision
Two EU officials who spoke with the ABC said they were “surprised” Australia did not sign the statement in the end. However, a different official involved in the negotiations said that while Australia had signaled it was open to signing on, Canberra never finalized a decision to join the coalition.
The ABC also reported that some of the diplomatic sources it spoke with attributed Australia’s decision not to join the statement to domestic politics.
Sources speculated that criticism from Australian Jewish groups following the Bondi Beach terror attacks and increased antisemitism may have played a part in Australia’s decision not to level sanctions on Israeli settlements.
Another source told the ABC that the UK’s characterization of Israel’s policy in the West Bank took officials by surprise.
British Secretary of State, Edward Miliband, told parliament that settler violence against Palestinians constituted “ethnic cleansing” and that Israel’s government was turning a “blind eye” to it.
One EU source claimed that Miliband’s language departed from the agreed-upon final joint statement.
Last week the Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Australia was “pursuing further targeted measures in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence.”
In June of this year, Australia, the UK, Canada, France and Norway all announced sanctions against Israeli firms connected to financing and “enabling” settler violence in the West Bank.
Australia said it was “ready to take more action if the Government of Israel does not take urgent steps to address the situation on the ground.”
